text: **Keros depths**: The Keros type is set by how far the cribriform plate sits below the ethmoid roof, which is the height of the lateral lamella: type 1 is 1-3 mm, type 2 is 4-7 mm, and type 3 is 8-16 mm. Type 3 has the tallest and thinnest lateral lamella and the highest risk of an iatrogenic skull-base injury and CSF leak. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 7)

**Sinus development and adult size**: The maxillary sinus forms first, in utero, and grows in two bursts (around age 3 and again from 7 to 18 years). At about 15 mL it is the largest adult sinus. The ethmoid is the most developed sinus at birth (3-4 cells, rising to 10-15 cells by age 12-15). The sphenoid reaches adult size (0.5-8 mL) by 12-18 years. The frontal sinus is last: it starts pneumatizing at 5-6 years and reaches 4-7 mL in adolescence, and is aplastic or hypoplastic in about 5-10% of people. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 4-7)

**Ethmoid lamellae and recessus terminalis**: From front to back, the ethmoid lamellae are the uncinate (1st), the bulla (2nd), the basal lamella of the middle turbinate (3rd) and the superior turbinate lamella (4th). The basal lamella runs vertically to the cribriform plate in front, obliquely to the lamina papyracea in the middle, and horizontally to the lateral wall at the back. In about 80% of people the uncinate inserts on the lamina papyracea. This forms a blind recessus terminalis, and the frontal sinus then drains medial to the uncinate. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 3-7)

**Lateral wall dehiscence rates**: The internal carotid canal is dehiscent in the lateral sphenoid wall in about 25% of patients (in 20-25% only a thin plate separates it), and the optic canal in about 5%. The posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery crosses the face of the sphenoid just below the natural ostium. This is why widening the ostium inferiorly bleeds, and why this vessel is the pedicle of the nasoseptal flap. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 7, 67)

**24-12-6 rule and external ethmoid ligation**: Through a Lynch (medial canthal) incision, the anterior ethmoid foramen lies about 24 mm behind the anterior lacrimal crest. The posterior ethmoid foramen lies about 12 mm behind that, and the optic canal about 6 mm behind the posterior foramen. Use these distances for external anterior/posterior ethmoid artery ligation in anterosuperior bleeding. Stop after the posterior ethmoid artery to protect the optic nerve. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 5-6, 33)

**Historical and salvage arterial control**: Transantral (Caldwell-Luc) ligation of the distal internal maxillary artery in the pterygopalatine fossa was the classic operation for posterior bleeding. Endoscopic SPA ligation has largely replaced it. External carotid ligation is a last resort for life-threatening bleeding: tie it above the lingual artery origin, and expect it may fail because of extensive collaterals. Ligation risks include periorbital ecchymosis, retrobulbar hematoma, optic or infraorbital nerve injury, and clip dislodgement. Ligation is preferred over embolization for postoperative hemorrhage. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 33-34)

**Woodruff plexus definition**: Pasha describes Woodruff's plexus as an arterial confluence on the posterior lateral wall, behind the inferior and middle turbinates, fed by the sphenopalatine and ascending pharyngeal arteries, and a common source of posterior bleeding. Other sources (and the site's rhinology content) describe it as a posterior venous plexus. For boards, know it as the posterior lateral-wall plexus behind the turbinates that is linked to posterior epistaxis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 28)

**Posterior packing specifics**: A posterior pack (gauze, Foley, or a double-balloon catheter) must be backed by a formal anterior pack to make a closed, tamponaded space. It stays in for about 2-4 days, and anterior packs for 2-5 days. Because of airway and hypoxia risk, posterior packing needs inpatient monitoring (ICU if bilateral). Other risks are alar pressure necrosis, eustachian tube dysfunction, sinusitis and toxic shock syndrome. For volume replacement, the book's rule of thumb is about 300 mL of crystalloid for every 100 mL of blood lost. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 31-33)

**HHT features**: HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu) is an autosomal dominant defect of the elastic and muscular layers of vessel walls. Nosebleeds usually begin at or after puberty. Telangiectasias appear on the lips, tongue, oral mucosa, fingertips and GI tract, and AVMs occur in the lung (about 40%) and brain. Because of this, a new HHT diagnosis calls for screening for pulmonary and cerebral AVMs, not just treating the nose. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 29)

**HHT treatment ladder**: Start with moisture and avoiding trauma. Then use repeated endoscopic laser or coblation/cautery ablation, with embolization as needed. For refractory bleeding, septodermoplasty (Saunders) replaces telangiectatic septal mucosa with a split-thickness skin graft, and the Young procedure closes the nasal vestibule. Systemic options include tamoxifen/estrogens, antifibrinolytics and anti-angiogenic therapy (bevacizumab). Consider rapid-sequence intubation so that mask and airway manipulation do not trigger bleeding. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 29-31, 34)

**Mucociliary system**: Ciliated pseudostratified epithelium begins at the limen nasi. It carries a two-layer blanket: a thin periciliary sol layer underneath and a viscous gel layer on top. This blanket moves at about 1 cm/min toward the natural ostia and nasopharynx. Mucus is about 95% water, 3% mucin glycoproteins and 2% salts, plus IgA, bacteriolytic lysozyme and bacteriostatic lactoferrin. Clearance is disrupted in CF, PCD and smokers. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 12)

**Saccharin clearance test**: A saccharin particle is placed on the anterior inferior turbinate, and the time until the patient tastes sweetness is recorded. A prolonged time suggests impaired mucociliary clearance, which points toward ciliary biopsy with electron microscopy, motility studies or nasal nitric oxide. Rhinomanometry gives an objective resistance value but is rarely used clinically because it is slow, costly and variable. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 16)

**Autonomic mediators and nasal cycle**: Hypothalamic sympathetic tone, relayed through the superior cervical ganglion, keeps the nasal venous sinusoids constricted. Its mediators are norepinephrine and neuropeptide Y. Parasympathetic fibers drive secretion and dilate resistance vessels through acetylcholine, VIP and PHI. The normal nasal cycle alternates sides every 2-7 hours. A symmetric congestive response lasting 15-30 minutes can follow exercise, lying down, cold air or irritants. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 11-12)

**UPSIT scoring**: The UPSIT is a 40-item scratch-and-sniff test scored 0-40. Scores above about 33-34 are normal and 6-18 indicates anosmia. A score below about 6 is worse than chance and suggests malingering, because a true anosmic should still guess about a quarter correctly. Electrophysiologic tests (odor event-related potentials, electro-olfactogram) and olfactory epithelial biopsy are research tools. Basic labs can include thyroid function, zinc, vitamin D and B12. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 26)

**Ranking of causes and Kallmann syndrome**: The most common causes of smell loss, in order, are obstructive sinonasal disease, post-URI/viral loss and head trauma. Traumatic loss is more frequent after occipital blows, which shear olfactory fibers at the cribriform plate. Kallmann syndrome is congenital anosmia (absent or hypoplastic olfactory bulbs) plus hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, from failed migration of GnRH neurons. MRI of the olfactory bulbs and an endocrine workup are indicated. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 26-27)

**Olfactory epithelium cell types**: The epithelium contains bipolar receptor neurons, sustentacular cells, microvillar cells and basal cells. Globose basal cells are the stem cells that replace receptor neurons, which turn over about every 60 days. The odorant dissolves in mucus from Bowman's glands, binds a G-protein (cAMP) coupled receptor, and the signal converges on glomeruli where mitral/tufted cells relay it. Trigeminal fibers sense irritants such as ammonia and vinegar, so 'smelling' ammonia does not prove that CN I works. About 80% of patients who complain of taste loss actually have a smell disorder. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 13, 25)

**UPMC staging**: The UPMC system stages JNA by route of extension and by residual vascularity after embolization. Stage I is the nasal cavity or medial pterygopalatine fossa. Stage II is the sinuses or lateral PPF without residual vascularity. Stage III is skull-base erosion, orbit or infratemporal fossa without residual vascularity, and stage IV is the same with residual vascularity. Stage V is intracranial extension with residual vascularity, with M/L suffixes for medial or lateral spread. Residual vascularity predicts blood loss and recurrence better than extent alone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 20)

**Nonsurgical options and their limits**: Radiation is reserved for unresectable or intracranial residual disease, or for nonsurgical candidates, because in adolescents it risks malignant transformation, growth retardation, hypopituitarism and cataracts. Chemotherapy is reserved for failure of surgery and radiation. Hormonal agents (estrogen, flutamide) can shrink the tumor and reduce vascularity but are not routine. Do not biopsy in clinic. Histology shows a vascular, fibrous stroma that is rich in mast cells. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 19-20)

**Osteoma epidemiology and Gardner syndrome**: Osteoma is the most common benign sinonasal tumor (frontal more often than ethmoid). Multiple osteomas should prompt evaluation for Gardner syndrome (familial adenomatous polyposis with osteomas and soft-tissue tumors), because the colonic polyps carry a very high risk of turning malignant, so colonoscopy/GI referral is required. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 20)

**Vascular benign lesions**: Septal hemangioma usually arises at Little's area or the inferior turbinate. Excise it with a cuff of mucoperichondrium, with embolization first if it is large. Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a friable septal polyp linked to trauma or pregnancy ('pregnancy tumor') and often regresses after delivery. Glomangiopericytoma (sinonasal hemangiopericytoma) is a pericyte-derived tumor of low malignant potential, and a better prognosis goes with an actin-positive, CD34-negative immunophenotype. Treat it by excision; about 10% recur. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 20-21)

**Schneiderian papilloma subtypes**: There are three Schneiderian papillomas. Fungiform (exophytic) is the most common. It arises on the septum, is linked to HPV 6/11, and has very low malignant potential. Inverted papilloma arises on the lateral wall and carries malignant risk. Oncocytic (cylindrical cell) papilloma also arises on the lateral wall or sinuses. Vestibular squamous papillomas (warts) are excised or laser-ablated with a cuff of normal tissue to prevent recurrence. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 18-19)

**Tornwaldt cyst**: A Tornwaldt cyst is a midline cyst on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall, derived from a notochord remnant. It is usually incidental (T1/T2 hyperintense on MRI) and is observed, or marsupialized if infected or symptomatic. Tell it apart from nasopharyngeal carcinoma (which usually starts off-midline in the fossa of Rosenmuller) and from adenoid retention cysts. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 21)

**Antrochoanal polyp and pediatric foreign body**: An antrochoanal polyp is a solitary polyp from the maxillary antrum that passes through the ostium into the choana and nasopharynx, typically in a child or young adult with unilateral obstruction. Histology lacks the eosinophilia of polyposis. Cure requires endoscopic removal of the intrasinus pedicle (antral portion), not just the nasal part. A nasal foreign body or rhinolith is the most common cause of unilateral purulent rhinorrhea in children. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 17-18)

**Site-specific malignancy and recurrence**: Malignant transformation (about 10%) arises mainly from lateral-wall lesions and is rare from the septum. Calcification may be seen on CT. Radiation is not part of treatment for benign IP. Most recurrences appear within the first 2 years, and late recurrence after that is uncommon. Polyps differ from IP by being translucent, bilateral and less vascular. IP is linked to HPV 6/11 and EBV. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 19)

**Most common cause and repair pearls**: Prior septal surgery is the most common cause (over half), especially when opposing mucoperichondrial tears line up. Biopsy the edge of a granular or abnormal perforation to look for vasculitis, sarcoid, TB, syphilis or cancer. A silastic button can be placed in the office but needs periodic replacement and can crust. If a small perforation whistles and cannot be closed, enlarging it posteriorly can stop the whistle. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 24)

**Valve contribution and causes of collapse**: The internal valve accounts for about half of total nasal airway resistance. The septum-upper lateral cartilage angle is about 10-15 degrees in White patients and is typically wider in Black, Asian and Hispanic noses. Causes of valve collapse include over-resection of the lateral crus or scroll, caudal septal deflection, aging, trauma and facial nerve paralysis (loss of the nasal dilators). Dorsal septal deviation is the most common cause of internal valve obstruction. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 22-23)

**Relative durability of techniques**: Outfracture alone is easy but gives poor long-term results. Intramural cautery or radiofrequency is office-friendly but fades, especially if rhinitis goes untreated. Submucosal resection of erectile tissue (with or without bone) that spares the medial mucosa gives the most durable benefit. Total turbinectomy is avoided because of atrophic rhinitis and empty nose syndrome. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 23-24)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **EGPA classification criteria**: Classic EGPA (Churg-Strauss) criteria require 4 of 6: asthma, peripheral eosinophilia above 10%, mono- or polyneuropathy, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, paranasal sinus abnormality, and biopsy showing extravascular eosinophils (sensitivity about 85%, specificity about 99.7%). Coronary arteritis can cause myocardial infarction, and hearing loss may occur. Treatment is corticosteroids, with cyclophosphamide for organ-threatening disease and rituximab or anti-IL-5 options. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 43-44)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Rhinoscleroma**: Rhinoscleroma is chronic granulomatous infection with Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, endemic in Eastern Europe, North Africa, South Asia and Latin America. It passes through three stages: catarrhal (purulent rhinorrhea, crusting), granulomatous (painless nodules, epistaxis, septal destruction, possible laryngeal or subglottic spread) and fibrotic (stenosis). Histology shows Mikulicz cells (foamy macrophages full of bacilli) and Russell bodies. Treatment is long-term culture-directed antibiotics (tetracycline or ciprofloxacin) plus debridement, with airway evaluation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 45-46)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Rhinosporidiosis**: Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection with Rhinosporidium seeberi, acquired from contaminated water (South Asia, Africa). It causes a friable, strawberry-like, bleeding polypoid nasal mass and can involve the conjunctiva. Histology shows large sporangia with spores and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Treatment is excision with cautery of the base, sometimes with dapsone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 46)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Other systemic nasal findings**: Sarcoidosis gives submucosal yellow nodules (cobblestoning), crusting and perforation. Langerhans cell histiocytosis can present as a nasal mass or perforation. Lupus causes septal ulceration and perforation, and polyarteritis nodosa can cause nasal mucosal lesions. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma ('lethal midline granuloma') destroys midline structures and needs deep, repeated biopsies. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 21-22)

**NARES specifics**: NARES presents with perennial allergic-type symptoms (paroxysmal sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, itch) but negative skin and serum testing. A nasal smear shows eosinophilia (about 10-20%). It can be a forerunner of AERD and nasal polyposis. It responds best to intranasal corticosteroids. By contrast, a nasal smear with more than about 25% eosinophils in an atopic patient supports allergic rhinitis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 38, 46-47)

**Rhinitis of pregnancy**: Rhinitis of pregnancy is the most common hormonal rhinitis. Congestion without sneezing typically starts near the end of the first trimester and resolves after delivery. It may relate to estrogen-driven cholinergic effects and mucosal hyaluronic acid. Manage it with saline, avoidance, and an intranasal steroid if needed (budesonide has the most reassuring pregnancy data). Avoid decongestants. Other hormonal causes are oral contraceptives, hypothyroidism and puberty. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 47)

**Vidian neurectomy and posterior nasal nerve ablation**: The vidian nerve forms from the greater superficial petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic) in the pterygoid canal at the floor of the sphenoid. It runs to the pterygopalatine ganglion. Endoscopic division (reached through the sphenopalatine foramen, following the canal posterolaterally) reduces rhinorrhea but causes dry eye (shown on Schirmer testing), nasal and palatal dryness, and cheek or dental numbness. Posterior nasal nerve cryoablation in the posterior middle meatus is a less invasive option, with headache, dry eye, epistaxis and synechiae as possible side effects. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 43, 49)

**Weaning rhinitis medicamentosa**: Topical decongestants should be limited to 3-5 days. To wean, stop the decongestant and start saline and an intranasal steroid. A short oral steroid burst works well for severe rebound. Long-term overuse can cause persistent mucosal change. Defer turbinate surgery until the patient is fully weaned. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 41, 48)

**Primary atrophic rhinitis (ozena)**: Atrophic rhinitis can be primary or secondary. The primary (idiopathic) form, ozena, is seen mainly in endemic regions and is linked to Klebsiella ozaenae, nutritional deficiency (vitamins A and D, iron) and endocrine factors. It causes glandular and nerve degeneration, squamous metaplasia, foul crusting and a wide nasal cavity. The secondary form follows over-resection, radiation or trauma. Treatment includes irrigation, crust removal, vitamin and iron replacement, antibiotics for infection, and, when refractory, nostril closure (Young procedure) or lateral-wall augmentation. Decongestants are avoided. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 47-48)

**Classic exam stigmata**: Look for allergic shiners (infraorbital venous darkening), Dennie-Morgan lines (lower-lid creases), a transverse nasal crease from the 'allergic salute', and pale or bluish boggy turbinates that shrink with decongestant. Other signs are cobblestoned posterior pharyngeal lymphoid tissue, open-mouth 'adenoid facies' and middle ear effusion. About one-third of patients with allergic rhinitis have asthma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 36-38)

**Pharmacotherapy by symptom target**: Intranasal steroids are the single best maintenance therapy. They act on both early and late phases but need regular use and more than a week for full effect. Second-generation antihistamines (loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine) are less sedating than first-generation agents, which cause sedation, anticholinergic dryness and urinary retention. Ipratropium targets rhinorrhea only. Montelukast blocks the late phase and helps when asthma coexists. Cromolyn works only as prophylaxis before a known exposure. Topical decongestants should be used no more than 3-5 days. Oral pseudoephedrine avoids rebound but raises blood pressure and causes insomnia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 40-41)

**Steroid potency equivalents**: Equivalent doses are prednisone 5 mg = methylprednisolone 4 mg = hydrocortisone 20 mg = cortisone 25 mg = dexamethasone 0.75 mg. Side effects of systemic steroids include hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypokalemia, gastric irritation, psychosis or insomnia, posterior subcapsular cataract and avascular necrosis of the femoral head. This is why routine depot or repeated oral bursts are avoided in rhinitis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 42)

**Avoidance specifics**: The dust-mite allergen is in mite feces. Control measures are encasing the mattress and pillows, hard floors, washing, and acaricides such as benzyl benzoate. A HEPA filter removes 99.97% of particles of 0.3 micrometers. For pollen, keep windows closed, use air conditioning, and shower after outdoor exposure. For mold, cut indoor humidity and remove damp sources. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 37, 40)

**Skin endpoint titration (SET) scheme**: Make serial 5-fold dilutions (1 mL of the stronger solution plus 4 mL of diluent). Pasha starts from a 1:100 w/v extract, so #1 = 1:500, #2 = 1:2,500, #3 = 1:12,500, #4 = 1:62,500, #5 = 1:312,500 and #6 = 1:1,562,500. The AAOA convention instead starts from a 1:20 concentrate, so its #1 = 1:100; check which numbering a question uses. Each intradermal bleb starts at about 4 mm and grows to about 5 mm when negative. A wheal of 7 mm or more (at least 2 mm larger than the previous negative) is positive. The endpoint is the first positive dilution that is followed by a confirming wheal at least 2 mm larger at the next stronger dilution (for example 5-5-7-9). The endpoint dilution is a safe starting dose for immunotherapy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 38-39)

**Test preparation and in vitro role**: Hold antihistamines about 48-72 hours before skin testing. Beta-blockers are a relative contraindication because they blunt rescue epinephrine. In vitro specific IgE (RAST/ELISA/ImmunoCAP) is indicated for dermatographism or eczema, high anaphylaxis risk, uncooperative young children, unstoppable medications, or equivocal skin results. A negative skin test alone is NOT an indication. In vitro tests are highly specific and carry no anaphylaxis risk, but they are less sensitive, slower and more costly. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 38-39)

**Duration and contraindications**: Benefit is usually seen by about 1 year, and therapy is typically continued for 3-5 years (Pasha recommends 5 years) for lasting tolerance. Contraindications include uncontrolled asthma, significant cardiovascular disease, beta-blocker use (it increases reaction severity and blunts epinephrine), severe immunodeficiency or autoimmune disease, and nonadherence. Do not start therapy during pregnancy; current practice allows a stable maintenance dose to continue, whereas Pasha lists pregnancy as a contraindication. SCIT suits multiple allergens and requires a monitored setting. SLIT suits a single allergen, is given at home, and has mainly local side effects. Local nasal immunotherapy is a rarely used pollen option. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 42-43)

**Bent and Kuhn criteria**: There are five major criteria: nasal polyposis, type I hypersensitivity to fungi (skin test or specific IgE), characteristic CT (heterogeneous, serpiginous hyperattenuation), eosinophilic mucin, and noninvasive fungal elements on staining. Minor criteria are bone erosion, unilateral predominance, Charcot-Leyden crystals, peripheral eosinophilia and a positive fungal culture. The usual organisms are dematiaceous molds (Bipolaris, Curvularia, Alternaria), then Aspergillus. Postoperative antifungals are not indicated. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 55)

**Histology and treatment**: Mucorales show broad, ribbon-like, nonseptate hyphae branching at about 90 degrees. Aspergillus shows narrow septate hyphae with acute (about 45 degree) branching. Endoscopy looks for pale, insensate or black mucosa, and frozen-section biopsy of the middle turbinate or septum confirms the diagnosis quickly. Treatment is urgent debridement to bleeding tissue plus IV antifungals: amphotericin B for Mucorales, voriconazole for Aspergillus. Also correct the underlying problem (DKA, neutropenia). Mortality is about 50% once the CNS or cavernous sinus is involved. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 55-56)

**Chronic invasive and granulomatous forms**: Chronic invasive fungal sinusitis is rare and occurs in immunocompetent or mildly impaired hosts. It invades slowly over months and can present as CRS with orbital apex syndrome, blindness or cerebritis. The chronic granulomatous subtype (Aspergillus flavus, classically from Sudan and South Asia) forms noncaseating granulomas. Treatment is debridement plus long-term voriconazole or amphotericin, and the prognosis is far better than for the acute form. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 56)

**Retention cyst versus mucocele**: A mucous retention cyst is a submucosal collection from a blocked seromucinous gland. It is a dome-shaped lesion, usually on the maxillary floor, found incidentally on about 10% of CTs, with no expansion or bone remodeling. It is observed unless it obstructs. A mucocele fills and expands the whole sinus with bone thinning. Mucoceles are most common in the frontoethmoid, then maxillary, then sphenoid sinus, and can be primary or secondary to surgery, trauma or tumor. Odontogenic radicular or follicular cysts are in the differential. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 57)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **PCD specifics and surgery**: Missing outer dynein arms are the most common ultrastructural defect. Kartagener's triad (sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus) occurs in about half of patients. Male infertility from sperm dysmotility and chronic otitis are common. Because the cilia do not clear mucus toward the natural ostium, a standard middle-meatal antrostomy may fail. A gravity-dependent drainage operation (inferior antrostomy or endoscopic medial maxillectomy) can be considered for refractory disease, along with aggressive irrigation, and ear tubes for OME. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 57-58)

**Compartment-specific features**: Meningitis is the most common intracranial complication overall. It comes mostly from ethmoid and sphenoid disease, pneumococcus is the usual organism, and seizures and SNHL can follow. Epidural, subdural and brain abscesses come mainly from frontal sinusitis. On imaging, an epidural abscess is biconvex and can cross the midline, while subdural empyema is crescentic, stops at the falx, and has more neurologic deficits. Brain abscess moves through stages of cerebritis/encephalitis, a quiet latent phase, expansion with raised ICP, and rupture. Lumbar puncture is done only after imaging excludes mass effect. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 59-60)

**Cavernous sinus thrombosis details**: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually caused by S. aureus. It presents with spiking 'picket-fence' fevers, bilateral chemosis and proptosis, palsies of CN III, IV and VI, V1-V2 sensory change and papilledema. Treat with high-dose IV antibiotics that cross the blood-brain barrier (for example vancomycin plus cefepime plus metronidazole), drain the sinus source once the patient is stable, and consider anticoagulation (controversial). Superior orbital fissure syndrome (CN III, IV, VI and V1) becomes orbital apex syndrome when CN II is also involved. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 59, 61)

**Diagnostic criteria and outcome tool**: Adult CRS requires at least 2 of 4 cardinal symptoms (nasal obstruction, mucopurulent drainage, facial pain or pressure, reduced smell) for 12 weeks or more, plus objective inflammation on endoscopy or CT. ABRS is 4 weeks or less. The SNOT-22 is the standard validated patient-reported measure of CRS symptom burden and is used to track response to medical therapy, surgery or biologics. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 51, 54)

**Bitter taste receptors and other cofactors**: The T2R38 bitter taste receptor on sinonasal cilia detects bacterial quorum-sensing molecules and triggers nitric oxide-mediated clearance. Patients with nonfunctional variants ('nontasters') more often have refractory CRS that needs surgery. Biofilms and osteitis mark recalcitrant disease rather than being primary causes. Staphylococcal enterotoxins act as superantigens in CRSwNP. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 50-51)

**Anti-inflammatory antibiotics**: Long-term low-dose macrolides are an option for CRSsNP, especially the non-type-2 or low-IgE phenotype, because of their anti-inflammatory effect. A short course of doxycycline can shrink polyps in CRSwNP. Pasha also lists 3-6 week broad-spectrum courses. Current guidance limits antibiotics to documented bacterial exacerbations or specific phenotypes rather than routine prolonged courses. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 54)

**Open frontal procedures**: An osteoplastic flap (bicoronal, brow or midforehead approach, with the template from navigation or a Caldwell view) gives the best exposure of the whole frontal sinus. Obliteration requires removing all mucosa, burring the bony walls and plugging the recess with fat. Late mucocele (often years later), contour deformity and chronic pain are the risks. Trephination through the medial brow helps with lateral disease or acute complicated frontal sinusitis. The Lynch fronto-ethmoidectomy is quick but often fails from recess stenosis. Riedel (removal of the anterior wall and floor) is disfiguring. Killian keeps a supraorbital bar. Endoscopic frontal surgery is contraindicated in an aplastic frontal sinus. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 63-64)

**Retrobulbar hematoma timing and adjuncts**: Irreversible vision loss can occur within about 60-90 minutes. If it occurs intraoperatively, stop the case, control bleeding, avoid tight packing and examine the eye. Perform immediate lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis, and get an ophthalmology consult. Adjuncts are mannitol (1-2 g/kg) and high-dose steroids; medial (Lynch) or endoscopic orbital decompression are alternatives. Orbital fat floats in irrigation, which helps identify a lamina breach. Orbital emphysema after nose-blowing is managed by observation and no nose-blowing. Diplopia most often comes from medial rectus or superior oblique injury. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 65-66)

**Complication rank and carotid injury**: Synechiae between the middle turbinate and lateral wall are the most common complication of ESS. Prevent them with mucosal preservation, medialization and debridement. Internal carotid injury in the sphenoid is immediately life-threatening. Pack firmly, compress the carotid in the neck, call for neurointerventional angiography (and possible stenting or sacrifice) and neurosurgery, and maintain blood pressure. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 66-67)

**Humoral defects by subtype**: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency. It is often silent but associated with atopy, autoimmunity, IgG subclass deficiency, and anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products. IgG2 deficiency is the most common subclass deficiency in children (poor polysaccharide responses to encapsulated organisms). IgG3 deficiency is the most common in adults (viral, M. catarrhalis, S. pyogenes). Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinemia (BTK defect, absent B cells) presents after about 6 months, once maternal IgG wanes. CVID presents in early adulthood and carries autoimmune and lymphoma risk. Treatment is IVIG plus infection control. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 70-72)

**Rhinosinusitis in HIV**: Up to about 75% of untreated HIV patients develop rhinosinusitis. With a CD4 count above 200, organisms and management resemble those of immunocompetent hosts. Below 200, expect Pseudomonas, CMV, mycobacteria, fungi (including Mucor) and Pneumocystis. Have a low threshold for culture-directed therapy, early CT/endoscopy, biopsy (Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma) and early surgery. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 56)

**HIV/AIDS head and neck map**: AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells/microliter, a CD4 percentage below 14%, or an AIDS-defining illness. Head and neck clues include benign lymphoepithelial cysts of the parotid (bilateral cystic parotid enlargement), persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia, necrotizing gingivitis, Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and SNHL or facial palsy from opportunistic infection. Screening is by immunoassay with confirmatory testing. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 73-74)

**Cartilage histology**: thyroid, cricoid, and most of the arytenoid are hyaline cartilage (they can ossify with age), whereas the epiglottis, corniculates, and cuneiforms are elastic/fibroelastic. Because fibroelastic cartilage has a tightly adherent perichondrium, the epiglottis is rarely the site of chondritis, and a calcified triticeous cartilage in the thyrohyoid ligament can be mistaken for a foreign body on a radiograph. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 76)

**Myoelastic-aerodynamic theory**: adducted, tensed folds are blown apart once subglottic pressure exceeds their resistance; tissue elasticity plus the Bernoulli negative pressure through the narrowed glottis pull them back together. Opening and closing both proceed inferior to superior (vertical phase difference, not seen well on stroboscopy), while the mucosal wave travels medial to lateral across the superior surface. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 79)

**Objective voice-lab norms**: mean speaking fundamental frequency is about 128 Hz in men and about 256 Hz in women; normal jitter about 0.4%, shimmer about 0.5 dB, harmonic-to-noise ratio about 11 dB; mean transglottal airflow about 100 mL/s, glottal resistance 30-50 cm H2O/L/s, and subglottic pressure 6-8 cm H2O. Perceptual scales: GRBAS rates Grade, Roughness, Breathiness, Asthenia, Strain each 0-3; CAPE-V uses visual analog scales and adds pitch and loudness. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 80, 83)

**AAO-HNS Hoarseness CPG (2018)**: do not give antireflux medication for hoarseness without reflux signs/symptoms (option if chronic laryngitis signs), do not routinely give oral steroids before the larynx is visualized, strongly avoid routine antibiotics, examine the larynx before prescribing voice therapy, and scope when hoarseness lasts >4 weeks or sooner with red flags (tobacco/alcohol, neck mass, hemoptysis, dysphagia, otalgia, airway compromise, neurologic signs, recent intubation or neck surgery). Botulinum toxin is recommended for spasmodic dysphonia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 81, 83-84)

**Drug-induced dysphonia**: anticoagulants, thrombolytics, and PDE-5 inhibitors predispose to vocal fold hematoma; bisphosphonates cause chemical laryngitis; inhaled steroids cause mucosal irritation and candidiasis; ACE inhibitors cause cough; androgens/danazol virilize the voice; antipsychotics can cause laryngeal dystonia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 80-81)

**Granulomatous and chronic infectious laryngitis**: TB laryngitis is usually secondary to pulmonary TB and favors the posterior larynx (interarytenoid), producing ulcerated granulation that mimics carcinoma; syphilis causes painless edema (secondary) or destructive gummas (tertiary); scleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) and blastomycosis both produce pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia that can be misread as SCC; leprosy causes supraglottic ulceration (treated with dapsone). Biopsy with cultures/special stains is the key step. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 91-93)

**Fungal laryngitis spectrum**: Candida (white friable plaques, inhaled steroids, immunosuppression, radiation, antibiotics), Aspergillus (allergic to invasive), blastomycosis (red ulcers/miliary nodules on the folds), histoplasmosis (anterior larynx/epiglottic ulcers), and coccidioidomycosis (nodular mass). All may mimic malignancy, so biopsy before assuming cancer; treat with systemic antifungals and secure the airway if needed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 93)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Laryngeal chondritis/perichondritis**: caused by infection, trauma, tracheotomy, radiation (chondronecrosis), malignancy, or relapsing polychondritis (larynx involved in about half). The thyroid cartilage is most often affected; the epiglottis is spared because its fibroelastic cartilage has adherent perichondrium. Presents insidiously with pain, odynophagia, tenderness, and dyspnea; complications are subperichondrial abscess and stenosis; treat with airway control, aggressive antibiotics, drainage, and debridement of necrotic cartilage. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 93)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Laryngeal site signatures of systemic disease**: sarcoidosis favors the supraglottis (pale, turban-like epiglottis); GPA favors the subglottis (biphasic stridor); amyloidosis presents as a smooth submucosal (often subglottic/ventricular) mass treated by endoscopic debulking when symptomatic; rheumatoid arthritis affects the cricoarytenoid joint (pain, hoarseness, fixation that mimics paralysis). (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 94-95)

**Risk factors beyond smoking**: LPR, voice abuse, chronic throat clearing/cough, and hypothyroidism (screen TSH in a deep-voiced patient). Reinke edema itself is not considered premalignant; treat smoking, reflux, and thyroid disease first, reserving microflap evacuation of the gelatinous superficial lamina propria for persistent symptoms. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 96)

**Saccular cyst vs laryngocele**: a laryngocele is air-filled and communicates with the laryngeal lumen (laryngopyocele if infected); a saccular cyst is a mucus-filled dilation of the saccule that does NOT communicate with the lumen. Other mimics: ductal (mucus retention) cysts of the supraglottis and ventricular prolapse (ventricle mucosa herniating between true and false folds). External laryngoceles are more common than purely internal ones in Pasha. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 96-97)

**Acquired subglottic cysts**: retention cysts from mucous gland obstruction after even short intubation; present as post-extubation stridor with smooth lateral subglottic cysts and are treated by endoscopic marsupialization/excision (laser or cold). They require less trauma than granuloma formation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 97)

**Sulcus classification**: type I is a physiologic groove into the superficial lamina propria; type II (sulcus vergeture) has loss of SLP with mucosa adherent to the vocal ligament; type III (sulcus vocalis) extends into the ligament or deeper. Voice is often worse than the exam suggests; stroboscopy shows reduced mucosal wave, and microlaryngoscopy with palpation may be needed for diagnosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 100)

**Material durations (Pasha)**: Gelfoam about 4-6 weeks (overinject ~30%); carboxymethylcellulose carrier gel about 1-2 months; hyaluronic acid about 6-8 months; micronized AlloDerm about 6 months; collagen 4-9 months; calcium hydroxylapatite 12-18 months; autologous fat is long-lasting but resorbs up to about half by 6 months (overinject ~40%). Teflon is obsolete because of granuloma, migration, and stiffening. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 103-104)

**Isshiki framework types**: type I medializes (implant through a thyroid cartilage window, done awake, reversible, preserves mucosal wave); type II lateralizes via midline cartilage split (titanium bridge for adductor SD); type III shortens/relaxes the folds to lower pitch; type IV (cricothyroid approximation) lengthens/tenses to raise pitch (gender-affirming). Mnemonic: 3 is lower than 4. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 104)

**Airway target**: tracheotomy is the gold-standard stabilizer; before decannulation, a lateralizing procedure should create at least about 4 mm of posterior glottic airway. Options include laser posterior cordotomy, partial/total arytenoidectomy, arytenoidopexy/suture lateralization, and reinnervation of the PCA with a neuromuscular pedicle. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 105)

**Prevention**: consider tracheotomy when intubation is expected to exceed roughly 10-14 days to limit posterior glottic injury; established stenosis is treated with the same lateralizing options as bilateral paralysis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 105-106)

**Workup specifics**: image the entire vagal/RLN course from skull base to the aortopulmonary window/arch; consider labs (Lyme, treponemal, thyroid, glucose, heavy metals) when no cause is evident. Idiopathic paralysis may recover for up to about 12 months. Cuff pressure in the proximal subglottis can cause RLN neurapraxia after intubation. Congenital lesions affect the right side more (shorter nerve), and Wallenberg (PICA) infarcts produce central vagal palsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 102-103)

**Elicitation phrases**: adductor SD worsens on voiced, vowel-initial phrases (count 80-90, 'We eat eggs every day'); abductor SD worsens on voiceless consonant-vowel transitions (count 60-70, 'The puppy bit the tape'). Symptoms typically worsen with stress and improve with alcohol; whispering, singing, and laughing are often spared. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 106)

**Compensatory swallow maneuvers**: supraglottic swallow (hold breath, swallow, cough) and super-supraglottic (with effort) close the airway before the swallow; Mendelsohn maneuver holds laryngeal elevation to prolong UES opening; Masako (tongue held between teeth) strengthens posterior pharyngeal wall contraction; effortful swallow increases tongue-base pressure. Chin tuck protects the airway; turn the head toward the weak side and tilt toward the strong side. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 113)

**Adjunct tests**: esophagram (structure/motility) and water-soluble contrast first when perforation is suspected; esophageal manometry is the gold standard for motility disorders; blue-dye testing in tracheotomized patients detects aspiration of dyed feeds on suctioning; scintigraphy can quantify aspiration; EAT-10 is a validated symptom scale. FEESST adds air-pulse testing of the laryngeal adductor reflex. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 110-112)

**Escalation ladder for intractable aspiration**: cuffed tracheotomy (aids toilet but does not stop microaspiration and impairs laryngeal elevation), endolaryngeal stent (short-term), glottic closure or epiglottopexy (epiglottopexy permits voicing and is potentially reversible), subperichondrial cricoidectomy (irreversible, aphonic), laryngotracheal separation or Lindeman diversion to the esophagus (potentially reversible), and narrow-field laryngectomy (spares hyoid and straps; definitive). (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 113-114)

**Routine trach care rules**: keep cuff pressure under capillary perfusion pressure (<25 cm H2O) to avoid stenosis, tracheomalacia, and tracheoinnominate erosion; keep the cuff up at least 1 day postop; never cap or place a one-way speaking valve (e.g., Passy-Muir) on an inflated cuff. Before decannulation, the original indication must be resolved and the patient should tolerate capping (Pasha: 24 hours on 3-4 consecutive days), with endoscopic airway check as needed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 88-89)

**Percutaneous dilational tracheotomy selection**: suited to intubated ICU patients with palpable landmarks and neck extension; avoid with emergent/difficult airway, nonpalpable cricoid, obesity, children, cervical spine limitation, neck mass or recent neck surgery, infection, uncorrectable coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, or high airway pressures (>20 cm H2O). Also watch for post-obstructive (negative-pressure) pulmonary edema after relieving chronic obstruction, treated with positive pressure. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 88-90)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Localizing obstruction by sound**: stertor = nasopharynx/oropharynx ('hot potato' voice oropharynx); inspiratory stridor = supraglottis; inspiratory or biphasic = glottis; biphasic with barky cough = subglottis; expiratory stridor/wheeze = intrathoracic trachea/bronchi. Heliox (80/20 or 70/30) lowers gas density to improve laminar flow past a stable obstruction as a temporizer; a non-rebreather gives FiO2 about 0.6-0.8, nasal cannula 0.24-0.44. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 84-85)

**Pharyngoesophageal weak points**: Killian triangle/dehiscence (posterior, between oblique inferior constrictor and cricopharyngeus) gives Zenker, which bulges to the left in about 80-90%; Killian-Jamieson space (lateral, below the cricopharyngeus, near the RLN entry) gives lateral diverticula; Laimer-Haeckermann space lies between cricopharyngeus and the circular esophageal fibers. Zenker is a false pulsion diverticulum. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 120)

**Achalasia**: loss of Auerbach plexus neurons yields aperistalsis and a nonrelaxing hypertensive LES; esophagram shows a dilated esophagus with bird's-beak taper and air-fluid level. Endoscopy excludes pseudoachalasia from cardia cancer. Treatment: pneumatic dilation (perforation about 1-5%), Heller myotomy with fundoplication, or Botox; calcium channel blockers/nitrates are weak options. It raises esophageal SCC risk; Chagas disease (T. cruzi) produces an identical picture. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 118, 124)

**Muscle-type localization of systemic disease**: scleroderma affects the smooth-muscle lower two-thirds and produces a weak/incompetent LES with aperistalsis and severe reflux (contrast achalasia's tight LES; CREST variant). Polymyositis/dermatomyositis affects striated muscle, so the pharynx and upper third fail (nasal regurgitation, aspiration); dermatomyositis carries higher malignancy risk. Presbyesophagus is reduced peristalsis and LES tone in the elderly. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 119, 124)

**Spastic and vascular dysphagia**: diffuse esophageal spasm shows simultaneous normal-amplitude contractions (corkscrew esophagram) versus high-amplitude peristalsis in nutcracker esophagus; treat with nitrates/CCBs. Dysphagia lusoria is compression by an aberrant right subclavian artery from the descending aorta (retroesophageal), associated with a right nonrecurrent laryngeal nerve, often presenting in middle age; CT angiography confirms. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 122-123)

**Webs and rings**: webs are thin, eccentric mucosa-submucosa membranes, usually proximal; rings are circumferential, include muscularis, and are usually distal (Schatzki ring at the squamocolumnar junction). Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome = postcricoid web + iron-deficiency anemia + glossitis/cheilitis, mostly in middle-aged women, with increased hypopharyngeal/upper esophageal SCC risk; iron and dilation treat it. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 123-124)

**Diverticulum taxonomy**: true diverticula contain all wall layers, false only mucosa/submucosa; pulsion results from high intraluminal pressure, traction from adjacent inflamed nodes. Zenker = false pulsion (hypopharynx); midesophageal = true traction (often from mediastinal granulomatous nodes, usually asymptomatic); epiphrenic = false pulsion above a distal obstruction or motility disorder, so the underlying cause must also be treated. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 119-120)

**Esophagitis types**: reflux (distal erosions), candidal (white plaques, immunosuppression/antibiotics), HSV/CMV (ulcers; biopsy and culture), pill esophagitis (doxycycline/tetracycline, potassium chloride, NSAIDs/aspirin, quinidine, clindamycin; prevent with water and upright posture), bullous dermatoses, and radiation esophagitis with strictures 6-18 months after treatment. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 121)

**Esophageal neoplasms**: leiomyoma is the most common benign tumor (intramural, distal two-thirds); polyps are the most common intraluminal lesion (cervical). Adenocarcinoma is now most common, distal, linked to Barrett/GERD/obesity; SCC is usually mid-esophageal, linked to tobacco/alcohol, prior head and neck cancer, Plummer-Vinson, caustic injury, achalasia, and tylosis. The absence of serosa allows early transmural spread; 5-year survival is poor (<15%). (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 124-125)

**Mallory-Weiss vs Boerhaave**: Mallory-Weiss is a partial mucosal tear from retching (upper GI bleed, usually self-limited); Boerhaave is a full-thickness spontaneous rupture, typically distal posterior-left, with chest pain, dyspnea, and shock. Tachycardia is often the first sign; Hamman sign is a mediastinal crunch from pneumomediastinum. Instrumentation remains the most common cause of perforation; start with water-soluble contrast. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 121-122)

**Validated LPR scores**: Reflux Symptom Index has 9 items scored 0-5 (total 0-45), abnormal >13; Reflux Finding Score has 8 laryngoscopic items (subglottic edema/pseudosulcus, ventricular obliteration, erythema, fold edema, diffuse edema, posterior commissure hypertrophy, granuloma, thick mucus) scored 0-26, abnormal >7. Dual-probe pH testing places probes 5 cm above the LES and just above the UES; DeMeester score >14.7 is abnormal; impedance detects nonacid and gaseous reflux. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 91-92, 117)

**Sandifer syndrome**: episodic torticollis or arching neck posturing in infants and children with reflux, a protective posture that can be mistaken for a neurologic or musculoskeletal problem. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 116)

**Medication pearls**: PPIs taken 30-60 minutes before meals (twice daily if needed); H2 blockers for uncomplicated GERD; prokinetics (metoclopramide raises LES pressure but risks tardive dyskinesia; erythromycin is a motilin agonist); sucralfate coats ulcerated mucosa; liquid antacids after meals for mild disease. Agents that lower LES tone include nitrates, calcium channel blockers, beta-agonists, alcohol, nicotine, chocolate, fat, and mint. Fundoplication success is best predicted by prior response to acid suppression. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 115, 117-118)

**Scintigraphy agents**: Tc-99m pertechnetate is trapped but not organified (cheap, single visit, image at ~30 min); I-123 is trapped and organified, imaged at 4 and 24 hours, low radiation, best diagnostic sensitivity; I-131 carries a high radiation dose and is used for whole-body metastatic surveys and ablation/therapy. Cold nodules carry roughly 5-20% malignancy risk in older series versus about 4% for hot nodules. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 132-133)

**Bethesda versions**: Pasha's table (2017-era Bethesda) lists malignancy risks I 1-4%, II 0-3%, III 5-15%, IV 15-30%, V 60-75%, VI 97-99%; the site uses the current 2023 (3rd edition) figures (I 13%, II 4%, III 22%, IV 30%, V 74%, VI 97%). Older question banks may use 2017 numbers; management categories are unchanged. Cytologic clues: amyloid stroma (Congo red) suggests medullary carcinoma; Hurthle cells also appear in Hashimoto thyroiditis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 131-132)

**Thyroid cysts**: usually degenerated benign nodules but can represent cystic papillary carcinoma; aspiration relieves symptoms and provides cytology. Consider lobectomy for cysts that recur after drainage or yield bloody aspirates, and sample any solid component. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 133)

**Named prognostic systems**: MACIS (Metastasis, Age, Completeness of resection, Invasion, Size) and AMES (Age - men >40/women >50, Metastasis, Extent, Size >=5 cm) stratify survival risk; the ATA system stratifies recurrence risk. Papillary carcinoma has about 95% 5-year survival; follicular 70-85%; Hurthle cell worse (about 50% in Pasha). (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 133-137)

**Remote-access thyroidectomy**: transoral endoscopic (vestibular), transaxillary, and other endoscopic/robotic approaches avoid a neck scar but require special training, lengthen operative time, add access-site morbidity, and gas insufflation can cause subcutaneous or mediastinal emphysema. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 139)

**Extent of neck surgery**: without clinical nodal disease, total thyroidectomy plus prophylactic central neck dissection; with neck disease, add therapeutic ipsilateral lateral dissection, and consider contralateral lateral dissection when preoperative calcitonin exceeds about 200 pg/mL. Check calcitonin and CEA 2-3 months postop, then every 6-12 months. Pentagastrin/calcium stimulation increases calcitonin specificity. Nodal involvement is present in about 50-60%. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 137-138)

**MEN eponyms and components**: MEN1 (Wermer) = parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic islet tumors, pituitary adenoma; MEN2A (Sipple) = MTC, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia; MEN2B = MTC, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus (no hyperparathyroidism). RET is on chromosome 10. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 137)

**Staging and imaging clues**: all anaplastic carcinomas are stage IV (IVA intrathyroidal, IVB gross extrathyroidal extension or nodal disease, IVC distant metastasis); median survival is about 5 months. Anaplastic masses are heterogeneous with calcification and necrosis, whereas thyroid lymphoma is typically homogeneous - core or open biopsy separates them when FNA is nondiagnostic. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 138-139)

**Thionamide toxicity**: methimazole and PTU can cause agranulocytosis (stop drug and check CBC for fever or sore throat), hepatotoxicity (worst with PTU), and rash; methimazole is avoided in the first trimester (PTU for pregnancy), then switched. Lithium also lowers hormone release. Radioiodine is the most common definitive therapy but is contraindicated in pregnancy and causes hypothyroidism. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 129-130, 143)

**Other thyroiditides to differentiate**: painless (silent/postpartum) thyroiditis mimics subacute thyroiditis without pain; acute suppurative thyroiditis is rare, painful, and febrile (look for a piriform sinus fistula, usually left, in children) and needs IV antibiotics/drainage; Riedel thyroiditis is a rock-hard fibrotic gland (now linked to IgG4-related disease) causing compression and hypothyroidism, treated with hormone replacement and isthmus division for airway compromise. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 145)

**Asymptomatic surgical criteria - versions**: Pasha cites the 4th International Workshop (2014): age <50, calcium >1 mg/dL above normal, 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg/day, CrCl <60 mL/min, stones/nephrocalcinosis, T-score <=-2.5 or vertebral fracture. The site uses the 5th Workshop (2022), which lowered hypercalciuria to >250 mg/day (women) or >300 mg/day (men); 5th is current. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 149)

**Acute hypercalcemia management**: volume repletion with saline first, then loop diuretic once euvolemic (avoid thiazides, which retain calcium); calcitonin acts within hours but tachyphylaxis develops; bisphosphonates work over days; glucocorticoids help granulomatous disease, vitamin D excess, or lymphoma; dialysis for life-threatening cases. Signs: stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones, short QT. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 146-147)

**Hypercalcemia differential**: beyond PTH-driven disease, consider malignancy (osteolytic metastases, PTHrP), granulomatous disease (sarcoid, TB, berylliosis), vitamin A/D excess, thiazides, lithium, milk-alkali syndrome, immobilization, Paget disease, hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and FHH. Intact PTH distinguishes PHPT (high/inappropriate) from malignancy (suppressed). PHPT often shows low phosphate and a mild hyperchloremic acidosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 146-148)

**Autotransplantation technique**: when a gland is devascularized or after total parathyroidectomy, mince about 20 mg of tissue and place it into pockets of sternocleidomastoid or the forearm brachioradialis (forearm allows later removal under local if hyperfunctioning). For persistent disease, a missed adenoma most often lies in an ectopic posterior/superior mediastinal (tracheoesophageal groove) position. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 149-150)

**Hypocalcemia signs and nonsurgical causes**: Chvostek (facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau (carpal spasm after 3 minutes of cuff inflation 20 mm Hg above systolic). Causes besides surgery: hypomagnesemia (correct Mg first), vitamin D deficiency, DiGeorge syndrome (third/fourth pouch agenesis), and pseudohypoparathyroidism (end-organ PTH resistance with high PTH). Elevated preoperative alkaline phosphatase predicts hungry bone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 150)

topic: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury During Thyroidectomy
text: **Nerve relationships**: the RLN ascends near the tracheoesophageal groove, crosses either deep or superficial to the inferior thyroid artery near the middle third, and enters the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint (inferior cornu). The internal SLN may anastomose with an RLN branch (loop of Galen). The right RLN is more oblique and the left longer; superior parathyroids sit dorsal to the RLN and inferior glands ventral. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, pp 128, 145)

**EEG staging signatures**: wake = alpha (8-13 Hz, occipital, eyes closed); N1 = low-amplitude mixed frequency, theta, vertex sharp waves, slow eye movements (<5% of sleep); N2 = K-complexes and sleep spindles 11-16 Hz (~50%); N3 = slow waves 0.5-2 Hz >75 uV occupying >20% of the epoch (~10-20%, first half of night); REM = low chin EMG, rapid eye movements, sawtooth waves (~25%). Epochs are 30 seconds. Benzodiazepines create drug spindles and suppress N3. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 155-158)

**Other AASM scoring rules**: RERA = arousal after >=10 s of increasing effort not meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria (RDI adds RERAs to AHI); Cheyne-Stokes = >=3 crescendo-decrescendo cycles with cycle length >=40 s; sleep hypoventilation = a PCO2 rise of >=10 mm Hg (or to >55 mm Hg) sustained >10 min; arousal = abrupt EEG shift >=3 s after >=10 s of sleep; PLM = 4 or more leg movements 0.5-10 s long separated by 5-90 s. Respiratory effort is best measured by esophageal manometry; RIP belts are standard. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 155-157, 161)

**MSLT/MWT protocols**: MSLT follows an overnight PSG with >=6 hours of sleep, after 1-2 weeks of regular sleep off stimulants; 4-5 nap opportunities at 2-hour intervals; narcolepsy if mean sleep latency <=8 min with >=2 sleep-onset REM periods. MWT (4 x 40-minute trials in a dim room) measures ability to stay awake for occupational/treatment assessment and needs no prior PSG. CSF hypocretin-1 <110 pg/mL (or <1/3 of normal) defines type 1 narcolepsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 161-162, 180)

**Narcolepsy mimics**: idiopathic hypersomnia features long (>10 h) unrefreshing sleep, naps that do not refresh, and short MSLT latency without SOREMPs; Kleine-Levin syndrome affects adolescent males with recurrent episodes of days-weeks of hypersomnia plus hyperphagia, hypersexuality, and cognitive change, normal between episodes. Chronic insufficient sleep remains the most common cause of hypersomnia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 179-181)

**Palatal surgery risks and snoring options**: complications include bleeding, nasopharyngeal stenosis, VPI, voice change, and postobstructive (flash) pulmonary edema requiring positive pressure. Excess palatal resection can create mouth leak and worsen later CPAP use. Palatal stiffening (implants, injection snoreplasty, radiofrequency) suits primary snoring with favorable anatomy (small tonsils, normal BMI) but has little effect on significant OSA. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 169-170, 174)

**Device types**: mandibular advancement splints are better tolerated and more effective than tongue-retaining devices; a tongue-retaining (suction) device is an option when dentition is inadequate or TMJ disease limits advancement. Predictors of success: lower BMI, lower AHI, positional OSA, and greater achievable protrusion. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, p 168)

**Mode selection**: auto-PAP is avoided in CHF, COPD, obesity hypoventilation, nonsnorers, and desaturation from non-OSA causes; bilevel PAP fits hypercapnia (COPD, OHS), neuromuscular disease, and high-pressure intolerance, with a backup rate for hypoventilation. PAP is contraindicated with CSF leak/pneumocephalus (e.g., after cribriform injury), untreated pneumothorax, bullous lung disease, or high aspiration risk. Nasal dryness is the most common side effect. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 167)

**Two-process model and markers**: homeostatic Process S builds with wakefulness; circadian Process C (SCN, entrained via melanopsin retinal ganglion cells by light) promotes alertness. Core body temperature minimum is about 2 hours before habitual waking; dim-light melatonin onset is 2-3 hours before habitual bedtime. Sleep restriction lowers leptin and raises ghrelin (weight gain) and causes insulin resistance; growth hormone peaks in early N3. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 152-154)

topic: Restless Legs / Periodic Limb Movement Disorders
text: **RLS genetics and drug pearls**: BTBD9 links to iron homeostasis and PLMs; secondary RLS occurs with iron deficiency (ferritin), renal failure, pregnancy, and drugs (SSRIs, TCAs, antihistamines, dopamine antagonists). Rebound = worsening at end of dose; augmentation = earlier, stronger, wider symptoms on dopaminergics. About 80% of RLS patients have PLMs, but PLMs are not required. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 174-175)

**Glasgow Coma Scale in the primary survey**: GCS sums eye opening (1-4), verbal response (1-5), and motor response (1-6), for a range of 3-15. A score of 8 or less marks severe head injury (and usually the need for a definitive airway), 9-12 is moderate, and 13 or more is mild. Record it before sedation or paralysis, because it sets the timing of facial fracture repair. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 633)

**Hemorrhage classes**: adult blood volume is about 7% of body weight (about 5 L at 70 kg); class I is about 10% loss and asymptomatic. Class II is about 20% (1 L): anxiety, narrowed pulse pressure, and tachycardia, the first reliable sign; class III is 30-40%: hypotension, diaphoresis, and confusion. Class IV is over 40%: lethargy or coma; start with two large-bore IVs (18G or larger) and an initial crystalloid bolus (2 L in adults, 20 mL/kg in children). Crystalloid replaces blood loss at about 3:1, and packed red cells are indicated once loss exceeds about 30% (class III-IV), using type O in an emergency. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 632-633)

**Penetrating facial trauma by division**: Division I (above the supraorbital rim) puts the frontal sinus and brain at risk and needs neurosurgical and CT evaluation; division II (supraorbital rim to oral commissure) threatens the globe, parotid duct, facial nerve, and maxilla. Division III (commissure to hyoid) is handled like neck zone II. A wound crossing the mandibular angle plane (a vertical plane from the mandibular angle to the skull base) needs carotid-sheath evaluation with angiography. **Sympathetic ophthalmia**: an unsalvageable ruptured globe may be enucleated early, because autoimmunity against uveal antigens can blind the uninjured eye. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 666)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Trauma airway options**: nasotracheal intubation needs no neck extension and is the preferred route for severe mandible fractures; orotracheal intubation carries more risk with C-spine injury. An LMA ventilates but does not protect the airway; **Needle cricothyroidotomy**: a 12-gauge or larger catheter through the cricothyroid membrane, connected to jet oxygen at about 1 s inflation to 4 s exhalation. It bridges only about 30 minutes before CO2 retention becomes dangerous; **Surgical cricothyrotomy**: vertical skin incision, horizontal incision through the membrane, spread, then a tube. It is faster and less bloody than tracheostomy because it sits above the thyroid isthmus; prefer urgent tracheostomy in young children and in laryngeal fracture or tracheal disruption. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 630-631)

**Occlusion clues to fracture site**: an anterior open bite suggests bilateral condylar or angle fractures; a posterior open bite suggests an anterior alveolar or parasymphyseal fracture. The chin deviates toward a subcondylar fracture, with an open bite on the opposite side; inability to open the mouth suggests a coronoid fracture or a depressed zygomatic arch impinging on the coronoid. Normal interincisal opening is about 4-5 cm. Lower-lip and chin numbness localizes injury to the inferior alveolar or mental nerve. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 635-637)

**Dental language for boards and consults**: the universal system numbers adult teeth 1-32, from the maxillary right third molar (#1) to the maxillary left third molar (#16), then the mandibular left third molar (#17) to the mandibular right third molar (#32). The 20 primary teeth are lettered A-T and are usually all shed by about age 12. **Kazanjian-Converse fracture classes**: Class I has teeth on both sides of the fracture, Class II has teeth on one side only, and Class III is edentulous. Class II and III fractures cannot rely on occlusion for reduction. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 638-639)

**Teeth in the fracture line**: remove a tooth in the line that blocks reduction or occlusion, is infected, is fractured or nonviable, or has exposed pulp; otherwise keep it, because extraction creates a portal for infection, removes height and stability (especially molars at the angle), and weakens fixation. **Typical MMF duration**: children about 2-4 weeks, adults about 4-6 weeks, elderly over 8 weeks, and condylar fractures only about 1-3 weeks (with elastics) to limit ankylosis. MMF requires an intact maxilla. **ORIF over MMF**: favor ORIF for unfavorable or comminuted fractures, multiple or bilateral fractures, poor pulmonary reserve, seizure disorder, pregnancy, unreliable patients, and the elderly. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 639-640)

**Approaches**: the transoral approach (no scar, no marginal mandibular risk) suits symphysis, parasymphysis, and body fractures; the submandibular (Risdon) approach exposes the posterior body, angle, and ramus; the retromandibular approach (incision about 0.5 cm below the lobule, behind the ramus, through or around the parotid) exposes the ramus and condylar neck. The preauricular approach is for the TMJ and condylar head; transbuccal trocar drilling lets you plate angle and body fractures through the mouth. **Hardware**: lag screws compress oblique symphyseal or body fractures; external fixation is for comminuted, infected, or bone-loss cases. A load-bearing locking reconstruction plate is the choice for atrophic edentulous mandibles; angle fractures have the highest complication rate of any site. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 640-642)

**Condylar fractures, classic open-reduction indications**: condyle displaced into the middle cranial fossa, lateral extracapsular dislocation, foreign body in the joint, inability to restore occlusion closed (for example, no occluding teeth), bilateral fractures with loss of ramus height, or associated midface fractures needing a stable vertical reference. These are historical 'absolute' indications (Zide-Kent), not current rules: modern trials favor ORIF more often for displaced subcondylar fractures in adults. Otherwise treat closed with short elastic MMF and early mobilization. Bilateral condylar neck fractures can compromise the airway and cause an anterior open bite. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 642)

**Complication pearls**: inferior alveolar or mental nerve hypesthesia is the most common complication and usually recovers; nonunion produces fibrous rather than osteogenic union and needs debridement, refixation, and often bone graft. An exposed plate can often be kept with local care until the bone heals; condylar avascular necrosis and TMJ ankylosis (opening limited to about 5 mm or less) follow prolonged immobilization or condylar injury. Fibrous ankylosis may respond to opening exercises, while bony ankylosis needs resection and joint reconstruction. Chlorhexidine rinses can stain teeth after about a week of use. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 642-643)

**Le Fort epidemiology and buttresses**: Le Fort II (pyramidal) is the most common pattern and Le Fort I the second most common; all Le Fort fractures cross the pterygoid plates. Pasha lists four vertical buttresses: nasomaxillary (medial), zygomaticomaxillary (lateral, the strongest load-bearer, starting above the first molar), pterygomaxillary (posterior), and the weak midline septovomerian; **Fixation targets**: Le Fort I is reduced (digitally or with disimpaction forceps) into MMF, then the NM and ZM buttresses are plated. Le Fort II needs at least ZM fixation, plus the nasofrontal or infraorbital rim as needed; Le Fort III usually needs coronal exposure. **Timing**: repair is ideal within 24-48 hours before edema, or within about 2 weeks before fibrosis and resorption set in. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 644-647)

**Palatal fractures**: these usually run parasagittal (paramedian), because the vomer reinforces the midline; reduce them (Rowe forceps or bone hooks) to restore maxillary arch width and dentoalveolar position before Le Fort fixation. Anterior palatal fractures can be plated; posterior ones are often managed with closed reduction and MMF, or a palatal splint. Edentulous patients need dentures or a splint, with or without MMF. An unreduced palatal split leaves a widened arch and crossbite. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 647)

**Isolated zygomatic arch and ZMC approaches**: the Gillies temporal approach uses an incision behind the temporal hairline through the temporoparietal fascia and the superficial layer of the deep temporal fascia; the elevator passes deep to that fascia layer and superficial to the temporalis muscle, sliding under the arch to reduce it without endangering the frontal branch. The Keen approach reaches the arch transorally through a gingivobuccal incision. Stabilizing a displaced ZMC usually takes at least two-point fixation (typically ZF and ZM). ZMC fractures are rare before about age 5, when the maxillary sinus is small. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 648-649)

**Traumatic optic neuropathy**: it comes from optic canal or SOF compression or shear; signs are reduced acuity, an afferent pupillary defect, and color loss. Immediate complete loss carries a very poor prognosis; for delayed or progressive loss, options are high-dose corticosteroids (with or without mannitol) and orbital or optic canal decompression when CT shows bony impingement. The evidence is weak, and CRASH-trial data raise concern about high-dose steroids in head injury; **Superior orbital fissure syndrome**: involves CN III, IV, VI, and V1 (ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, a dilated pupil, and forehead numbness). Vision loss added to this picture means orbital apex syndrome. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 650)

**Orbital floor repair: contraindications and endpoints**: delay or avoid repair with hyphema, retinal tear or detachment, globe perforation, an only-seeing eye, active sinusitis, or a frozen globe; ophthalmology should examine every patient first. Enophthalmos or hypoglobus of about 2 mm or more (measured with a Hertel exophthalmometer) supports repair; repair before swelling or after it settles (about 7-10 days); delay allows scar and bone resorption. Rebuild the floor back to the posterior ledge; do a forced duction test at the end of every repair. About 5 mm of enophthalmos is the most that can be corrected safely without stretching the optic nerve. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 650-651)

**Orbital approaches and their lid complications**: the subciliary approach gives wide floor and rim exposure but carries the highest risk of ectropion and scleral show; the transconjunctival approach (with or without lateral canthotomy) leaves no external scar but can cause entropion. The precaruncular (transcaruncular) approach reaches the medial wall and can be joined to a transconjunctival incision; an upper blepharoplasty or lateral brow incision exposes the frontozygomatic suture. The Caldwell-Luc route is a supplement for posterior or comminuted floors; treat postoperative ectropion with upward massage and steroid injection first, then surgery. Epiphora suggests canalicular injury, which is treated with probing or DCR. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 651-652)

**Outflow injury and mucocele**: injury to the nasofrontal outflow tract is the most common cause of a post-traumatic mucocele; mucoceles may appear years later, so long-term imaging follow-up matters. Sinus fluid persisting more than about 10 days after injury suggests outflow obstruction; if only one outflow tract is injured, an intersinus septectomy can let that side drain through the healthy one. Obliteration is reserved for injury to both outflow tracts or severe comminution; the frontal sinus is not radiographically present until about age 5-6, so these fractures are rare in young children. The anterior table is thick, while the posterior table and floor are thin. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 653-654)

**Canthal and lacrimal tests**: in the bowstring (lid traction) test, you pull the lower lid laterally while palpating the medial canthus; a loose tendon or a mobile bone fragment means canthal instability. Traumatic telecanthus is an intercanthal distance over about 32-35 mm in adults (over about 22 mm in infants), or wider than one palpebral fissure. It shows early as rounding of the medial canthus. The fluorescein (Jones) dye test checks lacrimal patency: dye placed in the eye should appear on an inferior meatus pledget within about 1-5 minutes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 656-657)

**Canthal and lacrimal repair principles**: rebuild the medial orbital wall before fixing the canthus; restore the canthal tendon (or its bone fragment) along its native posterior and superior vector, behind the lacrimal fossa, with slight overcorrection. Use transnasal wiring to the opposite side when the fragment is comminuted; wires placed too low or too anterior cause residual telecanthus and lid malposition. Canalicular lacerations are repaired over silicone stents (Crawford or Monoka), and the lower canaliculus matters most; obstruction distal to the sac needs DCR; proximal failure needs conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (a Jones tube). Late telecanthus is very hard to correct secondarily. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 657-658)

**Textbook timing and pediatric pattern**: Pasha gives a closed-reduction window either within about 3 hours of injury (before edema) or at 3-10 days (after edema, before bony union), which is consistent with the site's 2-10 day window. Children tend to have greenstick or dislocation injuries and a higher risk of septal hematoma; adults comminute more often. Avoid rigid plates on the nasal bones; fine wires or splints are used when needed. Persistent deformity after a failed closed reduction is corrected by septorhinoplasty after healing (about 3-6 months). (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 659-660)

**Classic numbers still tested**: longitudinal fractures make up about 75% (temporoparietal blow, conductive loss, EAC step-off, Battle sign); transverse fractures make up about 25% (frontal or occipital blow, SNHL and vertigo). Facial nerve injury occurs in about 30-50% of transverse or otic-capsule-violating fractures; however, most traumatic facial palsies overall come from longitudinal fractures because those are more common. Incudostapedial joint separation is the most common ossicular injury; Pasha times formal audiometry at about 2-8 weeks (sooner if a new loss is not explained by hemotympanum). Over 90% of traumatic CSF leaks stop with conservative care. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 661-663)

**Canal injury and late sequelae**: an EAC laceration almost always overlies a fracture; stent the canal (a wick or packing with antibiotic-steroid drops) to prevent stenosis. Repair a complete canal stenosis, because trapped skin forms canal cholesteatoma; epithelium trapped in the fracture line can cause delayed middle ear or mastoid cholesteatoma years later, which justifies long-term otologic follow-up. Persistent vertigo needs evaluation for perilymphatic fistula and BPPV. A complete unilateral vestibular loss is managed with a short course of suppressants and then vestibular rehabilitation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 663)

**Textbook numbers behind selective management**: about 5-15% of aerodigestive injuries are asymptomatic at first, and pharyngoesophageal injury is the most commonly missed neck injury; repair pharyngoesophageal tears primarily if found within about 24 hours; later ones generally need drainage or diversion. Contrast studies should start with water-soluble contrast; carotid injuries carry about 10-20% mortality. Repair is preferred over ligation, especially in a patient without an established stroke; vertebral artery injuries are usually embolized. Historically, 50-70% of mandatory zone II explorations were negative, which drove the move to selective and CTA-based care; Pasha measures zone I from the sternal notch (clavicles) to the cricoid. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 664-666, 668)

**Burn resuscitation and inhalation injury**: estimate TBSA with the rule of nines (head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior and posterior trunk 18% each, palm about 1%); Parkland: 4 mL x kg x %TBSA of crystalloid over 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours, titrated to urine output. Suspect inhalation injury with a closed-space fire, singed nasal hair, soot, carbonaceous sputum, or hoarseness; facial burn extent does not predict airway severity. Intubate early, confirm with laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy, and avoid tracheotomy through burned skin; carbon monoxide poisoning is significant above about 10% carboxyhemoglobin in nonsmokers (about 20% in smokers). Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated and worsen outcomes in inhalation injury; significant facial burns need admission or a burn center. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 674-676)

**Burn wound pearls**: silver sulfadiazine is painless but can cause leukopenia; mafenide penetrates eschar and cartilage (useful for the ear) and covers Pseudomonas, but it is painful and causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis through carbonic anhydrase inhibition. Silver nitrate penetrates poorly and causes electrolyte loss; bacitracin suits superficial facial burns. Do not neutralize chemical burns (the reaction is exothermic); irrigate instead; Pasha favors waiting up to about 10 days for deep facial burns to demarcate before excision, then grafting by aesthetic unit. Pediatric oral commissure electrical burns are managed conservatively, watching for delayed labial artery bleeding, with a commissure or oral splint to prevent microstomia; for auricular burns, avoid pressure on the ear and cover exposed cartilage early to prevent suppurative chondritis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 675-676)

**Local anesthesia and tetanus**: the maximum lidocaine dose is about 4 mg/kg plain and 7 mg/kg with epinephrine (in a 70 kg adult, about 30 mL vs 50 mL of 1%); regional blocks limit tissue distortion; supraorbital and infraorbital foramina lie roughly in the mid-pupillary line. The mental foramen lies below the second premolar; a ring block anesthetizes the auricle; do not irrigate wounds with hydrogen peroxide (it is cytotoxic). Remove tar with petroleum-based solvents and scrub out embedded debris early to prevent traumatic tattooing; **Tetanus (current CDC/ACIP)**: give Td/Tdap for clean minor wounds if 10 or more years since the last dose, and for all other wounds if 5 or more years. Add tetanus immune globulin for dirty wounds when the primary series is incomplete or unknown; Pasha states only the 10-year rule. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 670-671)

**Region-specific closure numbers**: Pasha allows primary closure of lip defects up to about one-half of the lip (many sources say one-third); mark the vermilion before injecting, place a key stitch at the vermilion border first, and close in three layers (mucosa, orbicularis, skin). Eyelid: up to about one-quarter of the lid can close primarily, and a lateral canthotomy adds about 10 mm; margin lacerations are aligned at the gray line, then the posterior margin and tarsus, without suturing orbicularis. Keep a parotid duct stent about 10-14 days; a hematoma is gelatinous at first and needs incision, but liquefies after about 1 week and can then be aspirated. A U-shaped flap with a beveled edge risks trap-door (pincushion) deformity: square the edges and undermine widely. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 672-673)

**Acute auricular trauma**: drain an auricular hematoma promptly by incision and drainage, then suture a through-and-through bolster to prevent reaccumulation, perichondritis, and cauliflower ear; lacerations are closed by approximating the perichondrium; exposed cartilage must be covered.
