Helical rim defects under about 2 cm can be closed primarily; larger ones use chondrocutaneous (Antia-Buch) advancement. A partial avulsion often survives on a skin pedicle as small as 1-2 mm. Complete avulsion warrants microvascular replantation when feasible; otherwise bury the cartilage in a postauricular or abdominal pocket for later reconstruction. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 674)

topic: Cranial Nerve Examination / Skull Base Localization
text: **Motor 'exception' rules**: CN XII supplies all tongue muscles except the palatoglossus (CN X); CN X supplies all palatal muscles except the tensor veli palatini (V3). The RLN supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid (external SLN); CN X supplies all pharyngeal muscles except the stylopharyngeus (CN IX). V3 also supplies the tensor tympani, mylohyoid, and anterior digastric; **Parasympathetic routes**: Edinger-Westphal nucleus -> CN III -> ciliary ganglion -> pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle. Inferior salivatory nucleus -> CN IX (Jacobson) -> lesser petrosal nerve -> otic ganglion -> auriculotemporal nerve -> parotid; superior salivatory nucleus -> nervus intermedius -> chorda tympani -> lingual nerve -> submandibular ganglion -> submandibular and sublingual glands. (Pasha 6e, Appendix B, pp 679-682)

**Immunobullous disease: histology and immunofluorescence**: pemphigus vulgaris is intraepithelial (suprabasilar) acantholysis from anti-desmoglein 1/3 antibodies, with a 'row of tombstones' basal layer and Tzanck cells; DIF shows intercellular deposits and serum IIF is positive; it is often fatal untreated. Mucous membrane (cicatricial) pemphigoid is a subepithelial split with linear basement-membrane DIF and usually negative IIF; it favors the attached gingiva in women in their 50s-60s, and ocular involvement (about 50-70%) can cause symblepharon and blindness, so it needs ophthalmology referral. Bullous pemphigoid affects older adults, is mainly cutaneous, and is rarely oral; both show a Nikolsky sign. Send perilesional tissue for DIF in Michel medium, not formalin. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 188, 190-191)

**Color clues to systemic disease**: a blue-gray gingival line (Burton line) means lead poisoning; perioral and labial melanotic macules suggest Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (GI hamartomatous polyps); diffuse mucosal hyperpigmentation suggests Addison disease. Mucosal telangiectasias suggest HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu); generalized pallor suggests anemia or thalassemia, and generalized redness suggests polycythemia or liver failure. Small yellow papules are Fordyce granules (ectopic sebaceous glands, normal); black hairy tongue is elongated filiform papillae. Black-brown discoloration can follow bismuth or arsenic; **Amyloidosis**: the tongue is the most common head and neck site (macroglossia); Congo red staining shows apple-green birefringence. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 187, 194)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Sarcoidosis in the head and neck**: cervical adenopathy is the most common head and neck presentation (about 25-50%); laryngeal sarcoid is classically a pale, diffuse supraglottic swelling, especially of the epiglottis. Other sites include the sinonasal tract (crusting, nodules, septal perforation), lacrimal glands, and orbit; Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) is uveitis, parotid enlargement, facial palsy (about 50%), and fever. Workup includes CXR (bilateral hilar adenopathy), serum ACE, calcium, and biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas; about 40% are asymptomatic at diagnosis. Treat symptomatic or organ-threatening disease with steroids; intralesional steroid or debulking is used for obstructing laryngeal disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 204-205, 241)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Tuberculosis**: cervical TB (scrofula) is the most common head and neck form; laryngeal TB favors the posterior glottis (interarytenoid area), epiglottis, and vocal folds and can mimic cancer. TB otitis causes painless watery otorrhea with multiple TM perforations; screen with an IGRA (unaffected by BCG) or a PPD. PPD induration is positive at 5 mm or more in HIV, immunosuppression, or close contacts; at 10 mm or more in health care workers, IV drug users, residents of congregate settings, and children under 5; and at 15 mm or more in low-risk people; diagnose nodal disease by FNA (AFB, culture, PCR) or excisional biopsy. Avoid incision and drainage, which leaves a chronic draining sinus; treat with multidrug therapy and isolate active pulmonary disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 243)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Syphilis**: primary syphilis is a painless chancre with adenopathy; secondary syphilis comes about 4-6 weeks later with rash, mucous patches, and condylomata lata. Tertiary syphilis brings gummas, neurosyphilis, and aortitis; otosyphilis can cause fluctuating or sudden SNHL with vertigo and positive Hennebert or Tullio signs. Congenital syphilis: Hutchinson triad (notched incisors, interstitial keratitis, deafness), mulberry molars, saddle nose, and Clutton joints; screen with RPR or VDRL and confirm with a treponemal test (FTA-ABS). Penicillin G treats all stages, with steroids added for otologic disease; desensitize penicillin-allergic patients when penicillin is essential. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 242)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Endemic mycoses that mimic laryngeal and oral cancer**: histoplasmosis (Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, bird and bat droppings) causes painful ulcerative lesions with heaped edges, mostly in disseminated disease; blastomycosis (Midwest/Great Lakes) causes verrucous laryngeal or skin lesions with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and broad-based budding yeast. Coccidioidomycosis (desert Southwest, 'valley fever') shows spherules filled with endospores; cryptococcosis (pigeon droppings, immunosuppression) causes meningitis with SNHL and is seen as an encapsulated yeast on India ink. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can be misread as SCC, so request fungal stains and cultures. Treatment is an azole or amphotericin B. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 244)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **GPA by the numbers**: sinonasal disease is the most common head and neck finding (about 60-90%); other rates: nasopharyngeal ulceration about 75%, laryngeal ulceration about 25%, subglottic stenosis under about 20%, serous otitis media/CHL about 20-25%, and ocular disease about 40%. Lungs are involved in about 90%, and renal disease causes most deaths. c-ANCA/PR3 supports the diagnosis; nasal biopsies have low yield (necrosis and inflammation), so take deep, generous tissue. Kidney, lung, or skin biopsies have higher yield; treat with induction immunosuppression (steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide), then maintenance. Add TMP-SMX prophylaxis and use saline irrigation and debridement for local care. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 247-248)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Giant cell arteritis**: it is the most common systemic vasculitis; it typically affects patients over 50, usually women, and about half have polymyalgia rheumatica. Features are new headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw or tongue claudication (claudication can mimic TMJ or dental pain), with visual symptoms; about one-third of untreated patients go blind; ESR and CRP are elevated. Start high-dose steroids immediately; do not wait for the biopsy; temporal artery biopsy is the reference standard, but skip lesions cause false negatives (up to about 40%), so take a long segment (Pasha says 2-5 cm). Pasha advises a contralateral biopsy if the first is negative; current ACR guidance starts unilateral and adds vascular ultrasound or imaging. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 248)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Connective tissue disease in the head and neck**: rheumatoid arthritis involves the TMJ in about 50% (usually bilateral); cricoarytenoid arthritis or ankylosis causes hoarseness, globus, or stridor and must be told apart from bilateral vocal fold paralysis (palpate the arytenoids or use LEMG). Ossicular joint involvement is rare; RA is linked to secondary Sjogren syndrome; SLE causes oral ulcers with an erythematous halo, septal perforation, autoimmune SNHL, parotid swelling, and cricoarytenoid disease. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific; ANA is a sensitive screen; discoid lupus affects skin and oral mucosa without visceral disease. Mixed connective tissue disease has overlap features with high-titer anti-U1 RNP. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 245-247)

**HIV head and neck findings**: benign lymphoepithelial cysts are multiple, bilateral, cystic parotid enlargements in HIV; manage them with antiretroviral therapy, serial aspiration, or sclerotherapy (for example, doxycycline) rather than routine parotidectomy. In HIV adenopathy, the most common cause is follicular hyperplasia. Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy is defined as nodes at 2 or more extrainguinal sites for over 3 months with no other cause. Biopsy enlarging, asymmetric, over 2 cm, or FNA-suspicious nodes, or nodes with mediastinal disease, because lymphoma, mycobacteria, and Kaposi sarcoma are more common. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 207, 232-233)

**Noninfectious gland enlargement mimics**: Kuttner tumor (chronic sclerosing sialadenitis) is an IgG4-related, firm submandibular enlargement that looks like a tumor; it is diagnosed and treated by excision. Mikulicz disease is IgG4-related, persistent, symmetric lacrimal plus salivary swelling with mostly preserved function, and it responds to steroids. Sialadenosis is painless, bilateral, noninflammatory parotid enlargement from metabolic or nutritional causes (diabetes, alcohol/cirrhosis, bulimia/malnutrition, endocrine disorders) or drugs; treat the cause. Radioiodine sialadenitis is the most common complication of I-131 therapy; refractory cases can be treated with sialendoscopic duct irrigation and dilation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 205-206)

**Necrotizing sialometaplasia, a cancer mimic**: a benign, self-limited ischemic process of minor salivary glands. It most often presents as a painless or mildly painful hard-palate ulcer or nodule, sometimes after trauma, surgery, or intubation. Histology shows lobular necrosis with squamous metaplasia of ducts and acini, plus pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and it can be misread as SCC or mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Biopsy confirms it, and it heals on its own over weeks; avoid radical resection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 207)

**Histotype pearls**: mucoepidermoid is the most common salivary cancer in adults and children (and after radiation); low grade has about 90% 5-year survival; high grade about 50%; adenoid cystic is the most common submandibular and minor-gland cancer. Its histology is cribriform 'Swiss cheese' (best), tubular, or solid (worst); it spreads perineurally and to the lungs; 5-year survival is about 75-80% but 15-20-year survival is only about 10-30%; nodal spread is uncommon, so elective neck dissection is usually not needed. Acinic cell is the second most common pediatric salivary cancer and is bilateral in about 3%; carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma arises in a small percentage of PAs (Pasha says 2-3%); SCC in the parotid is usually metastatic from skin. Clear cell tumors require excluding metastatic renal cell carcinoma; undifferentiated carcinoma has the worst prognosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 210-214)

**Facial nerve trunk landmarks in parotidectomy**: the tragal pointer (the trunk lies about 1 cm deep, anterior, and inferior to its tip); the tympanomastoid suture (the trunk lies about 6-8 mm deep to its inferior end; the most reliable landmark). The posterior belly of the digastric (the nerve lies at about the same depth, just superior to its attachment at the digastric ridge); other options: retrograde dissection from a peripheral branch, or mastoidectomy to find the vertical segment in revision or distorted fields. **Counseling numbers**: greater auricular numbness usually improves within about 9 months if the nerve was not cut; a salivary fistula usually closes within 2-3 weeks with aspiration and pressure. Frey syndrome can appear up to years after surgery. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 214-215)

**Benign tumor pearls**: rule of 80s: about 80% of parotid tumors are benign and about 80% of salivary tumors arise in the parotid; enucleation of a pleomorphic adenoma has historically recurred in about 30% because of pseudopods; formal parotidectomy gives over 90% long-term control, and PA is radioresistant. Warthin tumor: older male smokers, about 10% bilateral and 10% multicentric, 'motor oil' aspirate, and avid on Tc-99m pertechnetate scanning (mitochondria-rich oncocytes), as is oncocytoma (about 1% of salivary tumors). Monomorphic adenomas lack chondromyxoid stroma: basal cell adenoma (parotid) and canalicular adenoma (upper lip minor glands). A clear-cell tumor requires excluding metastatic renal cell carcinoma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 208-211)

**Parotid hemangioma**: hemangioma is the most common salivary gland tumor in children; it appears in the first weeks of life as a soft, compressible preauricular mass, often with bluish overlying skin. It proliferates for about 6-12 months, then involutes. About half of patients have coexisting cutaneous hemangiomas. Do not mistake it for a solid parotid neoplasm requiring parotidectomy: imaging and clinical course usually settle the diagnosis, and propranolol is first-line when treatment is needed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 211)

**Textbook stone numbers**: about 80-90% of stones form in the submandibular gland; about 90% of submandibular stones are radiopaque and about 90% of parotid stones are radiolucent, so plain films miss most parotid stones; use ultrasound or noncontrast CT. Gout (urate stones) and smoking are associations; sialendoscopic basket retrieval works for small stones (about 3 mm or less in the parotid, 4 mm or less in the submandibular gland). Stones of about 5-10 mm usually need intraductal laser or mechanical fragmentation; palpable stones over about 1 cm near the hilum are removed transorally, and the gland is excised for intraparenchymal or multiple stones not reachable transorally. Sialography is contraindicated during acute infection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 202, 204)

**Lesser-taught spaces**: the masticator space (masseteric, pterygoid, superficial and deep temporal compartments) is usually seeded by mandibular third molars and presents with marked trismus and posterior ramus swelling; buccal space infection is odontogenic and can spread via the angular and facial veins to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis. Carotid space infection causes torticollis away from the affected side, plus thrombophlebitis or blowout; visceral space infection usually follows esophageal perforation. The prevertebral space runs from skull base to coccyx (Pott abscess is tuberculous spondylitis); retropharyngeal nodes drain the nose, sinuses, and nasopharynx, which is why retropharyngeal abscess is a pediatric disease. On a lateral film, prevertebral soft tissue wider than about half the vertebral body width (over about 7 mm at C2) is abnormal. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 235-240)

**Actinomycosis and nocardiosis**: Actinomyces israelii is a normal oral commensal (anaerobic, gram-positive, branching) that invades after extraction or mucosal injury; it forms a woody, purplish mass with sinus tracts and sulfur granules that ignores fascial planes and can mimic malignancy. Diagnosis needs anaerobic culture (1-2 weeks) and histology; treatment is debridement plus prolonged high-dose penicillin. Nocardia is an aerobic soil organism (modified acid-fast), usually spreading from the lung, and is treated with sulfonamides. Mnemonic SNAP: Sulfa for Nocardia, Actinomyces gets Penicillin. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 189-190, 245)

**Adult neck mass framework**: an adult neck mass lasting 2 weeks or more without a clear infectious cause should be treated as possibly malignant, with a full head and neck exam, imaging, and FNA; nodes over about 2 cm, firm, fixed, or nontender raise suspicion. Use KITTENS for the differential: Congenital, Infectious/Iatrogenic, Toxins/Trauma, Endocrine, Neoplastic, Systemic (Kikuchi, Kawasaki, sarcoid). Open biopsy is reserved for nondiagnostic or indeterminate FNA after a complete workup. Be ready to complete a neck dissection if frozen section shows SCC. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 228-231)

**Pilomatrixoma**: a benign hair-matrix tumor with a bimodal age peak (about 5-15 and 50-65 years). About 50-60% occur in the head and neck, usually as a firm, calcified, skin-tethered nodule 3 cm or smaller on the cheek, neck, or preauricular region, sometimes with bluish skin and a 'tent sign'. Ultrasound shows a calcified subcutaneous nodule. Treat with complete excision, including the attached skin, to prevent recurrence. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 233)

**Modified radical neck dissection subtypes**: all remove levels I-V; type I preserves only the spinal accessory nerve, type II preserves CN XI and the internal jugular vein, and type III (functional or Bocca dissection) preserves CN XI, the internal jugular vein and the sternocleidomastoid. Radical neck dissection is now reserved for nodal disease with extranodal spread directly involving the SCM, IJV or CN XI. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 276)

**Named selective dissections**: supraomohyoid (anterolateral) removes levels I-III and the extended version adds level IV, used for oral cavity cancer with an N0 or limited mobile N1 neck; lateral removes II-IV for selected supraglottic, oropharyngeal and hypopharyngeal primaries; posterolateral removes II-V plus retroauricular and suboccipital nodes for posterior scalp primaries. Radical dissection also takes the submandibular gland, and loss of SCM coverage raises carotid blowout risk. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 275-276)

**Level boundary landmarks**: level II runs from the skull base to the hyoid (surgical landmark) or carotid bifurcation (radiologic), split into IIA and IIB by CN XI; level III runs from the hyoid to the cricoid (or omohyoid); level IV from the cricoid to the clavicle; level V is split into VA and VB by the cricoid plane; level VI lies between the carotid sheaths and includes the Delphian (prelaryngeal) node; level VII runs from the suprasternal notch into the superior mediastinum. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 272)

**When the neck is unresectable**: the following are generally treated as unresectable: encasement of more than 270 degrees of the carotid circumference, invasion of the prevertebral fascia or vertebrae, brachial plexus, floor of neck/mediastinum, or skull base. A carotid that is invaded but not encased can be resected en bloc if the patient passes a balloon occlusion test and accepts the stroke risk. Initial chemoradiation may shrink a fixed neck enough to allow later resection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 257, 275)

**Bilateral (N2c) necks**: treat with bilateral neck dissection plus adjuvant radiation. Dissect the less involved side first and try to save its internal jugular vein. If both IJVs are threatened, space the two dissections about 3-4 weeks apart so collateral venous drainage can develop, which avoids facial/cerebral edema, SIADH and blindness. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 275, 277)

**Incision design and fluid collections**: use designs that protect flap blood supply (apron/curvilinear, MacFee parallel incisions, modified Schobinger). Any trifurcation limb should leave the main incision at a right angle to avoid tip necrosis over the carotid. A major hematoma needs return to the OR. A small hematoma can be watched for about 7-10 days until it liquefies and then aspirated. Hematoma tends to appear early and seroma later. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 276-277)

**Chyle leak specifics**: usually from the left (thoracic duct), seen in about 1-2% of neck dissections, typically in the first few days and often after feeding starts. Start with pressure dressing, head elevation, a medium-chain-triglyceride/low-fat diet and electrolyte correction. Escalate to sclerotherapy (e.g., tetracycline), re-exploration, or thoracic duct ligation when conservative care fails or output stays above about 600 mL/day. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 277)

**AJCC 8 oral cavity T categories**: T1 is 2 cm or less with DOI of 5 mm or less. T2 is 2 cm or less with DOI over 5 to 10 mm, or over 2 to 4 cm with DOI of 10 mm or less. T3 is over 4 cm or DOI over 10 mm. T4a means invasion through cortical bone of the mandible/maxilla or into the maxillary sinus or facial skin; superficial erosion of a tooth socket by a gingival primary does not count. T4b means masticator space, pterygoid plates, skull base or internal carotid encasement. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 279-280)

**Oral cavity high-yield numbers and mimics**: oral cavity is the most common H&N cancer site (~30%) and has the highest second-primary rate (10-40%). More than 90% of occult nodal disease lies in levels I-III. Leukoplakia carries roughly 5-10% malignant potential versus up to 50% for erythroplakia. Necrotizing sialometaplasia and granular cell tumor can mimic SCC on biopsy because of pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 278, 280)

**Rule of 90s**: about 90% of lip cancers are on the lower lip, about 90% are SCC, and lesions under 2 cm have roughly 90% 5-year survival. Regional metastasis is 2-15% overall. Commissure involvement worsens prognosis. Embryologic fusion keeps upper-lip drainage ipsilateral. Early lip cancer does not need elective neck dissection, and primary radiation (about 50-70 Gy) is an alternative to excision. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 279, 281)

**Access and mandible rules**: small (<2 cm) anterior tumors can be removed transorally. Larger or posterior tumors need a mandibulotomy (lip-split with a stepped osteotomy and rigid fixation), a visor flap (keeps the mandible intact but gives poor posterior exposure and chin numbness), or a transcervical/TORS approach. CT-proven bone invasion calls for segmental mandibulectomy; tumor that only abuts periosteum allows marginal (rim) resection. Bony gaps over about 5 cm are reconstructed with fibula or iliac crest. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 282-283, 287)

**Open pharyngeal approaches**: lateral pharyngotomy enters between the hypoglossal and superior laryngeal nerves for small tongue-base or posterior-wall tumors without splitting the mandible. Transhyoid (suprahyoid) pharyngotomy goes above or through the hyoid and requires a tumor-free vallecula. Mandibulotomy gives wide exposure with less malocclusion than mandibulectomy, which is reserved for direct bone involvement. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 286-287)

**Nodal numbers by oropharyngeal subsite**: tongue base has more than 60% cervical metastasis (about 20% bilateral) and about 65% overall 5-year survival. Tonsil cancers present with nodes in 65-75% and may look like asymmetric tonsil enlargement or recurrent peritonsillar abscess. Soft palate cancers have 20-45% nodal spread. Bilateral drainage is expected with tongue base and soft palate primaries. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 283, 321)

**Lymphoma in the differential**: lymphoma makes up roughly 10-15% of tonsil and tongue-base malignancies. Unilateral tonsillar enlargement therefore needs tissue handled fresh for flow cytometry, not formalin only. In the oropharynx, SCC is over 95% of cancers and its nodal metastases are characteristically cystic. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 285)

**TORS scope and complications**: TORS is FDA-cleared for T1-T2 malignancies of the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx (not pediatric, not mandible-invading tumors). It trades haptic feedback for 3D magnified angled vision. Key complications are delayed hemorrhage (consider ligating lingual, facial and other external carotid branches when the neck is dissected), salivary/pharyngocervical fistula with a concurrent neck dissection, and lingual or hypoglossal injury or dysgeusia from retractor pressure. Release the suspension periodically to prevent nerve injury. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 330-332)

**p16 testing specifics**: p16 IHC is read positive with strong nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in more than 70% of tumor cells. p16 is a surrogate, not proof: 10-20% of oropharyngeal cancers are p16-positive without HPV, so ISH or PCR can confirm. Test all oropharyngeal SCC. High-risk types are HPV-16 (by far the most common), 18, 31 and 33. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 255, 284)

**Subsite numbers and AJCC 8 T staging**: piriform sinus is 65-75% of cases with about 75% nodal spread, and apical tumors do worse. Posterior wall is 20-25% (about 60% nodal). Postcricoid is under 5%, linked to Plummer-Vinson syndrome, with about 40% nodal spread. T1 is one subsite and 2 cm or less. T2 is more than one subsite or over 2 to 4 cm without hemilarynx fixation. T3 is over 4 cm, hemilarynx fixation, or esophageal extension. T4a involves thyroid/cricoid cartilage, hyoid, thyroid gland or central-compartment soft tissue. T4b involves prevertebral fascia, carotid encasement or mediastinum. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 288-289)

**Larynx-sparing limits and extent**: partial laryngopharyngectomy suits T1-T2 tumors of the medial piriform wall that stay more than 1.5 cm from the apex. Contraindications include thyroid cartilage, piriform apex, postcricoid, interarytenoid or cervical-esophageal involvement and vocal fold fixation. Most postcricoid tumors need total laryngectomy with partial pharyngectomy. Cervical esophageal spread requires laryngopharyngoesophagectomy, usually with gastric pull-up. Advanced disease includes level VI in the neck dissection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 289-290)

**Gastric pull-up complications**: anastomotic leak/disruption in 10-37% (risk of mediastinitis and death). Hypocalcemia can come from parathyroid devascularization and from poor calcium absorption after truncal vagotomy and loss of gastric acid. Other risks are posterior membranous tracheal tears, cardiopulmonary events from fluid shifts or pneumothorax, and abdominal problems such as pyloroplasty leak or splenic injury. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 290-291)

**Subsite boundaries and frequency**: the supraglottis (30-35% of laryngeal cancer) runs from the epiglottic tip to the junction of the ventricle and true fold, and is lined by respiratory epithelium. The glottis (60-65%) runs from the true fold's upper surface to 1 cm below it. The subglottis (about 5%) runs from there to the lower border of the cricoid. The supraglottis comes from the 3rd-4th arches and the glottis/subglottis from the 6th, and the fusion plane between them separates lymphatic and blood supply. The paraglottic space allows transglottic spread. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 291-295)

**Nodal risk by glottic T stage**: about 5% for T1 (including T1b), 5-10% for T2, 10-20% for T3, and 25-40% for T4. Spread goes to levels II-IV and paratracheal nodes. The anterior commissure has no inner perichondrium, which is why tumor there can reach thyroid cartilage. A fixed fold implies thyroarytenoid, cricoarytenoid or interarytenoid muscle, cricoarytenoid joint, or perineural involvement. For advanced glottic disease treated surgically, the ipsilateral neck plus paratracheal nodes is addressed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 294, 298)

**Supraglottic specifics**: the infrahyoid epiglottis is the most common subsite. Overall nodal risk exceeds 50%, so both necks are always treated. Tumors tend to grow upward toward the tongue base and pre-epiglottic space and have pushing rather than infiltrating borders, which supports horizontal resection. 'Marginal zone' aryepiglottic fold tumors (often basaloid) behave aggressively, like piriform sinus cancers. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 293, 300)

**Numbers for high-grade lesions**: severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ progresses to invasive cancer in roughly 15-25%. After excision (microflap preferred over stripping, to keep the mucosal wave), follow every 2-3 months for 5 years with a low threshold to re-biopsy. Microinvasive carcinoma can be re-excised every 3 months until two consecutive biopsies are negative. Radiation is an alternative, usually for recurrence. CO2 laser ablation gives no specimen. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 296-297)

topic: Transoral Laser Microsurgery for Laryngeal Cancer
text: **European Laryngological Society cordectomy types**: I subepithelial (epithelium only); II subligamental (epithelium, Reinke space, vocal ligament); III transmuscular (through part of the vocalis); IV total (down to the inner thyroid perichondrium); V extended: Va contralateral fold/anterior commissure, Vb arytenoid, Vc ventricle/false fold, Vd subglottis up to 1 cm. Classic cordectomy suits T1 midmembranous lesions that spare the vocal process, anterior commissure, ventricle and subglottis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 299-300)

**Numeric candidacy limits**: all open partial procedures need adequate pulmonary function (FEV1/FVC above roughly 50-60%) and consent to possible total laryngectomy. General contraindications are a fixed cord, extensive cartilage invasion, subglottic extension, interarytenoid involvement, significant oropharyngeal spread and extralaryngeal extension. Vertical hemilaryngectomy also needs no more than 1/3 of the opposite fold involved and subglottic extension under 10 mm anteriorly and 5 mm posteriorly. Supracricoid laryngectomy is excluded by arytenoid fixation, subglottic tumor reaching the upper cricoid, cricoid or hyoid invasion, invasion of the outer thyroid perichondrium, or heavy pre-epiglottic disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 299-301)

**What each operation removes**: supraglottic laryngectomy removes the epiglottis, AE folds, false folds, pre-epiglottic space and upper thyroid cartilage with part of the hyoid. It sacrifices the superior laryngeal nerve, so aspiration is expected; the transoral version preserves the SLN and hyoid and swallows better. Vertical hemilaryngectomy removes one true fold from the anterior commissure to the vocal process plus the false fold, ventricle, paraglottic space and thyroid ala, sparing a 3 mm posterior cartilage strip. Supracricoid laryngectomy removes the entire thyroid cartilage, both true and false folds, the paraglottic spaces and up to one arytenoid, then reconstructs by CHP or, if the epiglottis is spared, CHEP. Near-total (3/4) laryngectomy keeps one arytenoid to create a phonatory shunt. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 300-302)

**AJCC 8 NPC staging (unique N system)**: T1 is confined to the nasopharynx or extends to the oropharynx/nasal cavity. T2 involves the parapharyngeal space or pterygoid/prevertebral muscles. T3 involves skull-base bone, cervical vertebrae, pterygoid structures or sinuses. T4 means intracranial, cranial nerve, hypopharynx, orbit or parotid involvement, or spread beyond the lateral pterygoid. N1 is unilateral cervical and/or uni- or bilateral retropharyngeal nodes 6 cm or less, above the caudal cricoid. N2 is bilateral cervical nodes 6 cm or less above the cricoid. N3 is over 6 cm or below the caudal border of the cricoid. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 305)

**WHO types and EBV serology**: type I keratinizing SCC is sporadic, smoking-related, not EBV-linked, less radiosensitive and has the worst prognosis. Type II (nonkeratinizing) and type III (undifferentiated/lymphoepithelioma) are EBV-driven, endemic, radiosensitive and do better. IgA against viral capsid antigen (VCA) is the sensitive marker and IgA against early antigen (EA) the specific one; both are used for screening in endemic regions. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 304-306)

**Presentation frequencies**: a painless neck mass is the most common first sign (~70%), and unilateral serous otitis media is next (~50%). CN VI is the most commonly involved cranial nerve. Stage I-II disease is not surgical: treat with radiation to the primary and both necks whatever the nodal status. Stage III-IV gets concurrent cisplatin chemoradiation plus adjuvant chemotherapy; Intergroup 0099 showed 76% vs 46% 3-year survival over radiation alone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 259, 304, 306)

**Epidemiology and prognostic line**: the maxillary sinus is the most common site, then the nasal cavity among sites overall and the ethmoid among sinuses. About 90% have eroded more than one wall at presentation. Tumors posterosuperior to Ohngren's line (medial canthus to mandibular angle) do worse because of skull-base and perineural spread. Occult nodal risk is under 10%, so the N0 neck is usually not treated electively unless the nasopharynx or soft palate is involved. Exposures include nickel, chromium, mustard gas, hydrocarbons, radium and wood or leather dust (adenocarcinoma, ethmoid predominant). (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 306-309)

**Open approaches and maxillectomy types**: lateral rhinotomy is the standard route for medial maxillectomy. Weber-Fergusson (lateral rhinotomy plus lip split, sublabial and subciliary/transconjunctival limbs) gives access for total maxillectomy. Midfacial degloving avoids facial scars but exposes mainly the inferomedial maxilla. Inferior (infrastructure) maxillectomy treats alveolar and limited palatal tumors. Radical maxillectomy is total maxillectomy plus orbital exenteration. Exenterate for orbital apex involvement or invasion through the periorbita. Add craniofacial resection when tumor reaches above the cribriform plate or ethmoid roof. Cavernous sinus, optic chiasm, bilateral orbit, carotid or significant brain involvement generally contraindicates resection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 309-311)

**Reconstruction and complications**: palatal and inferior maxillary defects can be obturated: a surgical obturator is placed at the operation and later replaced with a definitive prosthesis. Dural defects need watertight pericranial/galeal, temporalis or free-flap closure. Complications to know: meningitis with CSF leak; tension pneumocephalus, which can come from over-draining a lumbar drain and needs emergent decompression; frontal lobe syndrome; epiphora from nasolacrimal injury (DCR if persistent); and cavernous sinus versus orbital apex syndromes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 311-312)

**Small round blue cell tumors and IHC**: the differential mnemonic MR SLEEP covers melanoma/Merkel, rhabdomyosarcoma, SNUC/small cell/sarcoma, lymphoma, Ewing sarcoma, esthesioneuroblastoma and PNET. Useful stains: S-100 (sensitive, not specific), HMB-45, melan-A/MART-1 and tyrosinase for melanoma; chromogranin, synaptophysin and NSE for neuroendocrine tumors; LCA and CD20/CD3 for lymphoma; cytokeratin for carcinoma; desmin and myoglobin for rhabdomyosarcoma. Esthesioneuroblastoma shows Homer-Wright (pseudo) or Flexner-Wintersteiner (true) rosettes and peaks in teens and older adults. Dulguerov T stages: T1 nasal cavity/sinuses sparing sphenoid and upper ethmoid; T2 adds sphenoid or cribriform; T3 adds orbit or extradural anterior fossa; T4 is brain. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 254, 308, 329-330)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **AJCC 8 T/N/M details**: T2 is over 1-2 mm, T3 over 2-4 mm and T4 over 4 mm, with 'a' meaning no ulceration and 'b' ulcerated. N1a/N2a/N3a are 1, 2-3 and 4 or more clinically occult nodes; 'b' means at least one node was clinically detected; 'c' means in-transit, satellite or microsatellite disease (N1c with no nodes); matted nodes make it N3. M1a is skin/soft tissue/distant nodes, M1b lung, M1c other viscera and M1d CNS, with suffix (0) or (1) for normal or raised LDH. Historic 5-year survival by pT: T1 over 95%, T4 10-30%. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 317, 321)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Clinical subtypes**: superficial spreading is the most common and has a prolonged radial phase. Nodular grows vertically early and has the worst prognosis. Lentigo maligna melanoma arises in older patients on sun-damaged head and neck skin from a long in-situ phase. Acral lentiginous occurs on palms and soles and is more common in darker skin. Desmoplastic and amelanotic variants are easily missed. About 10-25% of melanomas arise in the head and neck, most often on the cheek and scalp. Shave, curettage and laser removal are inappropriate when melanoma is suspected because they destroy depth measurement. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 315-316)

topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Clinical subtypes**: nodular (noduloulcerative) is the most common: a pearly, telangiectatic papule with rolled edges and central ulceration. Superficial BCC is mainly truncal. Morpheaform (sclerosing) looks like a flat, waxy scar with indistinct borders, recurs most and has the worst prognosis. Other forms are pigmented (mimics melanoma), fibroepithelioma, and basosquamous, which behaves aggressively like SCC. Risk factors include xeroderma pigmentosum, arsenic exposure, radiodermatitis, scars/burns and immunosuppression. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 312-313)

topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Modality-specific numbers**: curettage with electrodesiccation suits small (<2 cm) nonmorpheaform lesions and is contraindicated for morpheaform BCC. Cryosurgery (freeze-thaw-freeze with about a 5 mm margin) is for lesions under 1 cm. Standard excision uses about 4 mm margins. Radiation for these superficial lesions is delivered with electrons. Mohs clears about 96% or more and is indicated for recurrent, morpheaform, H-zone and cosmetically critical lesions. Follow up every 4-6 months for recurrence and new primaries. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 313-314)

topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Gorlin (nevoid BCC) syndrome**: an autosomal dominant condition with many BCCs at a young age, keratocystic odontogenic tumors (jaw keratocysts), bifid ribs, scoliosis, frontal bossing, medulloblastoma and possible cognitive impairment. Manage by excising cancers with close follow-up every 3-6 months. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 314)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Book high-risk markers and variants**: overall metastatic potential is 1-4%. Risk rises with Marjolin ulcers (SCC in burn scars or chronic wounds), fusion-plane sites, de novo lesions on non-sun-exposed skin, depth over 6 mm and size over 2 cm. Spindle cell (in scars or burns) and adenoid/acantholytic (periauricular skin of older adults) variants are more aggressive. The verrucous variant is low grade. Bowen disease is SCC in situ. Excision margins are about 4-6 mm for early lesions and 1-2 cm for advanced ones. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 314-315)

**Staging and specimen handling**: Ann Arbor stage I is one nodal region or one extralymphatic site, II is two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm, III is both sides of the diaphragm, and IV is diffuse extralymphatic organ involvement. The suffix A or B records B symptoms. Labs include CBC, LDH, beta-2 microglobulin and LFTs; staging uses CT/PET of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis and bone marrow biopsy. Send the excised node fresh, not in formalin, for flow cytometry, and avoid steroids before biopsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 325-326)

**Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin**: Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal age peak and spreads to contiguous nodes, and its prognosis depends on stage. Lymphocyte-predominant has the best outlook and lymphocyte-depleted the worst. NHL is mostly B-cell, spreads noncontiguously and often extranodally (Waldeyer ring, sinonasal, salivary, thyroid, orbit), and its prognosis depends on grade. Diffuse large B-cell is the most common H&N NHL. Burkitt is EBV-linked, with jaw involvement in the endemic form. MALT lymphoma is low grade and linked to H. pylori. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 324-327)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Fractionation schemes**: conventional is 1.8-2.2 Gy once daily, 5 days a week. Pure hyperfractionation gives twice-daily smaller fractions over the same total time to a higher total dose and lowers late toxicity. Accelerated fractionation shortens total time to counter repopulation but raises acute toxicity. Concomitant boost adds a second daily fraction during the last 2 weeks. Hypofractionation uses large fractions for tumors that repair sublethal damage well, such as melanoma. Meta-analysis shows a survival advantage for hyperfractionation over conventional radiation. Larger tumors have hypoxic cores and resist radiation, and ulcerative or infiltrative tumors respond worse than exophytic ones. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 267-268)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Dose levels and modality choices**: gross disease gets about 70 Gy and the elective (N0) neck or adjuvant bed about 50-55 Gy ('shrinking fields'). On the RTOG pre- vs postoperative trial, survival did not differ but locoregional control was better postoperatively; postop RT needs larger fields and higher dose because the surgical bed is hypoxic. Neutron therapy is used for unresectable salivary cancers such as adenoid cystic carcinoma. Proton therapy offers tighter dose distribution. HDR brachytherapy (e.g., iridium-192) delivers a localized dose through temporary catheters. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 268-269)

**WHO oral mucositis grades**: grade 1 is erythema and soreness. Grade 2 is erythema and pain with solids still possible. Grade 3 is ulceration with a liquid-only diet. Grade 4 is ulceration so severe that oral intake is impossible. Supportive care includes oral rinses, cool foods, topical anesthetic 'magic mouthwash' mixtures and stopping tobacco and alcohol. Candida, HSV and bacterial superinfection are common. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 269-270)

**Late-effect numbers**: about 20-25% of patients become hypothyroid after neck radiation, so check TSH every 6-12 months. The lens is the most radiosensitive tissue, and cataracts can follow as little as about 6 Gy. Mandibular ORN risk rises above about 50-60 Gy and with post-radiation extractions. Laryngeal chondroradionecrosis can mimic recurrence. Radiation-induced thyroid, salivary and temporal bone cancers, sarcoma and leukemia can appear after a latency of about 20 years. Ear effects include otitis externa, serous otitis media and auricular chondritis. Nonfunctional larynx occurs in up to about 12% at 1 year after chemoradiation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 270-271)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Other cytotoxics**: 5-FU blocks thymidylate synthase (S-phase) and causes mucositis, diarrhea, myelosuppression and cardiac toxicity. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, is renally cleared, has been the traditional palliative single agent, and its toxicity is rescued with leucovorin. Bleomycin is known for pulmonary fibrosis and cyclophosphamide for hemorrhagic cystitis. Taxanes stabilize microtubules and cause neutropenia, alopecia and mucositis. Cisplatin ototoxicity is bilateral, cumulative, dose-limiting and high-frequency, from injury to outer hair cells and the stria vascularis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 263-264)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Drug naming and targeted-agent pearls**: antibody suffixes are -omab (mouse), -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanized) and -umab (fully human); -tinib marks tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Cetuximab (anti-EGFR) causes acneiform rash, diarrhea and hypomagnesemia; it improved survival with RT over RT alone (Bonner) and with platinum/5-FU in recurrent/metastatic disease (EXTREME). Gefitinib did not beat methotrexate. Vismodegib blocks SMO for advanced BCC. Cabozantinib and vandetanib (RET/VEGFR/MET) treat medullary thyroid cancer. Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4 and vemurafenib targets BRAF V600E melanoma. Trial phases: I safety and dose, II efficacy, III randomized against standard care, IV after approval. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 257, 264-266)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Induction and adjuvant trial landmarks**: TAX 324 showed docetaxel-cisplatin-5-FU (TPF) induction before chemoradiation beat PF induction for survival. GORTEC 2000-01 showed TPF raised larynx preservation over PF. Intergroup 0034 found no survival gain from adding adjuvant chemotherapy before postoperative RT. Concurrent high-dose cisplatin with postoperative RT is the adjuvant standard for high-risk resected disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 261-263)

**RTOG 9501 long-term nuance**: on 9-10 year follow-up, adding cisplatin to postoperative RT still improved locoregional control, disease-free survival and overall survival for positive margins and/or extranodal extension. Patients whose only risk factor was more than 2 positive nodes got no benefit. This is the evidence for limiting adjuvant chemoradiation to margin-positive or ENE disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 263)

topic: Head & Neck Cancer Surveillance / Second Primaries
text: **NCCN follow-up schedule**: history and physical with mirror or flexible exam every 1-3 months in year 1, every 2-6 months in year 2, every 4-8 months in years 3-5, then yearly. Get baseline post-treatment imaging of the primary and neck within 6 months (PET/CT no sooner than about 12 weeks after definitive therapy). Check TSH every 6-12 months if the neck was irradiated. Monitor EBV DNA for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Include speech/swallow, hearing, dental and depression screening. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, p 258)

topic: Head & Neck Cancer Surveillance / Second Primaries
text: **Prognosis and causes of death**: overall 5-year H&N cancer survival is about 66% (SEER 2010-2016). About 50-60% of deaths come from locoregional failure, 20-30% from distant metastasis and 10-20% from second primaries. Regional nodal disease is the strongest single prognostic factor and can roughly halve survival; ENE, low-neck (IV-V) nodes, skip metastases and higher node counts worsen it further. Histologic grade adds little. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 258-259)

**Unknown-primary specifics**: about 90% of primaries are found with full workup (PET/CT before panendoscopy, directed biopsies, bilateral tonsillectomy ± tongue-base resection). If none is found, the case is T0: EBV-positive nodes are staged as nasopharyngeal cancer and p16-positive nodes as HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer. Supraclavicular adenocarcinoma points below the clavicles, so workup includes PSA (men), mammography (women) and abdominal CT. Thyroglobulin and calcitonin stains look for a thyroid source. About 4% of melanomas present as nodal disease with no primary. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 321-323)

**Foramen of Huschke and vascular strip**: The foramen of Huschke (foramen tympanicum) is a persistent developmental gap in the anteroinferior tympanic ring that links the medial canal to the parotid and glenoid fossa; like the fissures of Santorini it lets infection and canal cancers escape the temporal bone, and it can present as glenoid soft-tissue herniation or TMJ fluid draining from the ear. The vascular strip is the richly vascular canal skin between the tympanosquamous and tympanomastoid sutures and is often swollen and inflamed in AOM. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 335–336)

**Mastoid landmarks: Koerner septum, Donaldson line, Citelli angle**: Koerner (petrosquamous) septum is a bony plate between squamous and petrous air cells that can be mistaken for the medial antral wall (a "false bottom"); the antrum lies deep to it. Donaldson line runs through the lateral semicircular canal and perpendicularly bisects the posterior semicircular canal, marking the upper limit of the endolymphatic sac. The sinodural (Citelli) angle lies between sigmoid sinus and tegmen, and Trautmann triangle is bounded by the bony labyrinth, sigmoid sinus, and superior petrosal sinus/dura. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 337)

**Retrotympanum and IAC landmarks**: The sinus tympani is bounded by the ponticulus above (ridge from pyramidal eminence to promontory), the subiculum below (ridge behind the round window niche), and the facial nerve laterally, and is a classic site of residual cholesteatoma. At the lateral IAC, "Mike's dot" marks where the superior vestibular nerve leaves toward the vestibule and helps locate the facial nerve during translabyrinthine dissection. Hyrtl fissure (tympanomeningeal hiatus) is an embryologic channel from hypotympanum to subarachnoid space that can carry otitic infection or CSF. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 339–340, 379)

**Arrest-week timeline**: Pasha ties each malformation to the gestational week of arrest: Michel aplasia (week 3), common cavity (week 4), cochlear aplasia (week 5), cochlear hypoplasia (week 6), and Mondini/incomplete partition (week 7), with normal development by week 8. Earlier arrest means more severe deformity and worse hearing; first-trimester teratogens (in utero infection, radiation, aminoglycosides, thalidomide) or genetic errors are the usual causes. Michel aplasia contraindicates cochlear implantation, whereas Mondini and other cochlear deformities do not. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 340, 360)

**Hair-cell innervation numbers**: Inner hair cells (one row) get about 95% of cochlear afferents via myelinated type I bipolar neurons, with 10–20 fibers converging on each inner hair cell. Outer hair cells (three rows) get only about 5% via unmyelinated type II pseudomonopolar fibers, with one fiber serving about 10 outer hair cells, but receive most of the olivocochlear efferent input. Outer hair cells are tightly coupled to the tectorial membrane, generate OAEs, and are more vulnerable to noise and ototoxins. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 344–345)

**Resonance and localization numbers**: Natural resonances: concha 4–6 kHz, ear canal 2–3 kHz (speech range), tympanic membrane 0.8–1.6 kHz, ossicles 0.5–2 kHz (basis of the Carhart notch), middle ear about 800 Hz. Localization uses interaural level differences above about 2 kHz (head shadow of 5–15 dB) and interaural time differences of up to about 0.6 ms carried by low frequencies. Primary auditory cortex is Heschl transverse temporal gyrus (Brodmann 41), with association cortex in area 42; the E COLI mnemonic gives the ascending order (eighth nerve, cochlear nucleus, superior olive, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus). (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 346)

**Degree of hearing loss and masking numbers**: Adult degree categories used by Pasha: ≤25 dB normal, 26–40 mild, 41–55 moderate, 56–70 moderately severe, 71–90 severe, ≥91 profound. Interaural attenuation is about 70 dB for insert earphones, about 40 dB for supra-aural earphones, and 0 dB for bone conduction. The maximal pure conductive loss is about 60 dB (as with ossicular discontinuity behind an intact drum); a gap beyond that implies a sensorineural component. Rollover (word score falling at higher intensity) and tone decay suggest retrocochlear disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 349–350)

**Pseudohypacusis tests**: Clues: test–retest variability beyond 5 dB, SRT more than 10 dB better than the PTA, present acoustic reflexes despite claimed severe loss, and no crossover (shadow curve) in a claimed dead ear. The Stenger test presents the same tone to both ears, louder in the claimed bad ear; a malingerer denies hearing anything because the sound is perceived only in the louder ear. The Lombard test (voice rises when masking noise is added) and delayed auditory feedback (speech disrupted by hearing one's own delayed voice) also expose functional loss; ABR/ASSR confirm true thresholds. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 353–354)

**OAE types**: Spontaneous OAEs occur in only about half of normal ears, so they are not used for screening. Transient-evoked OAEs (click-evoked) are the newborn-screening test and are generally absent once cochlear thresholds exceed roughly 30 dB HL. Distortion-product OAEs (two primary tones; the 2f1–f2 product) are more frequency-specific at high frequencies, persist in some mild–moderate SNHL, and are used for ototoxicity and noise monitoring. Middle-ear disease, vernix, or cerumen can abolish OAEs without cochlear damage. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 352–353)

**ASSR, ECoG ratio, and ABR modifiers**: ASSR uses continuous amplitude/frequency-modulated tones to estimate frequency-specific thresholds and can measure losses beyond about 80 dB HL, where click ABR runs out of output. ECoG: an SP/AP ratio of about 0.45 or more (normal about 0.2) supports hydrops and is seen in roughly two-thirds of Ménière patients; a transtympanic promontory electrode is most accurate. ABR is not affected by sedation but can be altered by phenytoin, lidocaine, diazepam, and halothane, and may be unrecordable when SNHL exceeds about 60 dB; only waves I, III, and V are seen at birth. Intraoperatively, wave V amplitude/latency changes precede loss of wave V and then wave I. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 354–356)

**Hearing-aid styles by loss severity**: Behind-the-ear aids give enough gain for mild to profound loss; mini-BTE open-fit and receiver-in-canal designs are now the most common, but chronic otorrhea can destroy the in-canal receiver. In-the-ear aids suit moderate–severe loss; in-the-canal aids are feedback-limited to mild–moderately severe loss; completely-in-canal aids fit mild–severe loss and need less gain because they sit near the drum, but are hard to handle. Venting reduces the occlusion effect and moisture; binaural fitting is preferred for bilateral loss; assistive devices (FM, infrared, telecoil) improve signal-to-noise in specific settings. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 356–358)

**Implantable middle-ear devices**: Middle-ear implants drive the ossicular chain with an electromagnetic or piezoelectric actuator, partially or totally implanted, and are aimed at moderate–severe SNHL. They avoid occlusion effect and feedback but are costly, may need battery-change surgery, and carry facial nerve and chorda tympani risk. For single-sided deafness, a bone-conduction implant requires normal bone-conduction thresholds in the hearing ear and does not restore localization. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 358–359)

**Textbook candidacy numbers**: Pasha's criteria: children from 9 months (FDA labeling) with bilateral profound SNHL (severe–profound after about 18–24 months) and minimal hearing-aid benefit, implanted earlier after meningitis because of ossification risk. Children 5 years and older and adults may be implanted for single-sided deafness or asymmetric loss (profound loss in one ear, at least a 15-dB PTA difference). Ear choice: the more recently deafened ear if neither benefits from aids, the poorer ear if some benefit exists, but the better ear after long-standing deprivation. Contraindications include Michel aplasia, absent or sectioned cochlear nerve, active infection, and inability to participate in rehabilitation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 360)

**Device types including ABI**: Hybrid (electroacoustic) arrays are shorter/thinner to preserve apical low-frequency hearing for steep high-frequency loss; split (double) arrays serve ossified cochleae. The auditory brainstem implant places an electrode pad on the cochlear nucleus and is indicated in NF2, with cochlear nerve aplasia, Michel aplasia, and severe ossification as investigational indications. Up to 22 electrodes exist but only about 8–10 channels are functionally independent because of current spread; better outcomes come with short deafness duration, postlingual onset, and early implantation in children. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 360–361)

**Complication rates**: Wound problems (infection, flap breakdown) occur in about 1–2%; permanent facial nerve injury about 0.1%; meningitis under 0.1% in adults with normal cochleae (higher with malformations; vaccinate against pneumococcus). Gusher and aberrant facial stimulation are more frequent with malformations such as Mondini/incomplete partition. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 359–360)

**Non-vascular objective tinnitus**: Palatal myoclonus causes a rapid clicking (about 0.7–3.3 Hz) from rhythmic palatal/eustachian tube muscle contraction; confirm with awake nasopharyngoscopy or EMG, image the brain to exclude a central lesion, and try muscle relaxants. Tensor tympani or stapedius myoclonus produces low-pitched fluttering often triggered by sound, visible as rhythmic tympanometric change; manage with reassurance and stimulant avoidance, and only rarely tendon section. Pulsatile tinnitus from idiopathic intracranial hypertension classically occurs in young obese women, is often bilateral, may come with mild SNHL and CN VI palsy, and is confirmed by lumbar puncture opening pressure; treat with weight loss and acetazolamide. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 366–367)

**Masking parameters**: Hearing aids are the simplest direct masker when tinnitus accompanies hearing loss. Maskers use pitch-matched band noise; a minimal masking level above about 10–15 dB predicts poor success, and residual inhibition (quieting after 1 minute of masking) usually lasts seconds to minutes. Cochlear implantation for single-sided deafness reduces or abolishes tinnitus in a large majority of reported patients, and treating coexisting anxiety or depression lowers tinnitus impact. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 367–369)

**Otomycosis and chronic/eczematous otitis externa**: Otomycosis is mostly Aspergillus niger (black conidiophores on white hyphae), with Candida less often; treat with debridement and acidifying, drying, or antifungal drops, using gentian violet or cresyl acetate for refractory cases. Chronic otitis externa is defined as lasting more than 6 weeks, often with dry, flaky, itchy skin from dermatitis or psoriasis; manage with cleaning, topical steroid (with nystatin if fungal), dermatology input, and canalplasty with split-thickness skin graft for recalcitrant stenosing disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 370–371)

**Nuclear imaging roles and prognosis**: Pasha separates the scans: technetium-99m bone scan shows osteoblastic activity and helps establish the diagnosis early but stays positive long after cure, whereas gallium-67 (or indium-111 WBC) scanning reflects active inflammation and normalizes with resolution, so it is used to follow treatment. Cranial nerve involvement runs CN VII, then X, then XI; mortality is about 10–20%. Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for refractory disease and surgical debridement for failed medical therapy or abscess. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 371–372)

**Mastoidectomy variants**: Canal-wall-up preserves the posterior/superior canal for a water-safe ear but has higher residual/recurrent disease risk and needs a second look or non-echo-planar DWI. Canal-wall-down (modified radical) suits eroded canal wall, lateral semicircular canal fistula, extensive or recurrent disease, unreliable follow-up, or an only-hearing ear, at the cost of cavity care and caloric vertigo with wind or water. The Bondy modified radical leaves an intact drum and ossicles for attic/mastoid disease with good hearing; a radical mastoidectomy exteriorizes the middle ear, closes the eustachian tube, and does not reconstruct. Priority order: a safe, dry ear first, hearing second. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 376–377)

**Atypical chronic otitis and aural polyp**: Tuberculous otitis media presents with painless, odorless, scant drainage, multiple small perforations, and pale granulation, usually from a pulmonary source; GPA can present with granulation, effusion, mixed loss, and facial palsy. An aural polyp signals underlying middle-ear disease (tube, cholesteatoma, foreign body, malignancy); biopsy unclear polyps and treat with debridement, silver nitrate, and steroid–antibiotic drops, with persistence prompting excisional biopsy. Myringosclerosis is drum-only and does not affect hearing; tympanosclerosis in the middle ear can fix the ossicles. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 375, 387–388)

**Underlay versus overlay**: Medial (underlay) grafting under the annulus and drum remnant is quicker, technically easier, and sufficient for most, especially posterior, perforations. Lateral (overlay) grafting suits large or anterior perforations but takes longer and risks anterior blunting, lateralization, entry into the glenoid fossa, and more postoperative conductive loss. Temporalis fascia is the most common graft; cartilage, perichondrium, fat, and acellular dermis are alternatives. A perforation gives a flat tympanogram with canal volume above about 1.5 mL. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 377–378, 388)

**Reconstruction options and targets**: The incus lenticular/long process is the most common erosion site because of its tenuous blood supply. Options: incudostapedial joint prosthesis or hydroxyapatite bone cement for a small gap, sculpted autologous incus, PORP to an intact stapes capitulum (target air-bone gap ≤20 dB), and TORP to the footplate (target ≤30 dB), with cartilage between prosthesis and drum to prevent extrusion. Cadaveric homograft ossicles have largely been abandoned in the US because of disease-transmission concerns; always check for lateral chain fixation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 378)

**Named abscess sites and high-risk organisms**: Postauricular subperiosteal abscess is most common. Extratemporal spread: Bezold abscess beneath the sternocleidomastoid from the tip, Citelli abscess along the digastric groove, and Luc abscess at the zygomatic root deep to temporalis. Mastoid fluid on CT alone is not mastoiditis; coalescence requires loss of bony septa. High-risk organisms for complications are type III pneumococcus (intracranial predilection), H. influenzae type B, and coexisting anaerobes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 379–380)

**Nystagmus direction by labyrinthitis type**: Serous (toxic) labyrinthitis gives irritative nystagmus beating toward the affected ear with usually recoverable hearing, while suppurative bacterial labyrinthitis destroys function, so nystagmus beats away, hearing loss is typically permanent, and labyrinthitis ossificans or meningitis can follow. Syphilitic labyrinthitis may show Tullio and Hennebert signs. Viral labyrinthitis differs from vestibular neuritis by the presence of hearing loss. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 383–384)

**Classic signs and differential**: About 10% of white adults have histologic otosclerosis but under 1% become clinical; tinnitus is common (about 80%), and paracusis of Willis (hearing better in noise) is classic. Histology of active foci shows blue mantles of Manasse; CT shows fissula hypodensity, and cochlear otosclerosis gives a pericochlear halo (double ring). Mimics: congenital stapes fixation (present from birth, larger gap, ossicular and facial nerve anomalies, CT to exclude inner-ear malformation), osteogenesis imperfecta/van der Hoeve (blue sclerae, fractures), and Paget disease (whole skull, raised alkaline phosphatase, rarely the footplate). Sodium fluoride and bisphosphonates are controversial medical options. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 389–391)

**Indications, outcomes, and intraoperative surprises**: Typical indications are an air-bone gap of at least 25 dB with a negative 512-Hz Rinne, good bone conduction and word recognition; do the poorer ear first and wait 6–12 months before the second. Expect about 90% gap closure within 10 dB, roughly 1% worse and 1% dead ear; revisions succeed about 65% of the time with higher SNHL risk. A persistent stapedial artery (with absent middle meningeal artery) may be worked around if the posterior footplate is free, otherwise abort; after separating the incudostapedial joint, always test for lateral (malleus/incus) chain fixation, which needs mobilization or ossiculoplasty rather than stapedotomy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 391–392)

**Glasscock-Jackson staging and named signs**: Glasscock-Jackson tympanicum: I promontory only, II fills middle ear, III into mastoid, IV into mastoid/canal and anterior to the carotid. Jugulare: I jugular bulb/middle ear/mastoid, II under the IAC, III into petrous apex, IV clivus or infratemporal fossa (any with or without intracranial extension). Signs: Brown sign (blanching with positive pressure), Aquino sign (pulsation fades with carotid compression), and Collet-Sicard (IX–XII) or Villaret (IX–XII plus sympathetics) syndromes; CT erosion of the caroticojugular spine indicates a jugular tumor. Consider DOTATATE PET for multicentric disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 393–394)

**Presentation details**: Asymmetric high-frequency SNHL is the usual presentation, but 10–20% present with sudden SNHL. The Hitselberger sign is reduced sensation of the posterosuperior canal and concha from pressure on CN VII sensory fibers; clinically significant facial weakness occurs in under 5% of vestibular schwannomas, versus over half of facial nerve schwannomas. Histology shows dense Antoni A (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas; about 95% are sporadic and 5% NF2-related. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 395, 427, 434)

**Natural history and surveillance interval**: Average growth is about 1–2 mm per year and roughly half of small tumors do not grow for long periods, though hearing can decline without growth. Pasha's observation schedule: MRI every 6 months for the first year, then yearly for 2 years, then every other year indefinitely; observation is typical for tumors under about 1.5 cm, and radiosurgery is usually offered for growing tumors under about 2.5 cm. Radiation risks include delayed hearing loss years later and very rare malignant change (<0.1%). (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 395–396)

**Non-schwannoma CPA lesions**: Meningioma is the second most common CPA tumor (about 3–15%), female predominant, eccentric to the IAC with calcification, hyperostosis, and dural tail; histology shows whorls and psammoma bodies. Epidermoid (CPA cholesteatoma) causes more cranial neuropathy and headache than hearing loss and can rupture into aseptic meningitis; arachnoid cyst mimics it on T1/T2 but does not restrict diffusion. Venous malformation (old 'hemangioma') of CN VII favors the IAC and geniculate, causes facial weakness disproportionate to size, and shows stippled calcification and irregular margins on CT. Metastases come from breast, lung, prostate, and melanoma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 396–397)

**Endolymphatic sac tumor**: A low-grade papillary adenocarcinoma arising from the endolymphatic sac behind the labyrinth; it often mimics Ménière disease (SNHL, vertigo, fullness) and is sporadic or part of von Hippel-Lindau disease, in which bilateral tumors occur. Treatment is gross total resection; the role of radiation is undefined. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 400)

**Approach tradeoffs**: Translabyrinthine: most direct, minimal cerebellar retraction, early facial nerve identification, but sacrifices hearing, has a higher CSF leak rate, is limited by a high jugular bulb or anterior sigmoid, and is contraindicated with active otitis. Retrosigmoid: any size, early brainstem view, hearing preservable, but more postoperative headache and limited lateral IAC access. Middle fossa: intracanalicular tumors under about 1 cm with serviceable hearing, but temporal lobe retraction and more transient facial weakness. Retrolabyrinthine preserves hearing but gives little IAC exposure; it is used mainly for vestibular nerve section or combined petrosal approaches. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 397–398)

**Cystic apex lesion signal table**: Mucocele: expansile, T1 low/T2 bright, nonenhancing. Apicitis: irregular non-expansile erosion, T1 low/T2 bright, enhancing. Cholesteatoma: expansile, T1 low/T2 bright, nonenhancing, restricts diffusion. Cholesterol granuloma: expansile, bright on T1 and T2, contains brown 'motor oil' fluid. Chondrosarcoma arises off midline at the petrooccipital synchondrosis, unlike midline chordoma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 398)

**Fibro-osseous, histiocytic, and uveitic disorders**: Fibrous dysplasia replaces temporal bone marrow with ground-glass fibro-osseous tissue, narrowing the canal (canal cholesteatoma risk) and rarely the otic capsule; McCune-Albright adds precocious puberty and café-au-lait spots. Langerhans cell histiocytosis mimics chronic otitis with granulation and otorrhea. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome resembles Cogan syndrome (hearing loss and vertigo) but with granulomatous uveitis, poliosis/vitiligo, and aseptic meningitis; Cogan's keratitis is nonsyphilitic and interstitial. Middle-ear adenoma presents with conductive loss and is cured by excision. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 399, 420)

**OSHA and acoustic trauma numbers**: OSHA requires a hearing conservation program at an 8-hour average of 85 dBA; the permissible exposure limit is 90 dBA for 8 hours, halving with every 5-dB increase (95 for 4 h, 100 for 2 h, 105 for 1 h); NIOSH is stricter. Temporary threshold shift usually recovers within 24 hours. The stapedial reflex has about 10 ms latency, so it cannot protect against impulse noise; a rifle injures the ear opposite the shooting arm. Single exposures above about 140 dB cause acoustic trauma with permanent shift, and above about 180 dB can rupture the drum or fracture ossicles. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 403–404)

**Drug-specific patterns**: Streptomycin and gentamicin are mainly vestibulotoxic, and aminoglycoside cochleotoxicity starts above 8 kHz; vancomycin and loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid) potentiate aminoglycoside injury. Cisplatin damages outer hair cells, stria, spiral ganglion, and vestibular system. Aspirin is the most common drug cause of tinnitus and is reversible; antimalarials (quinine, chloroquine) are also ototoxic. Monitoring with high-frequency audiometry or OAEs allows early detection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 362, 404)

**Steroid trial length**: Pasha recommends a high-dose oral steroid trial of at least 30 days with serial audiograms; response supports the diagnosis, and rheumatology can add steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, cyclophosphamide). Up to half of patients have vestibular symptoms, women aged 20–50 predominate, and serologies (including the 68-kD inner-ear antigen) do not correlate with outcome. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 403)

**Caloric and rotary-chair interpretation**: Calorics: head up 30° to make the horizontal semicircular canal vertical; a side-to-side difference over about 20–25% is unilateral weakness, and a directional preponderance means nystagmus one way exceeds the other. Total slow-phase velocity for all four irrigations below roughly 12–24°/s indicates bilateral weakness; failure of fixation suppression suggests a central lesion. Rotary chair: gain is eye/chair velocity (normal about 1); an acute unilateral loss gives low-frequency phase lead with high-frequency asymmetry, and loss of asymmetry signals compensation; bilateral loss lowers low-frequency gain. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 412–414)

**Bedside and functional tests**: Dynamic visual acuity drops 2–3 Snellen lines with 2-Hz head oscillation when the VOR fails; head-thrust is abnormal with more than about 50% reduced response. Fukuda stepping, Romberg, and past-pointing assess vestibulospinal function; Frenzel lenses remove fixation. Posturography quantifies function rather than localizing, and better scores on harder conditions suggest malingering. Cervical VEMP uses about 95 dB clicks and records the saccule–inferior vestibular nerve–SCM pathway; superior canal dehiscence lowers its threshold by roughly 20 dB. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 409–410, 414)

**Other maneuvers and surgery**: Semont (liberatory) is an alternative to Epley for posterior canal disease; Brandt-Daroff exercises work through habituation. Dix-Hallpike nystagmus has a 2–15 s latency and lasts 10–60 s; posterior canal is involved about 90%. For intractable cases, posterior semicircular canal occlusion has largely replaced singular (posterior ampullary) neurectomy and vestibular nerve section. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 412, 415–416)

**Variants and bilaterality**: Cochlear hydrops has hearing loss, fullness, and tinnitus without vertigo; vestibular hydrops has episodic vertigo without auditory symptoms. Lermoyez syndrome is worsening hearing and tinnitus that improve abruptly after a vertigo attack; Tumarkin otolithic crisis is a sudden drop attack without loss of consciousness. Delayed endolymphatic hydrops follows an earlier profound loss in one ear with later Ménière symptoms. Disease becomes bilateral in about 25–30%, and the glycerol dehydration test (rarely used) improves hearing in active hydrops. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 417–418)

**Surgical options with success rates**: About 10–15% of patients need surgery. Endolymphatic sac decompression or shunt preserves hearing and balance with low morbidity, with 60–80% vertigo control (close to the spontaneous remission rate). Vestibular nerve section via craniotomy spares hearing and controls vertigo in about 90%. Labyrinthectomy controls vertigo in up to about 90% but is limited to nonserviceable hearing (worse than about 50–60 dB or <50% word recognition) and is avoided if the other labyrinth is weak or contralateral disease is likely. Diet: sodium below about 1.5 g/day with even meal spacing. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 418–419)

**Posterior-circulation syndromes**: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome from vertebral or PICA occlusion: acute vertigo and nystagmus, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral limb ataxia, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, with hearing spared. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency gives brief vertigo with neck extension or rotation plus the '4 Ds' (dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, drop attacks). Subclavian steal causes vertigo with arm use, an interarm blood pressure difference, and a weak radial pulse. Multiple sclerosis presents with vertigo in about 10–15%. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 421–423)

**Segment dimensions and dehiscence**: Meatal segment about 8–10 mm; labyrinthine segment about 4 mm long and 0.61–0.68 mm wide (narrowest, at the meatal foramen); tympanic segment about 11 mm and the most common site of dehiscence (40–50%) and of iatrogenic injury; mastoid segment about 13 mm. The chorda enters the middle ear via the iter chordae posterius and exits via the iter chordae anterius (canal of Huguier); the pes anserinus usually splits into temporozygomatic and cervicofacial divisions. In the IAC, 'seven-up, Coke down' and cochlear nerve anterior ('business in front'). (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 423–424, 433)

**Electrodiagnostic timing details**: ENoG is only meaningful in complete (HB VI) paralysis and not until Wallerian degeneration has occurred (after about 24–72 hours); it compares compound action potential amplitude with the normal side. EMG shows fibrillations 1–2 weeks after denervation and polyphasic potentials with reinnervation; any voluntary motor units mean some nerve continuity. Older tests: nerve excitability test (side difference ≥3.5 mA is significant) and maximal stimulation test are subjective and rarely used; topognostic tests (Schirmer, stapedial reflex, salivary flow) have been replaced. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 427–430)

**Bell, Ramsay Hunt, Lyme and Melkersson-Rosenthal prognosis**: Bell palsy: about 70–85% recover fully by 6 months, 7–12% recur, and any residual movement predicts a good outcome; decompression (middle fossa, covering meatal foramen, labyrinthine segment, and geniculate) is considered only for >90% ENoG degeneration with no voluntary EMG activity within 2 weeks. Ramsay Hunt leaves residual weakness in 30–50%. Lyme disease involves the facial nerve in about 10% (sometimes bilaterally) and typically recovers fully over 6–12 months with antibiotics. Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is recurrent facial edema, recurrent facial palsy, and fissured tongue starting in youth, with granulomas on lip biopsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 430–432)

**Traumatic and iatrogenic injury**: Complete paralysis after a penetrating facial wound should be explored and repaired within about 48–72 hours, while distal branches can still be stimulated; injuries medial to a vertical line through the lateral canthus usually recover without repair. With contamination or tissue loss, tag the ends and repair in a second stage at about 3–4 weeks. For paralysis noticed right after ear surgery, wait 2–3 hours for local anesthetic to wear off; if the nerve was seen intact, give steroids and follow electrically, and consider re-exploration for complete paralysis in selected cases. Delayed-onset or incomplete weakness usually recovers fully. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 433)

**Neoplastic and neurologic causes**: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the parotid tumor most often causing facial palsy (by prevalence), though adenoid cystic has the highest perineural rate. Facial nerve schwannoma presents with paralysis or spasm in over half of cases. Guillain-Barré is a common cause of acute bilateral facial palsy; myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness with ptosis; stroke spares the forehead. Möbius syndrome and myotonic dystrophy are congenital/hereditary causes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 427–428, 433–434)

**Ceiling of nerve repair and eye-protection cautions**: The best expected result after any nerve repair or graft is about House-Brackmann III, so counsel accordingly. Primary coaptation is ideally done within about 3 days, while distal branches still respond to stimulation; cable grafts typically restore tone and some spontaneous expression. Gold or platinum lid loads can be used for reversible or permanent paralysis but can extrude or migrate; tarsorrhaphy protects the eye at the cost of visual field and cosmesis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 434–436)

**Dimensions and orientation**: The adult tube is about 35 mm: the bony one-third opens into the middle ear, and the cartilaginous two-thirds ends at the torus tubarius. It angles about 45° in adults, but in infants it is about half as long and only about 10° from horizontal, favoring reflux and otitis. The tensor veli palatini (CN V3) is the main dilator; the salpingopharyngeus helps keep it closed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 339–340)

**Conservative regimen and fistula test sensitivity**: Initial care is bed rest with head elevation and strain avoidance (open-mouth sneezing, stool softeners) for about 5–10 days, with exploration and window grafting reserved for persistent symptoms or progressive hearing loss. The Hennebert fistula test is only about 10–40% sensitive, and there is no definitive preoperative test. Labyrinthine concussion (posttraumatic vertigo and SNHL without fracture) is a self-limited mimic that may leave BPPV. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 419–420)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Healing timeline numbers**: neutrophils arrive within about 6 hours and peak at 24–48 hours; macrophages (the essential cell, recruiting fibroblasts via PDGF) dominate by 48–96 hours; fibroblasts appear by about 48 hours and peak around day 15. Granulation tissue begins near day 4, type III collagen peaks at about 3 weeks with conversion to type I beginning then, and wound contraction by myofibroblasts is maximal at 12–15 days. Proline/lysine hydroxylation in collagen synthesis needs vitamin C and iron. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 441–442)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Tensile strength milestones**: a closed wound has about 3% of normal strength at 1 week, ~20% at 3 weeks, ~60% at 5–6 weeks, and plateaus at 70–80% by about 3 months; remodeling continues ~12 months but never reaches normal skin. Fetal skin heals without scar (less TGF-beta, more MMP activity). Collagen typing: I = bone/tendon/mature scar, II = hyaline cartilage, III = early scar/granulation tissue and vessels, IV = basement membrane. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 442–443)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Wound infection threshold and nutrition labs**: a wound is considered infected when quantitative culture exceeds 10^5 organisms per gram of tissue. Assess nutrition with albumin, prealbumin, transferrin, total lymphocyte count and nitrogen balance; loss of ~20% lean body mass, vitamin A/C/zinc deficiency and hypothyroidism all impair healing. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 443)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Hyperbaric oxygen**: 100% oxygen at about 2.5 atmospheres boosts oxygen delivery, fibroblast/macrophage activity and VEGF-driven angiogenesis for hypoxic wounds, radiation injury and compromised flaps.
