Absolute contraindications are untreated pneumothorax and certain drugs (cisplatin, doxorubicin, bleomycin, disulfiram); relative ones include eustachian tube dysfunction, seizure disorder, COPD/emphysematous blebs, pregnancy and claustrophobia. Complications include middle ear barotrauma (tubes may be needed first), seizures and oxygen lung toxicity. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 444)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Negative-pressure wound therapy**: wound VAC promotes granulation and angiogenesis, debrides, drains and lowers bacterial load; it can bolster a skin graft or rescue distal scalp flap loss but is contraindicated over exposed dura. Dakin's (hypochlorite), peroxide or povidone-iodine dressings aid local debridement. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 443–444)

**Material specifics**: porous polyethylene (Medpor) has interconnected 100–200 micron pores allowing soft-tissue ingrowth; ePTFE (Gore-Tex) allows limited ingrowth and can extrude; silicone becomes encapsulated with no ingrowth and has a high nasal extrusion rate; PMMA is rigid and molded in situ without ingrowth; titanium osseointegrates. Resorbable PLA/PGA plates last about 1 year (useful in children). Bone grafts need bone-to-bone contact and 8–12 weeks of immobility; cancellous bone carries more osteoblasts, cortical bone gives strength and BMPs. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 461–464)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Flap vascular classification**: random flaps ride the subdermal plexus fed by musculocutaneous perforators (about 3:1 length:width), whereas axial flaps follow a named direct cutaneous vessel. Mathes–Nahai muscle flap types: I one pedicle (tensor fascia lata), II dominant plus minor (gracilis), III two dominant (gluteus maximus), IV segmental (sartorius), V dominant plus segmental (latissimus); types I, III and V are most reliable. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 445–446)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Mandibular reconstruction rules**: anterior defects carry the most morbidity and are hardest to reconstruct; defects over 5 cm have about 10-fold more complications. Nonvascularized bone grafts are limited to defects under ~6 cm (failure ~75% above that) and are contraindicated with radiation or anterior defects. A plate with soft-tissue flap alone suits small posterior defects in frail patients but extrudes or fractures (failures within ~18 months), especially anteriorly. High lateral defects may be left unreconstructed; a retained condyle-coronoid stump may need coronoidectomy to limit temporalis/pterygoid pull. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 477–478)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Innervated flap pairings**: radial forearm (lateral antebrachial cutaneous to lingual nerve) for oral sensation; anterolateral thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous to lingual, or motor nerve to vastus to hypoglossal) or rectus (intercostal nerves) for glossectomy; gracilis (anterior branch of obturator nerve) for facial reanimation. Denervated muscle shrinks to about 20% of its bulk and transferred fat to 40–60%. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 446–447, 455)

**Free-flap numbers**: failure is under 5%, mostly in the first 24–72 hours, and about 50–75% of compromised flaps are salvaged on re-exploration. Tolerated warm ischemia: jejunum ~2 hours, bone ~6 hours, skin ~8 hours; the no-reflow phenomenon sets in around 12 hours. Neovascularization from the bed is complete by about 10 days, except jejunum, whose serosa prevents ingrowth so its pedicle can never be sacrificed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 455, 459)

**Anastomosis pearls**: handle only adventitia, keep adventitia out of the lumen, avoid endarterectomy of plaque (intimal injury causes thrombosis), and avoid hypothermia, hypovolemia and hypotension. Arteries are usually end-to-end; veins end-to-end or end-to-side. For a size mismatch over 2:1, fishmouth the smaller vessel or use end-to-side (up to ~3:1). Aspirin for 7–10 days postop is an option. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 455–456)

**Named geometric flaps**: the classic rhombic (Limberg) flap uses 60° and 120° angles with equal sides, placing maximal tension away from the defect; the Dufourmentel variant uses more acute angles for a broader base. Rotation flaps need a peripheral incision about 4–5 times the defect diameter and may use a back-cut or Burow's triangle. A-to-T (O-to-T) closure hides scars along the hairline, brow or upper lip; V–Y advancement lengthens tissue (lip, columella). Elliptical excisions need about 3–4:1 length:width with ~30° apices. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 447–450, 520)

**Tissue expansion**: conventional expansion (weekly fills over 4–6+ weeks, starting 2–3 weeks after placement) relies on biologic creep, which truly adds surface area; rapid intraoperative expansion (about three 3-minute cycles) relies on mechanical creep and gains no net area, only recruitment. The base should be ~2.5 times the defect, rectangular expanders yield the most (~38% vs ~25% round), and fat may lose up to 50% of its mass permanently. Remote ports essentially eliminate rupture risk; external ports avoid painful injections in children. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 464–466)

**STSG thickness and contraction numbers**: thin (Thiersch) STSG 0.008–0.012 inch, medium 0.012–0.018, thick 0.018–0.030; FTSG includes all dermis. Primary contraction (up to ~20%) is greater in FTSG; secondary contraction is greater in STSG and worse on granulation tissue or mobile areas, less on fascia. FTSG adheres by fibrin in ~24 hours, survives by imbibition for ~72 hours, and has restored flow within about a week. Melolabial skin is a thick FTSG donor for nasal tip/ala. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 462–463)

**Hughes and Tenzel details**: the Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap takes posterior lamella from the upper lid to rebuild the lower lid, leaving at least 4 mm of upper tarsus at the lid margin to avoid upper lid instability; it is covered by a skin flap or graft and divided at 2–6 weeks. The Tenzel semicircular flap with cantholysis covers defects up to ~75%. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 467)

**Canthal and lid anatomy**: horizontal support (canthal tendons) is the strongest support system. The medial canthal tendon attaches to anterior and posterior lacrimal crests (posterior limb via Horner muscle); the lateral canthal tendon inserts on Whitnall's lateral orbital tubercle. Upper lid margin rests 3–4 mm above the pupil center covering the superior limbus, with a crease 6–12 mm above the lashes (lower or absent in many East Asian lids); the lower lid sits at the inferior limbus. Mobility is the priority in upper lid reconstruction. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 466, 493)

**Defect-by-region rules**: conchal bowl defects heal by second intention or FTSG if perichondrium is intact (cartilage loss here causes no deformity). Helical rim is the site of about half of auricular skin cancers; wedge excision is acceptable for defects under ~15% of height (~2 cm), using a star-shaped wedge to avoid cupping, and up to 15% height asymmetry is not noticed. Lobule defects should never get STSG alone (contracture) and an auriculomastoid flap should be designed ~30% larger. Larger rim loss can use a tubed postauricular flap (3 stages), Antia-Buch advancement, or a contralateral composite graft. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 467–469)

**Nasal flap selection by skin and size**: thin-skinned upper nose suits FTSG; thick-skinned defects under ~1.5 cm suit a bilobed or nasalis myocutaneous flap, and larger ones need a regional flap. The dorsal nasal (Rieger) glabellar rotation-advancement flap handles mid-dorsal and tip defects in one stage. A superiorly based nasolabial flap reconstructs the ala/lower lateral nose, while an inferiorly based one serves the upper lip, nasal sill and columella. Lining options include septal hinge flaps (middle third), bipedicled vestibular flaps (lower third), turbinate flaps, and pericranium with a forehead flap. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 469–471)

**Lip reconstruction by defect size**: primary closure works for up to about one quarter of the upper lip or one third of the lower lip (V or W excision). For 1/3–2/3 defects: Abbe (central, two-stage, pedicle divided at ~2–3 weeks) or Estlander (commissure, single-stage) cross-lip flaps sized at the defect's full height but half its width, based on the labial artery. Karapandzic bilateral advancement keeps neurovascular supply and oral competence but risks microstomia; the Gillies fan flap gives more tissue but is denervated. For over 2/3 loss: Bernard–Burow cheek advancement (Webster variant for upper lip), bilateral nasolabial flaps, or a radial forearm free flap with a palmaris tendon sling. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 473–476)

**Lip anatomy pearls**: the modiolus lateral to the commissure is the convergence point of facial expression muscles; precise realignment of the white roll/vermilion border is key to cosmesis. Upper lip lymphatics do not cross midline and also reach preauricular/infraparotid nodes, while lower lip lymphatics cross midline to submental/submandibular nodes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 473)

**Cheek subunit principles**: lateral (preauricular) cheek skin is fixed to SMAS over the parotid and closes primarily only for defects under ~1 cm; medial cheek tolerates larger primary closure or V–Y island advancement into the perialar area. In the zygomatic subunit use M-plasty to avoid pulling the lateral canthus, and design infraorbital incisions to avoid ectropion. Elevate in the sub-SMAS plane only lateral to the zygomaticus major to protect facial nerve branches. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 476–477)

**Dedo cervical classification**: I youthful neck; II skin laxity; III excess fat; IV platysmal banding; V microgenia/retrognathia; VI low hyoid. Turkey-gobbler neck is loss of the cervicomental angle (over 120°) from failed platysmal decussation; ptotic submandibular glands are addressed with a platysmal sling. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 480, 501)

**Photography and reference lines**: Frankfort horizontal (top of tragus/EAC to infraorbital rim) orients all photos; use a 90–105 mm lens (35 mm equivalent), blue background and two lights at 45°. Rhinoplasty set: frontal, both laterals, both obliques, base and smiling lateral. The ideal chin lies on the Gonzalez-Ulloa zero meridian, a line through nasion perpendicular to Frankfort horizontal. Nasal ratios: columella:base:dorsum about 3:4:5, 2–3 mm columellar show, basal view isosceles triangle with columella 2/3 and lobule 1/3. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 480–483, 507)

**Nasolabial angle norms differ by source**: site states ~90–95° (men) and 95–110° (women); Pasha gives ~90–100° (men) and ~100–110° (women), with nasofrontal angle 115–135°. Teach the range and the sex difference rather than a single number. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 482)

**Poor aesthetic candidates and premature-aging syndromes**: unrealistic expectations, many prior surgeons, psychiatric instability, and smoking (over 12-fold skin slough risk). Cutis laxa (autosomal recessive, loose skin, hernias, emphysema) benefits from rhytidectomy; progeria and Werner syndrome do not. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 480, 500–501)

**Endonasal approach options**: nondelivery (cartilage-splitting via intracartilaginous incision, or retrograde via intercartilaginous incision) allows conservative cephalic trim with no major support disruption; delivery (intercartilaginous + marginal incisions) brings out the lower lateral cartilage as a bipedicled chondrocutaneous flap but divides the scroll, a major support. Open approach (marginal + transcolumellar) preserves major support but sacrifices the skin envelope attachment (minor). A complete transfixion incision releases medial crural–septal attachment and lowers projection. Preserve at least 6–10 mm of lateral crus to prevent alar collapse/notching. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 483–485)

**Projection and rotation maneuvers**: shield graft adds ~1–2 mm projection; a columellar strut supports but does not increase projection; plumping grafts at the columellar base open the nasolabial angle (illusion of projection). Rotation rises with caudal septal trim, lateral crural shortening/overlay, or lateral crural steal; decreases with caudal septal excision near the spine or dorsal augmentation (apparent). Tongue-in-groove fixes medial crura to the caudal septum to correct hanging columella or excess show. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 486–488)

**Osteotomy sequence and post-op care**: medial osteotomies first (free nasal bones from the perpendicular plate), then lateral 'high-low-high' osteotomies along the nasomaxillary groove, preserving a triangle of bone at the piriform aperture (Webster triangle) above the inferior turbinate to protect the airway and staying away from the lacrimal crest; intermediate osteotomy for excess convexity. Spreader grafts prevent inverted-V and middle-vault collapse, especially with short nasal bones. External splint off at ~7 days, intranasal splints 5–7 days. Revision rate is 8–15% and revision is usually delayed about 1 year. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 487–488)

**Late deformities and fixes**: pollybeak (supratip fullness) from under-resected dorsal septum, over-resected dorsum with dead-space scar in thick skin, or tip ptosis — early triamcinolone and taping, later resect or support the tip. Inverted-V from upper lateral cartilage separation/collapse — spreader grafts. Saddle from over-resection, trauma, cocaine, GPA or relapsing polychondritis — osteotomies for mild, dorsal onlay for severe. Bossae from dome scarring in thin skin; parenthesis tip from cephalically positioned lateral crura. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 488–490)

**Other auricular deformities and thresholds**: a protruding ear has an auriculocephalic angle over 40° (normal 25–35°, rim 15–20 mm from mastoid; height ~6 cm adult, ~20° posterior tilt). Cryptotia buries the upper auricle under mastoid skin (Z-plasty/skin graft, or cartilage graft if severe). Cup/constricted ear has a tight helix and scapha needing helical-scaphoid release. Associated syndromes include Treacher Collins, hemifacial microsomia/Goldenhar, CHARGE and Down. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 491)

**Farrior technique and complications**: Farrior combines posterior cartilage wedge excision with mattress sutures. Reverse telephone deformity is undercorrection of the middle third or overcorrection of upper pole and lobule; telephone ear is fixed by anchoring helical root to temporalis fascia and/or conchomastoid grafting. Best timing is age 5–6 when the ear is ~85% of adult size. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 492)

**Eyelid exam numbers**: MRD-1 normally 3–4 mm and MRD-2 about 5 mm; levator excursion normally 12–17 mm; upper lid crease ~10 mm (tarsal plate 8–9 mm upper, 4–5 mm lower). Schirmer test under 5 mm wetting in 5 minutes with anesthetic is abnormal; Bell's phenomenon is present in ~80%. Brow ptosis (male brow at the rim, female above it) must be corrected first or upper blepharoplasty will worsen it. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 493, 495–496)

**Operative sequence and lower lid approaches**: brow first, then upper lid, then lower lid. Mark upper lid skin by pinch upright and leave at least ~20 mm of lid skin to prevent lagophthalmos. Lower lid: skin–muscle flap (most common), skin-only flap (more retraction risk), or transconjunctival (fat excess with little skin, no external scar, less retraction). Fat can be repositioned over the rim into the SOOF to avoid hollowing. Upper lid has two fat pads (medial, central) with lacrimal gland laterally; lower lid has three, with the inferior oblique between medial and central. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 494, 496–497)

**Blepharoplasty complications**: milia are most common (cautery/unroof). Blindness from retrobulbar hemorrhage, usually after lower lid fat removal, can occur up to ~5 days and is heralded by pain — lateral canthotomy/cantholysis. Ectropion: conservative first, then lid-tightening or FTSG (upper lid skin best). Medial incisions within ~1 mm of the punctum create webbing (Z-plasty). Most common residual fat pocket is lateral lower lid; chemosis resolves in ~6 weeks; diplopia from inferior rectus/superior oblique injury usually resolves by 6 months. Blepharochalasis (recurrent inflammatory lid edema in young patients) differs from dermatochalasis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 494, 497–499)

**Resurfacing lasers**: CO2 (10,600 nm, water chromophore) ablates ~20–60 microns per pass, re-epithelializes in ~8 days with 3–6 months of erythema and more collagen tightening; hypopigmentation is its most common complication. Er:YAG (2940 nm) has 12–18 times more water absorption, ablates 3–5 microns, heals in ~5 days with 3–4 weeks of erythema and less tightening. Dermabrasion stops at the papillary dermis (pinpoint bleeding) and must spare the reticular layer's adnexa; pretreat with tretinoin and give antiviral prophylaxis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 508–510)

**Filler specifics**: hyaluronic acid lasts ~6–12 months and is reversible with hyaluronidase; calcium hydroxyapatite (Radiesse) is deep dermal, lasts ~12 months and has no reversal agent; poly-L-lactic acid (Sculptra) stimulates collagen over multiple sessions and is used for HIV lipoatrophy; PMMA (Bellafill/ArteFill) is permanent. Vascular compromise presents with pain and blanching or a violaceous pattern away from the site; treat within 24–48 hours with hyaluronidase, warm compresses, massage, aspirin and nitropaste. Delayed nodules may respond to triamcinolone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 513–515)

**Neuromodulator technique**: Dysport to Botox dose ratio is about 2.5:1 (Dysport spreads more and starts sooner). Inject frontalis at least ~2 cm above the brow; corrugator belly/tail for vertical glabellar lines, procerus for horizontal; crow's feet ~1 cm lateral to the orbital rim (medial spread causes lid ptosis, treated with apraclonidine); perioral within 5 mm of vermilion ('lip flip'). Avoid rubbing for several hours after injection. Phenol peel limits: under 25% of the face at a time with ~10-minute intervals. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 512, 516–517)

**Peel complications**: hyperpigmentation is the most common complication after TCA/superficial peels (sunscreen, hydroquinone, tretinoin); hypopigmentation is expected after deep phenol peels. HSV reactivation appears within about 24 hours (prophylactic antivirals). Phenol cannot be combined with an undermined rhytidectomy flap (necrosis) and is contraindicated on irradiated skin lacking adnexa. Milia peak about 1 month after dermabrasion. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 512–513)

**Norwood scale and candidate selection**: Norwood I–VII runs from minimal recession to a narrow horseshoe fringe (VI joins frontal and vertex loss). The best candidates have hair–skin color contrast that is low (blonde, gray, salt-and-pepper; dark skin with dark curly hair); the worst have pale skin with dark straight hair. Follicular units hold 1–4 hairs (1–2 micrograft, 3–4 minigraft). FUE uses ~0.8 mm punches and suits patients who want short hair, African American patients, and limited donor supply. Juri temporoparietal-occipital flaps are used for traumatic/burn alopecia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 517–518)

**Z-plasty geometry**: equal limbs and angles; length gain is ~25% at 30°, ~50% at 45°, ~75% at 60° (classic), ~120% at 90°. Angles under ~20° risk tip necrosis, over ~75° create dog-ears; the new central limb lies along the line joining the free limb ends, and peripheral limbs should parallel RSTLs. W-plasty uses limbs under ~6 mm and is 'regularly irregular' (no length gain); geometric broken-line closure (5–7 mm units, irregularly irregular) camouflages better. Use W-plasty/GBLC for long scars across RSTLs, along the mandible or hairline. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 521–523)

**Revision timing**: Pasha allows revision either around 12 months (mature) or at 6–9 weeks (peak fibroblast activity), and earlier for an obviously misplaced scar; the site frames any revision before 12–18 months as a failure. Teach both: elective cosmetic revision is usually deferred to maturity, but early revision is acceptable for clearly malpositioned or functionally distorting scars. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 519–520)

**Keloid protocol**: intralesional triamcinolone with massage every ~3 weeks; excision only combined with steroid (excision alone recurs frequently); pressure and silicone; radiation for severe/refractory keloids; pulsed-dye laser; cryotherapy for small lesions. Risk factors are age under 30, darker skin (5–15% incidence in Black and Hispanic patients), and tension; hypertrophic scars do not recur after excision. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 524–525)

**Selective photothermolysis and dermatologic lasers**: power density equals watts divided by spot size; each chromophore (water, oxyhemoglobin, melanin) has its own absorption spectrum. Er:YAG 2940 nm (water, very superficial), KTP 532 nm and argon (oxyhemoglobin), pulsed-dye ~585–595 nm (vascular lesions, less scarring), Nd:YAG 1064 nm (deep, scatters, nonablative). (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 509–510)

**Pediatric central apnea and hypopnea rules**: a pediatric central apnea is scored when it lasts at least 20 seconds, or at least 2 missed breaths if it is accompanied by an arousal or a desaturation of 3% or more. A hypopnea is a 30% or greater drop in airflow lasting 2 breaths with a desaturation of 3% or more or an arousal; RERAs are flow reductions that do not meet hypopnea criteria. Obstructive apnea is a drop of 90% or more for 2 baseline breaths, without a 10-second minimum. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 537–538)

**Infant and congenital central disorders**: congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine curse) comes from PHOX2B mutation. Autonomic control of breathing fails during sleep, and treatment is tracheotomy with ventilation during sleep or diaphragm pacing. Primary sleep apnea of infancy is central apnea of 20 seconds or more from brainstem immaturity, with bradycardia and hypoxemia, and it is most common in preterm infants. Periodic breathing (3 or more central apneas of over 3 seconds each within 20 seconds) is common in Chiari malformation. When central apnea predominates, look for Chiari, metabolic or cardiac disease, opioids, and high altitude. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 538)

**Infant sleep safety and behavioral insomnia**: daytime sleepiness in a child is never normal and needs investigation. SIDS peaks at 1–4 months, but the risk lasts to 12 months. Risk factors are male sex, prematurity, prone sleeping, multiple births, a teenage mother, maternal substance use and secondhand smoke. Prevention is back-to-sleep positioning on a firm mattress, with no bed sharing and no loose objects. Behavioral insomnia has two types: sleep-onset association (treat by gradually withdrawing parental intervention, stopping night feeds after 6 months, and using scheduled awakenings) and limit-setting (treat with consistent bedtimes, parent education and CBT). (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 536, 538–539)

**Medical therapy and analgesia**: for adenoid hypertrophy, a trial of intranasal steroid or montelukast is reasonable (warn families about behavioral and mood side effects of montelukast). For acute obstruction, use a nasal trumpet with a short steroid course. After tonsillectomy, give scheduled acetaminophen plus ibuprofen. Codeine and tramadol are contraindicated after tonsillectomy in anyone under 18 (FDA), because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers can make enough morphine to cause fatal respiratory depression. A single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose reduces postoperative nausea and vomiting (AAO-HNS 2019). (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 534, 539)

**Non-hemorrhagic T&A complications**: (1) Postobstructive (negative-pressure) pulmonary edema can follow sudden relief of long-standing obstruction; treat with PEEP and gentle diuresis. (2) Grisel syndrome is atlantoaxial subluxation from inflammatory laxity of the C1–C2 ligaments, with higher risk in Down syndrome; it presents as torticollis and neck pain and needs orthopedic or spine input and a collar. (3) Nasopharyngeal stenosis comes from circumferential scarring, recurs often, and may need flaps or stents. (4) VPI is more likely with submucous cleft or preoperative hypernasality; most cases resolve with speech therapy, and persistent cases warrant 22q11 testing. Avoid cautery or curettage at the torus tubarius to prevent eustachian tube stenosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 541–542)

**Adenoid grading and red flags**: grade the adenoid by the percentage of choanal obstruction on nasopharyngoscopy (1+ under 25%, 2+ 25–50%, 3+ 50–75%, 4+ over 75%), and note whether it abuts the torus tubarius. Unilateral tonsillar enlargement calls for exclusion of lymphoma, leukemia or atypical infection. With severe obstruction, consider screening for cor pulmonale (ECG, echocardiogram, CXR, capillary blood gas). Adenoidectomy is contraindicated in overt cleft palate or VPI; a superior partial adenoidectomy is the option when such a child has OSA. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 534, 540–541)

**Mandibular distraction specifics**: MDO uses bilateral osteotomies and proceeds in phases: latency of 1–5 days (shorter in infants; too short risks fibrous union, too long risks premature consolidation), active distraction at 1–2 mm/day until the tongue-base obstruction is relieved, consolidation for 4–12 weeks, then device removal. Complications include injury to the marginal mandibular and inferior alveolar nerves, tooth bud loss or dentigerous cyst, anterior open bite, relapse or nonunion, device failure and TMJ ankylosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 543)

**Syndromic associations by frequency**: Stickler is the most common associated syndrome (about 18%), then 22q11 deletion (about 7%), Treacher Collins (about 5%) and Goldenhar (about 3%). PRS does not require a cleft, but the classic cleft is U-shaped. Delay polysomnography until the infant is past term, because preterm studies have a high false-negative rate. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 601)

**Natural history and classification**: infantile hemangioma is about 3 times more common in girls. It may be absent at birth or show only a premonitory pale or red macule (herald patch). Rapid growth occurs in the first months, with most growth done by about 4–6 months and a plateau near 1 year. Classic teaching is 50% involution by age 5 and 70% by age 7; newer series show most involution finished by about age 4. Lesions are focal, segmental or multifocal. Segmental lesions in a beard (V3) distribution carry about a 60% risk of airway hemangioma and warrant a low threshold for endoscopy. More than 5 cutaneous lesions warrants abdominal ultrasound for hepatic hemangiomas. Maffucci syndrome is multiple venous-type vascular lesions with enchondromas, with about a 25% risk of chondrosarcoma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 543–545)

**Treatment triggers and propranolol cautions**: treat for complications such as threatened vision or hearing, airway compromise, impaired feeding, ulceration or cosmetically important sites, or high-output heart failure. Before starting propranolol, check vital signs and do a cardiopulmonary exam; ECG and glucose screening are not needed when the exam is normal. Response usually comes within 2–12 weeks. Continue until at least age 1, then taper, and watch for rebound. Contraindications include cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia, hypotension, heart block beyond first degree, heart failure and bronchial asthma. PHACES arterial anomalies raise stroke risk. Lesions that do not respond to propranolol should raise suspicion for a different vascular tumor such as KHE. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 545)

**Cutaneous–airway link numbers**: about 50% of infants with subglottic hemangioma also have a cutaneous hemangioma, but only about 1% of infants with a cutaneous hemangioma have a subglottic lesion. Airway lesions are sessile, often posterior or asymmetric (unilateral) in the subglottis, and stridor worsens with crying as the lesion engorges. Do not biopsy. Endoscopy is diagnostic, and AP neck films may show an asymmetric subglottic narrowing. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 544–545)

**de Serres staging**: stage I is unilateral infrahyoid, II unilateral suprahyoid, III unilateral supra- and infrahyoid, IV bilateral suprahyoid, and V bilateral supra- and infrahyoid. Some versions add VI (bilateral infrahyoid), VII (retropharyngeal) and an M modifier for mediastinal extension. Higher stages are more often microcystic and have more complications and residual disease. Cysts of 2 mL or more are macrocystic. Complete excision rarely recurs, but about half of lesions with gross residual disease regrow. Sclerosants include doxycycline and bleomycin. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 547)

**Epidemiology and approaches**: about 70% of atretic plates are mixed bony-membranous and about 30% are purely bony; purely membranous plates are rare. The bony components come from the vomer and the medial pterygoid plate. Choanal atresia is more common in girls and is usually unilateral (about 65%, more often right-sided). CHARGE is present in about half of bilateral cases; other associations are Apert, Crouzon, Treacher Collins, trisomy 21 and 22q11. Bedside tests are failure to pass a 6 French catheter and absent mirror fogging. The transpalatal approach is now rarely used because it can disturb palatal and dental growth. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 550)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **CF sinus surgery precautions**: almost all CF patients have pansinusitis, and about 10% have obstructive polyps. Operate for obstruction, mucocele, refractory pain or fever, fungal disease, or pulmonary exacerbations linked to sinus disease; it is not curative. Correct vitamin K deficiency before surgery, because fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption raises bleeding risk. Keep anesthesia short (aim for under about 1 hour) because retained pulmonary secretions make long anesthetics risky. Preserve landmarks, consider wide antrostomy or endoscopic medial maxillectomy for irrigation access, and plan inpatient recovery with aggressive irrigation and debridement. A sweat chloride above about 60 mmol/L is diagnostic. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 555–556)

**Pediatric sinusitis definitions and CT triggers**: suspect bacterial rhinosinusitis when symptoms persist beyond 10 days. Acute disease resolves completely within 30 days, chronic disease lasts over 12 weeks, and recurrent acute disease has symptom-free intervals. Frontal and sphenoid sinuses generally do not develop until about ages 8–12. Obtain CT for a toxic child, an acute episode not improving after 48–72 hours of treatment, immunocompromise or suspected complications. Polyps in a child should prompt CF testing. Recurrent sinusitis with pneumonia or bronchiectasis should prompt an immune workup. Adenoidectomy improves symptoms in up to about half of children. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 554–555)

**Pediatric airway numbers**: the infant larynx sits at about C2–C3 and descends to C6–C7 by adulthood. The cricoid is the narrowest point (about 4–5 mm in a term neonate), and a subglottic lumen under about 3.5 mm in a neonate is abnormal. Because resistance rises steeply as the radius falls, 1 mm of circumferential edema can cut a neonatal airway by more than half. Estimate uncuffed tube size as (age in years + 16)/4. When sizing at endoscopy, the correct tube leaks at about 20–30 cm H2O. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 556, 559, 564)

**Congenital laryngeal webs and atresia**: webs come from incomplete laryngeal recanalization around week 10. Most are glottic (about 75%) and anterior. They present at birth with a weak or absent cry and variable stridor. Anterior glottic webs are strongly associated with 22q11 deletion, so order genetic testing. Thin webs can be lysed endoscopically. Thick webs need lysis with keel placement, endoscopic or through a laryngofissure, sometimes with a tracheotomy. Complete obstruction (laryngeal atresia, or an obstructing mass such as teratoma or epignathus) presents prenatally as CHAOS on ultrasound and MRI and needs an EXIT delivery. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 562–564, 596)

**Congenital vs acquired SGS**: congenital SGS is membranous, cartilaginous (small or elliptical cricoid, or a trapped first tracheal ring telescoped under the cricoid) or mixed. It is usually milder and more likely to improve with growth than acquired stenosis, and it is associated with 22q11, Down syndrome and CHARGE. Grade I and some grade II lesions can be observed with surveillance. Cricotracheal resection fits severe stenosis that sits more than about 3 mm below the vocal folds. A subglottic cyst in a previously intubated preterm infant is treated by endoscopic unroofing; stage the procedure if the cysts are circumferential, and expect recurrence. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 564–565, 570)

**Syndromic associations**: laryngeal clefts come from failed development of the tracheoesophageal septum. They are associated with Opitz G/BBB syndrome (MID1, X-linked; hypertelorism, hypospadias, cleft lip/palate), Pallister-Hall syndrome (GLI3; bifid epiglottis, hypothalamic hamartoblastoma, polydactyly, imperforate anus), TEF/esophageal atresia, and congenital heart disease. Type I–II and selected type III clefts are repaired endoscopically; most type III and all type IV clefts need open repair. Diagnostic gel injection of the interarytenoid space can predict the benefit of formal repair. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 567, 600)

**Esophageal atresia/TEF (Gross) types**: type C (proximal atresia with distal fistula) is most common at about 85%. Type A (isolated atresia, no fistula) is next at about 10% and causes polyhydramnios with a gasless abdomen. The H-type isolated fistula without atresia can present late with cough during feeds and recurrent pneumonia. Diagnose with barium esophagram, bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy. After repair, expect tracheomalacia and esophageal dysmotility. Also consider brain MRI when aspiration has no explanation after a normal operative airway evaluation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 561, 568–569)

**Bacterial tracheitis and diphtheria**: bacterial tracheitis follows a viral prodrome. The child develops high fever, a toxic appearance and a tender trachea, and does not respond to standard croup therapy. S. aureus (including MRSA) is the main cause, followed by group A strep, pneumococcus, H. influenzae and Moraxella. Lateral films may show irregular tracheal membranes. Treatment is IV antibiotics plus bronchoscopy to remove membranes and send cultures, and intubation is often needed. Diphtheria forms a friable gray membrane over the tonsils, pharynx and larynx that bleeds when removed; treat with isolation, antitoxin and penicillin or erythromycin. In croup, heliox is an adjunct, and if intubation is needed use a smaller-than-usual uncuffed tube. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 570–572)

**Risk factors and onset types**: the classic juvenile risk triad is firstborn child, vaginal delivery and young mother of lower socioeconomic status. About half of affected children are born to mothers with active genital condylomas. Juvenile-onset disease (under 12) is multisite and more aggressive; adult-onset disease (12 and older) is more often single-site. Papillomas form at squamociliary junctions and at sites of squamous metaplasia. Avoid tracheotomy when possible, because it can seed distal tracheal disease. Intralesional cidofovir is a historical adjuvant for moderate to severe disease, alongside bevacizumab. Prevention is HPV vaccination. Consider periodic biopsy to exclude dysplasia, and chest imaging if pulmonary spread is suspected. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 572–573)

**EoE diagnostic threshold**: diagnosis needs 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field on biopsy, with multiple biopsies from the proximal, mid and distal esophagus taken after or alongside adequate reflux treatment. Endoscopy may show white exudates, rings (trachealization), linear furrows or pallor, or may look normal. EoE is linked with atopy, food impaction without a prior esophageal history, and failure of airway reconstruction when uncontrolled. Treatment is PPI, swallowed topical steroids, elimination diets and dilation of strictures. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 574–575)

**Pediatric salivary pearls**: obstructive sialadenitis is the most common pediatric salivary disease, and juvenile recurrent parotitis is second. Mumps (paramyxovirus) peaks at ages 4–6 in unvaccinated children. It causes painful parotid swelling that is bilateral in about 75%, sometimes after a prodrome with trismus. Complications are sudden unilateral SNHL, orchitis with infertility, encephalitis, pancreatitis and nephritis. Care is supportive with an audiologic check, and MMR vaccination prevents it. Sialendoscopy can remove stones under about 4 mm. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 578–579)

**Age-matched audiometry**: from birth to 6 months, use ABR and OAE (ear-specific) and behavioral observation audiometry. Behavioral observation only estimates the better ear. From about 6 months to 3 years, use visual reinforcement audiometry in sound field or with inserts; the operant-conditioning variant suits children over about 2. From 3 to 5 years, use conditioned play audiometry, which is ear- and frequency-specific. From 6 years on, use standard audiometry. Normal pediatric canal volume on tympanometry is about 0.4–1.0 mL, and hearing is normal up to 20 dB HL in children (21–25 dB is borderline). (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 579–580)

**Risk factors and late-onset surveillance**: risk indicators include TORCH infection, bacterial meningitis, family history, craniofacial anomalies, birth weight under 1500 g, hyperbilirubinemia needing exchange, Apgar under 4 at 1 minute or under 6 at 5 minutes, prolonged NICU stay, ECMO, mechanical ventilation and ototoxic drugs. A child who passed the newborn screen but has a risk factor still needs a diagnostic audiologic evaluation, by about 24–30 months in this source (JCIH 2019 sets risk-specific earlier timing). About 20% of congenitally deaf children have an imaging anomaly, and up to 50% of those with unilateral loss. ECG screening targets Jervell and Lange-Nielsen and Refsum disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 580–582)

**Usher syndrome subtypes**: Usher is the most common autosomal recessive syndromic hearing loss and the leading cause of combined deafness and blindness. Type I has profound congenital SNHL, absent vestibular function and retinitis pigmentosa beginning before adolescence; these children walk late and are early CI candidates. Type II, the most common, has moderate to severe congenital SNHL, normal vestibular function and later RP. Type III has progressive SNHL with variable vestibular loss. Diagnosis uses an ophthalmologic exam with electroretinography plus genetics. Pendred is the second most common recessive syndrome and Jervell and Lange-Nielsen the third. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 587)

**Dominant and X-linked syndromes**: the mnemonic WANT BCS covers the dominant syndromes. Waardenburg causes SNHL. Its causative genes are PAX3 (types I and III) or MITF (type II). Type I has dystopia canthorum, with about 50% SNHL. Type II lacks dystopia but has about 80% SNHL. Type III adds limb anomalies and type IV adds Hirschsprung disease. Stickler (COL2A1) causes progressive SNHL with myopia, retinal detachment, joint laxity and Pierre Robin sequence. Branchio-oto-renal syndrome (EYA1) causes mixed loss with pits/tags and renal anomalies, so order a renal ultrasound. Alport syndrome is mostly X-linked COL4A5. It causes progressive SNHL in the first decade with nephritis and lenticonus or myopia. X-linked POU3F4 causes congenital stapes fixation with a gusher; avoid routine stapedotomy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 588–590)

**Connexin and Pendred specifics**: about 80% of nonsyndromic hereditary loss is autosomal recessive (DFNB), about 18% dominant (DFNA) and about 2% X-linked (DFNX) or mitochondrial. About a third of hereditary loss is syndromic. DFNB1 (GJB2/connexin 26 and GJB6/connexin 30) causes about half of severe-to-profound recessive nonsyndromic loss, and 35delG is the most common GJB2 variant. In Pendred (SLC26A4), a euthyroid multinodular goiter appears around ages 8–14 with EVA or Mondini anatomy. The perchlorate discharge test is the historical diagnostic test. Thyroid hormone shrinks the goiter but does not change hearing. In Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (KCNQ1/KCNE1), treat the long QT with beta-blockers or a defibrillator. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 581, 586–588)

**Additional malformation facts**: Scheibe (cochleosaccular) dysplasia is a membranous defect of the cochlea and saccule with a normal pars superior. It is not visible on CT and is linked to Usher, Waardenburg and congenital rubella. Michel aplasia reflects arrest around week 3. Lateral semicircular canal dysplasia is the most common canal anomaly; semicircular canal aplasia suggests CHARGE. An IAC under about 3 mm suggests an absent or hypoplastic cochlear nerve and needs MRI. An IAC wider than about 10 mm raises the risk of CSF gusher and spontaneous leak. Incomplete partition II carries meningitis and gusher risk through a dilated cochlear aqueduct. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 584–586)

**Pediatric candidacy specifics**: under FDA labeling, children can be implanted from 9 months for bilateral profound SNHL. Severe-to-profound loss qualifies from age 2 through 17, with limited hearing-aid benefit (for example, under 30% on age-appropriate word tests such as the Lexical Neighborhood Test). Single-sided deafness or asymmetric loss is now an indication. After meningitis, implant early before the cochlea ossifies. Give pneumococcal vaccination. Optimize middle-ear disease beforehand; tympanostomy tubes do not raise CI meningitis risk, but treat AOM aggressively. Simultaneous bilateral implantation is preferred when possible. An auditory brainstem implant is used for cochlear nerve aplasia, ossified cochleae and NF2. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 584)

**Pediatric bone-conduction rules**: use a softband (nonimplanted) device from infancy. A percutaneous osseointegrated implant is FDA-approved from age 5 and needs about 3 mm of cortical bone. Young children often get a two-stage procedure with a 'sleeper' second fixture in case of extrusion. If microtia reconstruction is planned, do it first or place the implant more posterior and superior to keep the reconstruction skin pocket intact. Exposure of dura or sigmoid sinus is common in the thin pediatric skull. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 583–584)

**AAP 2013 antibiotic-vs-observation rules**: give antibiotics for any AOM under 6 months, for severe AOM at any age (moderate or severe otalgia, otalgia 48 hours or more, or temperature 39°C or higher), and for nonsevere bilateral AOM at 6–23 months. Nonsevere unilateral AOM at 6–23 months, and nonsevere AOM at 2 years or older, may be observed with treatment if there is no improvement in 48–72 hours. First-line is high-dose amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day). Use amoxicillin-clavulanate if amoxicillin was given in the past 30 days, with concurrent purulent conjunctivitis (nontypeable H. influenzae), or with a history of amoxicillin failure. For penicillin allergy use cefdinir, cefuroxime or cefpodoxime; ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for 3 days is an alternative. After a second failure, consider clindamycin with or without a third-generation cephalosporin and tympanocentesis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 590–591)

**Pediatric tympanoplasty timing**: success in children (roughly 35–94%) is lower than in adults because of URIs, ongoing eustachian tube dysfunction (especially with cleft palate, Down syndrome or craniofacial anomalies) and less reliable postoperative care. Results improve with age up to about 13. Many surgeons wait until the adenoid pad is regressing (about age 7) or regressed (about age 10), or first treat adenoid and nasal disease. The contralateral ear should be free of effusion, retraction and recurrent infection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 592)

**Congenital and neonatal facial palsy**: birth trauma (forceps, prolonged labor, large infant) is the most common cause of unilateral neonatal facial paralysis. The pediatric nerve is exposed because the mastoid tip does not develop until about age 2. Hemotympanum or periauricular bruising supports a traumatic cause, and most traumatic palsies recover with observation. Electrophysiologic testing (EMG/ENoG) helps separate traumatic from developmental palsy, and an ABR screens for associated hearing loss. Congenital unilateral lower lip palsy (asymmetric crying facies, from depressor anguli oris hypoplasia) is the most common congenital cause and carries about a 10% rate of cardiac defects. Möbius syndrome combines CN VI and VII palsies, sometimes bilateral, with limb anomalies (club foot), micrognathia and tongue weakness. Osteopetrosis (Albers-Schönberg) can compress CN VII and VIII in a narrowed IAC. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 594–595)

**Langerhans cell histiocytosis forms**: LCH is a proliferation of histiocytes that contain Birbeck granules (tennis-racket organelles on electron microscopy) and stain CD1a/S100-positive. The localized form, eosinophilic granuloma, causes lytic temporal or frontal bone lesions in children and young adults. It mimics mastoiditis or otitis with granulation tissue and has an excellent prognosis after curettage, with radiation reserved for recurrence. Hand-Schüller-Christian disease is the chronic disseminated form, with lytic skull lesions, exophthalmos and diabetes insipidus. Letterer-Siwe is the acute disseminated infant form (under 3) with hepatosplenomegaly and rash and a very poor prognosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 615–616)

**General ENT care in Down syndrome**: atlantoaxial instability is present in about 25%, and about 2% have subluxation. Screening radiographs do not reliably predict risk, so protect the neck in every patient during positioning and intubation. Expect subglottic narrowing and choose a tube about 2 sizes (about 1 mm) smaller. Do an ABR by 3 months and behavioral audiograms every 6 months until ear-specific testing is reliable (about age 4), then yearly; see the child every 3 months if the canals are stenotic. Get a baseline PSG by age 4 (AAP 2011). Adenotonsillectomy leaves residual OSA in more than half, so DISE-directed lingual tonsillectomy or posterior midline glossectomy may follow. The risk of Grisel syndrome after T&A is higher. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 597–598)

**Closure-pattern frequencies and 22q11 safety**: closure patterns are coronal (about 55%), sagittal (10–15%), circular (10–20%) and circular with a Passavant ridge (15–20%). Give at least 3–6 months of speech therapy to correct compensatory articulation before surgery. Severe cases can be repaired as early as about age 4. Before a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty in 22q11 deletion, palpate the posterior pharyngeal wall and consider MRA, because the internal carotids can be medialized. Nasometry adds objective resonance data. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 624)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Classification and epidemiology**: the Veau classification has 4 classes: I soft palate only; II soft and hard palate to the incisive foramen; III complete unilateral lip, alveolus and palate; IV complete bilateral. Incomplete cleft lip may have a Simonart band. About 45% of clefts involve both lip and palate, 30% the palate only and 25% the lip only. Cleft lip is more common in males and isolated cleft palate in females. Rates are highest in Asian and Native American populations. Concordance is 25–40% in monozygotic twins. Up to 10% have heart anomalies. Feeds over 25–30 minutes signal excessive energy use and need special feeders, such as Haberman, Pigeon or squeeze bottles. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 619–621)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Timeline and named techniques**: lip repair is classically at about 10–14 weeks by the rule of 10s (over 10 weeks, over 10 lb, hemoglobin over 10), with nasoalveolar molding or lip adhesion beforehand for wide clefts. Palate repair is at about 10–14 months. Alveolar bone grafting (iliac crest cancellous bone) is done at about 6–8 years, before the permanent canine erupts. Orthodontics follows, and definitive rhinoplasty and orthognathic surgery wait until skeletal maturity. Lip techniques include Millard rotation-advancement (the standard for unilateral clefts, with Mohler and Noordhoff modifications), Tennison-Randall triangular flaps and the Fisher anatomic subunit repair. Palate techniques include von Langenbeck bipedicle flaps, Bardach two-flap palatoplasty with intravelar veloplasty, Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty (lengthens the velum) and V-Y pushback. Children with cleft palate need an average of about 3 sets of tympanostomy tubes by age 7. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 621–623)

**Lingual thyroid**: lingual thyroid is failure of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum. It presents as a posterior midline tongue-base mass, more often in females, with dysphagia, dysphonia or stertor, and it is often hypofunctioning. In about 75% it is the only functioning thyroid tissue. Work it up with ultrasound or CT for cervical thyroid, thyroid function tests and an I-123 or technetium scan. Observe it if asymptomatic. Treat symptoms with suppression, excision (transoral or transcervical, with possible autotransplantation) or, in adults, RAI ablation. Most patients need lifelong thyroid hormone. The Sistrunk procedure cuts TGDC recurrence to about 3%, versus 20–50% without hyoid resection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 607–608)

**Other congenital masses**: a thymic cyst is a third-pouch remnant found anywhere from the mandibular angle to the mediastinum, usually on the left. Check calcium and consider 22q11, and expect possible mediastinal extension. Teratomas contain all 3 germ layers; dermoids contain ectoderm and mesoderm only. Epignathus is an oropharyngeal teratoma, often arising from the skull base or palate, with high airway mortality, and may need an EXIT delivery. Fibromatosis colli appears at 2–4 weeks, with the head tilted toward and chin rotated away from the affected SCM. Ultrasound confirms it, and biopsy can be misread as malignant. Most pediatric neck masses (80–90%) are benign. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 605, 608–609)

**Rhabdomyosarcoma specifics**: about 35–40% of rhabdomyosarcomas occur in the head and neck, most often in the orbit, nasopharynx, middle ear/mastoid and sinonasal tract. Parameningeal sites (middle ear/mastoid, sinonasal, nasopharynx, infratemporal fossa) do worse because of meningeal spread. The embryonal type (about 75%, young children, including botryoid) has the best prognosis. The alveolar type (about 20%, adolescents, often PAX-FOXO1 fusion) has the worst, and the pleomorphic type is mostly adult. Nodal spread is about 20% and rare with orbital primaries. Presentations include unilateral otitis media or aural polyp, rapid proptosis and cranial neuropathy. Treatment is multimodal chemotherapy and radiation, with surgery when complete resection is feasible. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 611–612)

**Other pediatric malignancies**: lymphoma is the most common pediatric head and neck malignancy. Burkitt is the most common pediatric NHL, with c-MYC translocation and a starry-sky pattern; it is EBV-positive in 90–95% of endemic and 15–20% of sporadic cases. Hodgkin lymphoma peaks in teenagers, often with a mediastinal mass. Diagnose it by excisional biopsy sent fresh, and avoid steroids before biopsy. Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood; neck disease can cause Horner syndrome and heterochromia, and urine catecholamines help with the diagnosis. Pediatric NPC is usually undifferentiated and advanced at presentation. Excluding hemangioma, infection and malformation, more than half of solid pediatric parotid masses are malignant. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common pediatric salivary malignancy, and acinic cell carcinoma is second. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 611–614)

**Pediatric DTC (ATA 2015 pediatric guideline)**: a pediatric thyroid nodule is much more likely to be malignant (about 22–26%) than an adult nodule (5–10%). Nodule size alone does not predict risk, so FNA is not tied to size thresholds. For Bethesda III or IV cytology in a child, do lobectomy with isthmusectomy rather than repeat FNA. Children present with more nodal (40–80%) and lung (up to about 25%) disease and recur more often, but survival is near 100%. Total thyroidectomy is standard for papillary carcinoma, which is more often bilateral; diffuse sclerosing variant is more common in children. Risk factors include prior radiation (highest under age 5), DICER1, PTEN/Cowden, APC, Carney complex and Werner syndrome. Use the lowest effective RAI dose. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 613–614)

**Jahrsdoerfer and de la Cruz**: Pasha calls atresiaplasty candidacy favorable at a Jahrsdoerfer score of 6 or more out of 10 (with stapes present worth 2 points), and higher scores predict better hearing. Jahrsdoerfer's original scale rates 7 as fair and 8 or more as good, which explains the 7/10 often quoted. Use 6 as the minimum candidacy floor and 8 or more as the good-prognosis tier. The de la Cruz scheme splits ears into minor malformations (normal pneumatization, oval window, facial nerve relation and inner ear; operable) and major malformations (poor pneumatization, absent oval window, aberrant facial nerve or inner-ear anomaly; favor a bone-conduction device). Atresiaplasty is done at about 7 years or older, after microtia reconstruction. Reported results are 30 dB HL or better in 50–75%. Complications are TM graft lateralization (about 25%), canal restenosis, SNHL (2–5%), facial nerve injury (about 1%) and TMJ symptoms. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 616–617)

**Atresia associations**: about 90% of aural atresia is nonsyndromic, and 20–30% is bilateral. Associated findings are microtia (55–93%), cholesteatoma (4–7%), cochlear malformation (about 5%), canal anomalies (about 10%) and stapes fixation (about 4%). A fused malleus–incus is the most common middle-ear finding; the footplate is usually normal. CT for congenital cholesteatoma is usually not needed before about age 4. In unilateral atresia with a normal contralateral screen, detailed testing of the affected ear can wait until about 6–7 months. Treat otitis in the hearing ear aggressively. Microtia is about 2.5 times more common in males, more often right-sided and bilateral in about 25%. Teratogens include isotretinoin and thalidomide. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 616–618)

**Pediatric fluid arithmetic**: give an initial resuscitation bolus of 20 mL/kg of warm isotonic crystalloid. A routine transfusion aliquot is 10 mL/kg, and circulating blood volume is about 70 mL/kg (higher in infants). Maintenance follows the 4-2-1 rule: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg and 1 mL/kg/h for each kilogram above that, using lean weight in obese children. Vital signs and urine output lag in children, so look for dehydration signs (sunken fontanelle, dry mucosa, delayed capillary refill, no tears). (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 625–626)

**Validating a patient-reported outcome instrument**: a usable quality-of-life questionnaire must show convergent validity (correlates with measures of the same construct), discriminant validity (does not track unrelated constructs), reliability (stable scores when disease impact is unchanged), and responsiveness (scores move when disease impact changes). Global instruments (e.g., the parent-completed Child Health Questionnaire) are often paired with disease-specific ones such as the OM-6, which caregivers complete for children 6 months to 12 years with chronic or recurrent otitis, rating 6 domains on a 1–7 scale plus a 0–10 global score. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Outcomes and Evidence-Based Medicine in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 61)

**Intention-to-treat and validity trade-offs**: intention-to-treat analyzes subjects in the arm they were randomized to regardless of crossover or dropout, protecting the balance that randomization created. Internal validity (is the effect real within the study) and external validity (does it generalize) trade off: tightly controlled trials gain internal validity but may not reflect real practice. Power (1 − beta, conventionally 80%–90%) rises with sample size, alpha, and the size of the difference judged clinically meaningful. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Outcomes and Evidence-Based Medicine in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 62–63)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Why routine pediatric coagulation screening fails**: in one cited series, preoperative coagulation panels had sensitivity of only about 9%, specificity about 98%, positive predictive value about 2%, and negative predictive value about 92% for post-tonsillectomy bleeding. The AAO-HNS position is to test only when history raises suspicion or family history is unavailable, and a structured bleeding history is preferred over universal screening. PT prolongs only when factor levels fall below roughly 30%, and the bleeding time is no longer recommended in children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Outcomes and Evidence-Based Medicine in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 59–60); (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 156–158)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Isolated prolonged aPTT before adenotonsillectomy**: the most common cause in children is a benign nonspecific inhibitor (e.g., a transient lupus anticoagulant), which prolongs clotting in vitro without raising bleeding risk. A mixing study separates the two: correction with normal plasma means a factor deficiency, and failure to correct means an inhibitor. Deficiencies of factor XII, prekallikrein, or high-molecular-weight kininogen also lengthen the aPTT without causing bleeding. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 157)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Factor XIII deficiency, the normal-labs bleeder**: PT and aPTT are normal because they end before cross-linking, so the diagnosis needs a specific factor XIII assay. Clues are delayed bleeding after surgery or trauma, delayed bleeding from the umbilical stump, and intracranial hemorrhage after minor trauma. Treat with cryoprecipitate or FFP; the long half-life (11–14 days) and low target level (>5%) make prophylaxis practical. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 163)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **von Willebrand disease subtypes**: type 1 (the most common, autosomal dominant) is a partial quantitative deficiency with mild to moderate bleeding. Type 2A lacks large multimers. In type 2B, gain-of-function binding to platelet GPIb clears multimers and causes thrombocytopenia. Type 2M impairs platelet adhesion with normal multimers. In type 2N, poor binding to factor VIII lowers factor VIII levels and mimics hemophilia A. Type 3 has nearly absent VWF and can cause joint and muscle bleeding. Estimated prevalence is about 1%, but symptomatic disease is closer to 1 in 1,000. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 161–162)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **VWD laboratory triad**: order VWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity (function), and factor VIII level, and record ABO type, since type O individuals have VWF antigen levels about 25% lower than average. Multimer analysis and ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation then define the subtype. Avoid platelet function testing within about 10 days of NSAIDs or aspirin, which can mimic a disorder. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 158)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **DDAVP in children**: desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg IV raises VWF and factor VIII 2- to 8-fold, with a peak at 30–90 minutes. Confirm response with a preoperative challenge. It does not work in type 3 VWD and is controversial in type 2B (transient thrombocytopenia). It can help mild hemophilia A with baseline factor VIII above about 5%–10%. Tachyphylaxis limits use to about 3–4 days. Hyponatremic seizures occur mainly in children younger than 2, so restrict fluids to maintenance, avoid hypotonic fluids, and check sodium. Many hematologists avoid DDAVP under age 2. Nonresponders and major surgery get plasma-derived VWF concentrate (load 40–60 VWF:RCo units/kg, then 20–40 units/kg every 8–24 hours). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 164–165)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Antifibrinolytics for oropharyngeal surgery**: saliva and oral mucosa have high plasminogen-activator activity, so aminocaproic or tranexamic acid helps stabilize clot after tonsil or dental surgery. One regimen cited for bleeding disorders is aminocaproic acid 50 mg/kg 1 hour before surgery, then every 6 hours for about 10 days. Use caution with hematuria, because urinary levels are very high, and in patients with thrombophilia or prolonged immobility. Topical use is also possible. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 165)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Hemophilia essentials**: hemophilia A (factor VIII) affects about 1 in 5,000 male births and hemophilia B (factor IX) about 1 in 30,000. Both are X-linked, but 20%–30% of severe hemophilia A cases have no affected relative. Severity is set by factor level: below 1% is severe, 1%–5% moderate, and 6%–40% mild (bleeds may occur only with surgery or trauma). The aPTT is prolonged. Each unit/kg of factor VIII raises plasma levels about 2%, versus 0.8%–1% for factor IX. Surgery needs 50%–100% levels. Inhibitors develop in about 30% of severe hemophilia A versus 3% of B and require bypassing agents (rFVIIa about 90 mcg/kg or activated prothrombin complex). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 161, 164)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Inherited platelet disorders with normal counts**: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (defective GPIIb/IIIa) gives early mucocutaneous bleeding, epistaxis, and menorrhagia. Aggregation is absent with ADP, epinephrine, and collagen but normal with ristocetin, and treatment is platelet transfusion. Bernard–Soulier syndrome (defective GPIb/IX) has giant platelets, variable thrombocytopenia, and abnormal ristocetin response but normal response to other agonists. Storage-pool defects occur with Hermansky–Pudlak and Chédiak–Higashi syndromes. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome causes small platelets. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 160–161)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Syndromes with hidden coagulopathy**: Noonan syndrome is linked to mild factor XI deficiency, platelet dysfunction, or thrombocytopenia (about one-third have a bleeding diathesis), so check coagulation before surgery. Isolated factor XI deficiency is autosomal recessive, concentrated in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, and bleeds mainly after trauma or surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 162); (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 52)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Pediatric blood-product dosing**: one platelet unit per 10 kg (or 10 mL/kg if under 10 kg) raises the count about 30,000–50,000. Target at least 50,000 for bleeding or invasive procedures. Destructive thrombocytopenia such as ITP responds poorly, so transfuse only for life-threatening bleeding. FFP is 10–20 mL/kg and is not a volume expander. Cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII, VWF) is 1 unit per 10 kg. Draw diagnostic coagulation studies before giving products when possible, because transfusion can obscure the diagnosis for days to weeks. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 157, 163)

**Evaluate for a bleeding disorder at the time of an unexpected bleed**: while stabilizing the child, send CBC with platelets, PT, aPTT, and a platelet-function closure time. Get pediatric hematology input for abnormal results or for unexplained bleeding despite normal results. Draw these before giving blood products when that is safe. Note whether an antiemetic was given at the first surgery: it can suppress the hematemesis that would otherwise reveal a large volume of swallowed blood. Check orthostatic vital signs and treat the child as having a full stomach. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 157); (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Anesthesiology", p 119)

**Pediatric recurrent epistaxis**: lifetime epistaxis approaches 60%, and most childhood bleeds come from local trauma or dryness of the anterior septum. A child whose bleeding is not controlled by pressure, cautery, or packing, or who keeps having recurrent bleeds, should get the same screening sequence as preoperative evaluation (CBC/platelets, PT, aPTT, closure time, then hematology referral). VWD is the most likely inherited cause. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Hematology: The Coagulation System and Associated Disorders", p 158)

**When the otitis-prone child needs an immune workup**: suspect primary immunodeficiency when infections are frequent, suppurative, unresponsive to antibiotics, or caused by unusual organisms. Also suspect it with mastoiditis or other complications, or with other serious infections, severe eczema, or failure to thrive. First exclude common contributors (daycare, smoke exposure, allergy, anatomic problems). Initial screening is quantitative immunoglobulins, CBC with differential, and vaccine-specific antibody titers. Re-immunize children with low titers and remeasure after 3–4 weeks. Total protein and albumin identify secondary hypogammaglobulinemia from protein loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergy and Immunology", p 128–129)

**Primary immunodeficiencies that present with otitis**: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia is suggested by recurrent otitis with tiny or absent tonsils and cervical nodes. In CVID, recurrent otitis occurs in about two-thirds of children. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome has the triad of small-platelet thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent otitis, although only about 27% show all three. About three-quarters of hyper-IgE patients have ear infections, and some need mastoidectomy. X-linked hyper-IgM, polysaccharide-specific antibody deficiency (± IgG2 subclass deficiency), and neutrophil disorders also cause recurrent otitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergy and Immunology", p 128–129)

**Allergy drugs do not treat OME**: controlled trials and Cochrane reviews find no benefit from antihistamines, decongestants, or steroids for OME, and guidelines make no recommendation for allergy management as a treatment for effusion. Children with proven hypogammaglobulinemia and poor specific-antibody responses need IV or subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement rather than repeated empiric antibiotics. Base antibiotic choice on myringotomy cultures. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergy and Immunology", p 128–129)

**Biofilms explain culture-negative effusions**: middle-ear fluid that looks sterile on standard culture often contains bacterial DNA by PCR and mucosal biofilms on microscopy. Culture recovers only about 1% of biofilm bacteria, and sessile biofilm bacteria can survive antibiotic levels about 1,000 times those that kill free-floating (planktonic) cells. Tubes may work partly by aerating the middle ear, which raises oxygen tension and restores the oxidative killing of neutrophils. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Role of Biofilms in Pediatric Otolaryngologic Diseases", p 191–195)

**Refractory tube otorrhea**: tubes removed from children with persistent otorrhea are often coated with biofilm, which acts as a nidus that antibiotics cannot clear. Removing or exchanging the colonized tube can end drainage that has failed topical therapy. Tube materials and coatings that resist adherence are being developed. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Role of Biofilms in Pediatric Otolaryngologic Diseases", p 196)

**Pediatric habit (psychogenic/somatic) cough**: a honking or barking cough, often with a chin-on-chest posture, typically starts after a URI and persists after other symptoms clear. It can occur many times a minute, disappears in sleep, lessens with distraction, and does not respond to antitussives, bronchodilators, or steroids. It accounts for 3%–10% of children with cough lasting more than 1 month. Spirometry and chest radiograph are normal. Distinguish it from a tic disorder, which has a premonitory urge and voluntary suppressibility. Paroxysmal (habit) sneezing, with eyes open and no sneezing in sleep, is a variant. Treat with reassurance, management of contributing conditions, and speech-therapy suppression techniques. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Psychiatric Disorders in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 100–101)

**Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma**: the orbit is the primary site in about 10% of childhood RMS (mean age about 7). Tumors favor the superior orbit and are usually embryonal. They present with rapid proptosis, ptosis, or a lid or subconjunctival mass, and inflammatory signs can mimic orbital cellulitis. Intergroup RMS clinical grouping: I = completely resected; II = microscopic residual; III = gross residual after biopsy; IV = distant metastasis. Orbital embryonal tumors have about 94% 5-year survival versus about 74% for alveolar. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Ophthalmology", p 151)

**NF1 in the head and neck**: NF1 (17q11.2, autosomal dominant, about 50% de novo) is diagnosed by the NIH criteria, which require two or more of the following: six or more café-au-lait macules (>5 mm before puberty, >15 mm after); two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma; axillary or inguinal freckling; optic glioma; two or more Lisch nodules; a distinctive bony lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, cortical thinning of a long bone); or an affected first-degree relative. Plexiform neurofibromas can involve the parotid, carotid, retropharyngeal, and masticator spaces. Cervical neurofibromas can be mistaken for lymph nodes. Resect for rapid growth (to exclude malignant change), pain or deficit, airway compression, or disfigurement. Legius syndrome (SPRED1) mimics the pigmentary findings. The criteria were revised in 2021 to add genetic and ophthalmic findings. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 138)

**NF2 criteria and the child with one acoustic neuroma**: NF2 is defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or by a first-degree relative with NF2 plus either a unilateral vestibular schwannoma or two of the following: neurofibroma, meningioma, glioma, schwannoma, or juvenile posterior subcapsular lens opacity. In a child, an isolated unilateral vestibular schwannoma alone does not imply NF2. If other neurogenic tumors are present, the risk of NF2 and of a contralateral tumor is high, so image routinely and offer NF2 genetic testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 139)

**Pediatric facial palsy specifics**: Bell palsy is the most common cause of acute unilateral facial weakness in children, and most recover nearly fully within weeks. Lyme disease is a major association in endemic areas, so order serology with Western blot confirmation. Recurrence occurs in about 7%. Bilateral palsy (<1%) should prompt a search for a systemic cause, such as Lyme, sarcoidosis (chest imaging, serum and CSF ACE), Guillain–Barré, or other polyneuropathy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 140)

**EEG and BPVC criteria**: children with recurrent episodic vertigo should have an EEG to exclude epileptic vertigo, with prolonged video EEG if the routine study is normal and no spell was captured. Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood requires at least 5 attacks of sudden vertigo resolving within minutes to hours, with normal neurologic, audiometric, and vestibular findings and a normal EEG between attacks. It typically affects ages 1–4, about 20% go on to typical migraine, and frequent spells can be treated with cyproheptadine prophylaxis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 136)

**Mitochondrial deafness beyond m.1555A>G**: MT-RNR1 and MT-TS1 variants cause nonsyndromic loss. Syndromic loss occurs in MELAS (m.3243A>G), Kearns–Sayre, deafness–dystonia, and Leigh syndromes, all maternally inherited. The loss is usually cochlear, progresses from high to all frequencies, and OAEs are typically absent. Cochlear implants work well in many mitochondrial patients. Coexisting central or cognitive disease limits outcomes, so include a mitochondrial specialist in perioperative planning. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 137–138); (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 40)

**First-tier test in the dysmorphic child**: chromosomal microarray (array CGH) is now recommended as the first-line genetic screen, in place of karyotype, for children with unexplained developmental delay and dysmorphic or craniofacial features. It detects gains and losses of about 300–500 kb, compared with 3–5 Mb for high-resolution karyotype. Exome sequencing is reserved for cases where tiered testing is negative (clinical diagnostic yield about 25%). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 31, 57)

**Congenital dacryocystocele as a mimic**: a bluish swelling below the medial canthal tendon in a newborn comes from combined proximal (valve of Rosenmüller) and distal (valve of Hasner) obstruction. It often has an associated intranasal cyst under the inferior turbinate that can obstruct the obligate nasal airway. Infected lesions are urgent because of spread toward the cavernous sinus: give systemic antibiotics, often IV. Definitive care is probing with endoscopic marsupialization of the intranasal cyst. Simple congenital nasolacrimal obstruction is common (about 5% symptomatic), and about 95% resolves by 1 year. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Ophthalmology", p 146–147)

**Reading reflux tests correctly**: multichannel intraluminal impedance-pH (MII-pH) has largely replaced pH-metry. It detects every retrograde bolus, including weakly acidic events (pH 4–7) that pH probes miss, and records how far up the esophagus the bolus travels. It shows only temporal association, not causation, and it cannot tell vomiting from reflux. Acid suppression usually need not be stopped before the study, and stopping a PPI abruptly causes rebound acid. Pharyngeal pH monitoring and lipid-laden macrophages in BAL are nonspecific. A PPI trial, if used, is about 1 mg/kg twice daily for 6–8 weeks. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Gastroenterology", p 201–203)

**Infant regurgitation is developmental**: about 50% of infants regurgitate, peaking near 4 months and usually resolving by 1 year. Thriving 'happy spitters' need only reassurance, with thickened feeds for excess volume loss. Placebo-controlled trials show empiric PPIs do not improve infant irritability or feeding complaints. Metoclopramide adds little and risks extrapyramidal effects and tardive dyskinesia. Fundoplication treats reflux but has no role in true vomiting. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Gastroenterology", p 200, 204–205)

**EoE specifics**: diagnosis needs at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field in a symptomatic patient. Endoscopy shows linear furrows, rings, white exudates, and strictures. Infants and toddlers present with feeding problems, and adolescents with dysphagia or food impaction. Diet options are allergy-test-guided elimination, the six-food elimination diet (milk, egg, soy, wheat, fish/shellfish, peanut/tree nut), which resolves esophagitis in about 70%, or an elemental diet. Swallowed topical steroids are fluticasone puffed from an inhaler without a spacer and swallowed, or budesonide nebulizer solution drunk as a liquid. Patients must not rinse, eat, or drink for 30 minutes afterward. These steroids clear inflammation in about 50%–80%, and oropharyngeal or esophageal candidiasis is the main side effect. Relapse is nearly universal when therapy stops. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Gastroenterology", p 205–208)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **CF diagnostics and numbers**: CF is autosomal recessive. About 1 in 25 white individuals are carriers, incidence is about 1 in 3,000, and ΔF508 is by far the most common variant. US newborn screening measures immunoreactive trypsinogen, with or without CFTR variant testing (sensitivity and specificity near 99%), followed by a confirmatory sweat chloride test by pilocarpine iontophoresis. A level of 60 mmol/L or higher is diagnostic. The book calls values below 40 normal and 40–60 borderline, and says infants under 6 months above 30 remain at risk. Current CF Foundation criteria call ≤29 unlikely and 30–59 intermediate. Nasal potential difference testing is a specialized adjunct. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 227)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **Sinus–lung interface in CF**: Pseudomonas aeruginosa from a child's sinus culture should prompt CF evaluation. Choose sinus antibiotics with the lower-airway flora in mind (S. aureus and H. influenzae in younger children, Pseudomonas later; about 80% of adults are colonized). Sinus surgery improves symptoms and quality of life but has not consistently improved lung function or prevented exacerbations, and polyps recur often. Chronic azithromycin and inhaled tobramycin each reduce pulmonary exacerbations. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 228–229)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **PCD versus CF clues**: PCD is autosomal recessive (about 1 in 15,000–30,000, likely underdiagnosed). Kartagener syndrome is the triad of bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and situs inversus. Suspect PCD with nasal congestion from birth, chronic wet cough, and severe recurrent otitis and sinusitis. Unlike CF, clubbing and nasal polyps are uncommon. Associations include complex congenital heart disease, polycystic kidney, biliary atresia, hydrocephalus, and infertility. Screening uses nasal or exhaled nitric oxide (low in PCD, often high in asthma) or the saccharin transit test. Ciliary ultrastructure or function studies confirm the diagnosis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 229–230)

**Bronchodilators can worsen malacia**: albuterol may relax the smooth muscle that supports a floppy segment and increase dynamic collapse. Some pulmonologists use ipratropium instead, judging response by individual trial. Airway clearance, positive expiratory pressure devices, and CPAP stent the airway open. Most primary tracheobronchomalacia improves by age 2–3 years, whereas TEF-associated malacia can persist. A monophonic wheeze points to a single large-airway narrowing (malacia, foreign body), whereas a polyphonic wheeze suggests asthma or bronchiolitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 218, 226)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Alveolar bone grafting and orthognathic timing**: graft the alveolar cleft just before the lateral incisor and canine erupt (variable, roughly ages 6–12, timed with dental radiographs). Orthodontic palatal expansion comes first, then cancellous iliac crest bone placed between nasal and oral mucosal closures, with gingiva on the oral side.
