Grafting closes the oronasal communication, supports the teeth, and improves nasal hygiene and speech. About 25%–50% of repaired cleft patients develop Class III maxillary hypoplasia needing Le Fort I advancement at skeletal maturity (14–16 years in girls, 16–18 in boys). Definitive rhinoplasty is delayed until after orthognathic healing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery: Craniofacial Growth and Interdisciplinary Surgical Care", p 240–242)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Recurrence counseling numbers**: clefting affects about 1 in 1,000 births. Empiric recurrence risk for a first-degree relative rises with severity: unilateral cleft lip about 4%, unilateral cleft lip and palate about 4.9%, bilateral cleft lip about 6.7%, bilateral cleft lip and palate about 8%, and isolated cleft palate about 3.5%. Recurrence is higher when the proband is the less commonly affected sex. Recognized teratogens include phenytoin, valproate, thalidomide, alcohol, and dioxin. Finding Stickler syndrome in a child with cleft or Robin sequence changes counseling from multifactorial risk to 50% autosomal dominant risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 43, 45); (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Phylogenetic Aspects and Embryology", p 23–24)

**22q11.2 deletion before pharyngeal surgery**: 22q11.2 deletion is the most common genetic cause of VPI, and up to about 8% of children with isolated cleft palate carry it. About 93% of deletions are de novo, and TBX1 is the key gene. Medially displaced, tortuous internal carotid arteries in the posterior pharyngeal wall are a recognized hazard, so many surgeons image the vessels (e.g., MRA) before a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty. The syndrome also brings cardiac defects (up to 85%), immune and calcium problems, and a higher rate of adult psychiatric illness. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 54–55)

**Stickler syndrome needs eye surveillance**: Stickler syndrome (autosomal dominant; COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2) is a leading syndromic cause of Robin sequence. It brings high myopia, cataract, and risk of retinal detachment, plus mixed hearing loss, midface flattening, and early arthropathy. Refer to ophthalmology and genetics early. A missed diagnosis leaves parents falsely counseled about low multifactorial recurrence risk when the true risk may be 50%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 45, 55)

**Cervical spine in Down syndrome**: about 15% of children with Down syndrome have atlantoaxial instability. No universal preoperative imaging rule exists, but symptomatic children (gait change, incontinence, neck pain) need flexion–extension films and neurologic evaluation before airway surgery. When instability is found, plan neutral-position intubation and positioning (with somatosensory monitoring if needed), which matters for adenotonsillectomy and DISE. Mucopolysaccharidoses carry a similar odontoid risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Anesthesiology", p 117)

**Pediatric condylar fractures**: injuries to the growing condyle need a short period of immobilization followed by structured physical therapy. Prolonged fixation or neglect risks TMJ ankylosis and growth disturbance, with later asymmetry or malocclusion. Follow these children through growth with orthodontic input, because secondary reconstruction may be needed. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery: Craniofacial Growth and Interdisciplinary Surgical Care", p 246)

**Odontogenic infections in children**: most severe pediatric dentoalveolar infections come from caries. They are polymicrobial (streptococci, Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, Klebsiella, Eikenella), so use broad bactericidal coverage that includes gram-negatives and anaerobes. Remove the carious tooth early along with drainage, because drainage alone often fails. Children can progress quickly to airway compromise, mediastinal spread, or necrotizing fasciitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery: Craniofacial Growth and Interdisciplinary Surgical Care", p 245–246)

**Usher syndrome urgency**: Usher syndrome (autosomal recessive) causes about half of deaf-blindness and up to about 10% of congenital severe-to-profound SNHL. Type 1 combines profound congenital SNHL with absent vestibular function (delayed sitting and walking), and retinitis pigmentosa appears later. Bilateral cochlear implants are indicated before age 2. Type 2 is the most common, with milder loss and normal vestibular function. Type 3 is progressive and is seen mainly in Finnish and Ashkenazi populations. ERG detects retinopathy before fundus changes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Ophthalmology", p 151)

**Inheritance and nomenclature**: about 70% of hereditary loss is nonsyndromic; of nonsyndromic cases roughly 75-80% are autosomal recessive, ~20% dominant, 2-5% X-linked and ~1% mitochondrial. Loci are named DFN (DeaFness, Nonsyndromic): DFNA = dominant, DFNB = recessive, DFN with no letter = X-linked, numbered in order of discovery. Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance; mitochondrial traits pass only through the mother, with variable expression from heteroplasmy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 467-468)

**GJB2 (DFNB1) specifics**: connexin 26 subunits assemble into connexons/gap junctions that recycle potassium from hair cells back to the stria. GJB2 accounts for up to half of recessive nonsyndromic deafness; 35delG predominates in people of European descent (about 2.5% carrier rate in the US Midwest) and 167delT in Ashkenazi Jews (~4% carriers). Truncating mutations give stable moderate-to-profound loss, whereas missense mutations tend to cause milder, progressive loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 469)

**Audioprofile clues in dominant nonsyndromic loss**: dominant loss is usually postlingual and progressive. Low-frequency (upsloping) loss points to WFS1 (DFNA6/14/38; ~75% of dominant low-frequency loss). A congenital, nonprogressive mid-frequency 'cookie-bite' loss points to TECTA (DFNA8/12). High-frequency progressive loss has many genes, classically KCNQ4 (DFNA2). DFNA9 (COCH) is distinctive for accompanying vestibular failure, which can precede and progress faster than the hearing loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 472-474, 491)

**Other named nonsyndromic genes**: OTOF (DFNB9, otoferlin) causes profound prelingual loss and frequently an auditory neuropathy phenotype with preserved OAEs. CDH23 missense mutations cause nonsyndromic DFNB12, while more severe CDH23 alleles cause Usher 1D (tip-link protein with protocadherin 15). MYO7A can cause Usher 1B, recessive DFNB2 or dominant DFNA11. POU3F4 (DFN3) is the most common X-linked nonsyndromic form: mixed loss with stapes fixation, a dilated IAC and perilymph gusher at stapes surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 469-475)

**Mitochondrial susceptibility numbers**: the m.1555A>G (12S rRNA, MTRNR1) variant makes the mitochondrial ribosome resemble the bacterial target, so even normal aminoglycoside doses can cause permanent loss, sometimes appearing months after exposure. It is found in 17-33% of aminoglycoside-induced loss and in about 1 in 500 people of European descent, prompting calls for pre-treatment screening in nonemergent settings (e.g., leukemia, tuberculosis). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 480, 484)

**Classic testing sequence taught by this text**: screen GJB2 first (if biallelic, no further testing needed); if CT/MRI shows EVA or incomplete partition, test SLC26A4 (Pendred/DFNB4); consider Usher genes next in severe-to-profound congenital loss (3-6% of such children, second to GJB2 among congenitally deaf CI users). Order MRI for suspected NF2, progressive loss or retrocochlear audiology. Up to 30% have no cause after history and examination. Modern practice replaces serial single-gene testing with comprehensive panels, but the phenotype logic still applies. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 490)

**Recurrence and prenatal counseling**: the empiric recurrence chance for a hearing couple who already have one deaf child is about 17.5% (higher than the older estimate of ~10%). Prenatal molecular diagnosis requires the familial variant to be known first; fetal DNA comes from chorionic villus sampling at 10-12 weeks or amniocentesis at 15-18 weeks, and preimplantation diagnosis is possible with IVF. Genetic counseling should occur before and after testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 491)

**Surveillance schedule after confirmed childhood SNHL**: audiologic testing about every 3 months in the first year, every 6 months through the preschool years, then yearly during school. Early amplification is the goal (JCIH: intervention by 6 months). A GJB2 diagnosis needs no additional specialty referral because it has no comorbidity, whereas JLNS needs cardiology/beta-blockade and Usher needs close ophthalmology follow-up. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 490-491)

**Behavioral test by developmental age**: behavioral observation audiometry (BOA, reflexive responses, no conditioning) at 6 months or younger is only a screen and needs physiologic cross-check. Visual reinforcement audiometry (head turn rewarded by a lighted toy/video) works best at 6-24 months and sometimes to 30 months. Conditioned play audiometry (peg-in-board) works best at about 3-5 years. Conventional hand-raise audiometry is used from about 5 years. Sound-field results reflect only the better ear, and unmasked bone conduction reflects only the better cochlea. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 320-322)

**Pediatric audiometric norms and cross-checks**: normal hearing in children is 15 dB HL or better; 25 dB HL or worse is educationally significant. The SRT should agree with the 500/1000/2000 Hz PTA within about 7 dB; an SRT much better than the PTA suggests poor conditioning or nonorganic loss, and much worse suggests distortion such as ANSD. A speech awareness threshold far better than the tonal thresholds flags a steeply sloping loss with residual low-frequency hearing. Pediatric word lists (PBK-50, WIPI, NU-CHIPS, ESP) are chosen by age and language level. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 319, 323)

**Transducer pitfall with tubes or perforation**: insert earphones are preferred in children, but with a patent tube or perforation they can create pressure artifacts of up to ~35 dB that mimic a low-frequency conductive loss; supra-aural earphones or sound field reduce this. A sound-field audiogram in a child with bilateral effusion and normal unmasked bone conduction does not exclude a severe unilateral SNHL. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 320-321)

**Newborn screening details**: AABR screens with a ~35 dB nHL click and detects ANSD; OAE screens miss ANSD and have high false-refer rates in the first 24 hours (vernix, mesenchyme), so rescreening before discharge, ideally with AABR, cuts over-referral. NICU stays over 5 days should be screened with AABR. In a program with a ~2% refer rate, about 1 in 5 referred infants (1 in 3 bilateral refers) has true hearing loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 346-347)

**JCIH risk indicators for congenital, delayed-onset or progressive loss**: caregiver concern; family history of permanent childhood loss; NICU care over 5 days or any of ECMO, assisted ventilation, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides) or loop diuretics, exchange-level hyperbilirubinemia; in utero infection (CMV, herpes, rubella, syphilis, toxoplasmosis); craniofacial anomalies; syndromes with hearing loss; postnatal bacterial meningitis; head trauma; chemotherapy. These children need ongoing surveillance even after a passed screen. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 345-346)

**School and preschool screening**: for children 3 years and older, screen pure tones at 20 dB HL at 1, 2 and 4 kHz in each ear. Tympanometric screening for effusion uses peak admittance and tympanometric width, and referral requires failing two screens about 6-8 weeks apart because effusions are transient. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 347-348)

**Nonorganic loss and auditory processing disorder in children**: suspect functional loss with inconsistent thresholds, exaggerated listening effort or SRT-PTA mismatch; the Stenger test helps in unilateral claims in older children, and the child's underlying psychosocial need should be addressed rather than simply labeled. Auditory processing disorder is a deficit in central auditory behaviors with normal intelligence and normal audiometric thresholds; evaluate only after cognitive and language causes are excluded, and manage with signal-to-noise strategies (FM/remote microphones, preferential seating, classroom acoustics). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 324, 348-350)

**ASSR and OAE limits**: the auditory steady-state response uses amplitude-modulated continuous tones at audiometric frequencies and can estimate thresholds in severe-to-profound loss beyond click-ABR output limits (~94-100 dB SPL). OAEs are generally absent once cochlear loss exceeds about 40-50 dB. ABR is unaffected by sedation; children from ~6 months to 6-7 years usually need sedation for diagnostic ABR. ABR referral indications include failed newborn screen, post-meningitis, sudden/fluctuating/progressive or unilateral SNHL, suspected eighth-nerve or brainstem disease, and the developmentally difficult-to-test child. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 341-344) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 466)

**Ototoxicity monitoring**: obtain a baseline before ototoxic therapy and notify the treating team when hearing shifts by 10 dB or more at one or more frequencies; high frequencies change first, so extended high-frequency audiometry and DPOAEs are the most sensitive monitors, although DPOAE change criteria are not yet standardized. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 348-349)

**Quantitative tympanometry in children**: tympanometric width (gradient) and peak compensated admittance are the best single predictors of effusion; width greater than ~200-250 daPa is highly specific for effusion, and peak admittance of 0.1 mmho or less strongly suggests fluid, whereas more than 0.6 mmho makes effusion unlikely. Width widens as disease worsens until the tracing becomes flat. Jerger letter types ignore gradient; type C is sometimes split at -100 to -200 daPa (C1) versus beyond -200 daPa (C2). Compare canal volume with the other ear when a perforation is suspected. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 327-331)

**Infant probe tone**: in infants under ~6 months a 226 Hz probe is insensitive to effusion; 660/678 Hz or 1000 Hz probes are used, and acoustic reflexes in neonates are usually measurable only with a high-frequency probe. A higher-frequency probe is also more sensitive to mass changes such as cholesteatoma or adhesions. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 326, 331-333)

**Misleading audiogram types**: a pseudoconductive pattern (air-bone gap with normal middle ear) occurs with third-window lesions such as enlarged vestibular aqueduct and superior semicircular canal dehiscence; a pseudo-sensorineural dip near 2 kHz (Carhart notch) occurs with stapes fixation; in ANSD the audiogram can take any shape and does not predict function. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 320)

**Middle-ear and canal acoustics**: the effective tympanic membrane-to-footplate area advantage is about 13:1 once only the vibrating drum is counted; losing the transformer (as in the old fenestration operation) costs ~25 dB or more. The middle ear resonates near 1.2 kHz (stiffness dominates below, mass above), and the ~2.5 cm ear canal resonates near 3.4 kHz. Head shadow produces 15-25 dB interaural level differences above ~2 kHz, while timing cues dominate at low frequencies. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Physical and Physiological Bases of Hearing", p 275-277)

**Pneumatic otoscopy details**: judge position, color, translucency and mobility. Effusion behind a translucent drum may show an air-fluid level or bubbles that shift with head position; a full, bulging drum obscures the malleus. Validated otoscopists achieve about 87% sensitivity and 74% specificity for effusion against myringotomy (target minimum 80%/70%). In the neonate the drum is nearly horizontal, the canal is filled with vernix for the first days and the soft inferior canal wall moves with pneumatic pressure, mimicking drum mobility; the drum takes an oblique position by about 1 month. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Clinical Examination: Ear and Related Structures", p 306-312)

**Tube otorrhea specifics**: a Gram stain with white cells suggests nasopharyngeal pathogens (pneumococcus, H influenzae, Moraxella), whereas absence of WBCs suggests canal flora (Pseudomonas, S aureus). Quinolone-steroid drops resolved tube otorrhea about 2 days faster than quinolone alone and cleared organisms better than oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (81% vs 59%). Fungi grow from only ~2% of tube otorrhea, and there is no proof quinolone drops cause fungal otitis. Otorrhea persisting beyond 7-10 days warrants drop-delivery check (tragal pumping), microscopic toilet and culture; beyond 10-21 days consider CT/biopsy for cholesteatoma, LCH, rhabdomyosarcoma or osteomyelitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otorrhea", p 432-440)

**Ototopical safety in a nonintact drum**: neomycin is the most common contact sensitizer in otic drops; sensitization mimics or perpetuates otitis (erythema, edema, pruritus, failure to heal), so a nonhealing ear on a neomycin drop should prompt a switch. Aminoglycoside drops can reach the inner ear through the round window and cause high-frequency/vestibular loss, so consensus guidance favors non-ototoxic (quinolone) drops whenever the TM is not intact. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otorrhea", p 437-439)

**Fungal and id reactions**: fungus in a draining ear may be a saprophyte (aural toilet only), a superficial secondary infection (add clotrimazole solution or tolnaftate powder), an allergen (steroids and immunotherapy) or invasive disease (systemic antifungals). A dermatophytid ('id') reaction is a sterile eczematous canal reaction to a fungal infection elsewhere in the body; treat the remote focus. Pseudomonas drainage classically smells sweet, whereas foul odor suggests anaerobes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otorrhea", p 431, 440-441)

**Retrotympanic vascular mimics on CT**: an aberrant internal carotid artery crosses the middle ear along the promontory and is continuous with the horizontal carotid canal (absent vertical segment); a persistent stapedial artery shows an absent foramen spinosum and an enlarged tympanic facial canal, and it supplies the middle meningeal artery; a dehiscent jugular bulb is continuous with the jugular vein (contrast settles doubt). Recognize these before biopsy or myringotomy of a red mass. Pediatric paragangliomas are often advanced and more often malignant, so screen for familial and multicentric disease. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination: Radiologic Aspects", p 383, 397-398) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tinnitus in Children", p 450)

**Imaging rules of thumb**: CT is first for external/middle-ear anomalies; inner-ear and nerve anatomy is best shown with high-resolution T2 MRI, with CT as an adjunct for bone. On CT the vestibular aqueduct should be no wider than the adjacent posterior semicircular canal. Congenital cochlear nerve deficiency often comes with a narrow IAC and cochlear-nerve aperture, whereas acquired atrophy shows a small nerve in a normal-caliber IAC. Normal IAC sagittal layout: facial nerve anterosuperior, cochlear anteroinferior ('7-up, Coke down'). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination: Radiologic Aspects", p 356, 373-374)

**Classic eponymous dysplasias**: Michel (complete labyrinthine aplasia), Mondini (small cochlea with deficient interscalar septum), Bing-Siebenmann (membranous labyrinth underdeveloped inside a normal bony capsule) and Scheibe (cochleosaccular, membranous-only dysplasia limited to the organ of Corti and saccule, normal on CT). Membranous dysplasias are invisible on imaging, which is why normal CT/MRI does not exclude an inner-ear cause. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 266)

**Timing of cochlear coiling**: this text places one cochlear turn at week 7 and completion of the full ~2.5-2.75 turns by week 8, with the adult labyrinth recognizable by week 10; otic-capsule ossification begins about week 15 from 14 centers and is complete by week 23, and each part ossifies only after reaching adult size. Sources differ by a few weeks on coiling, so teach 'coiling complete by about 8-10 weeks.' (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 263-265)

**Post-meningitic hearing loss numbers**: bacterial meningitis is the leading cause of acquired profound bilateral loss in children. Permanent loss follows 25-35% of pneumococcal versus 5-10% of H influenzae or meningococcal meningitis; low CSF glucose and ataxia/vestibular signs predict loss. Damage comes from the host inflammatory response, so prompt antibiotics with corticosteroids help prevent it. The book suggests audiology at 4-6 weeks so transient conductive loss can clear, but because labyrinthitis ossificans can develop within weeks, current practice is testing before or soon after discharge with urgent imaging if loss is found. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 483-484)

**Other ototoxins**: high-dose erythromycin causes a flat, bilateral loss within days that reverses after stopping (persists mainly with hepatic failure); evidence that vancomycin alone is ototoxic is weak, and many reports involve co-administered ototoxins. Loop-diuretic toxicity occurs within minutes, is usually reversible within 24 hours, and is less likely with slow infusion (e.g., ethacrynic acid under 15 mg/min). Carboplatin, once thought safer, can cause substantial loss at high dose. Aminoglycosides persist in inner-ear fluids for months, so repeated courses add risk; co-administered aspirin reduced gentamicin hearing loss from 13% to 3% in one trial (at the cost of GI effects). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 484-486)

**Noise dose**: damage is proportional to total sound energy, so a quieter sound for longer can equal a louder sound for less time. Exposure at or above 85 dBA is considered hazardous (ISO-1999; OSHA uses a 90 dBA permissible limit with an 85 dBA action level). Impulse noise above ~130 dB SPL causes direct mechanical injury with little individual variation, whereas 90-130 dB exposures cause metabolic injury with large individual variability. The cochlea is most susceptible at 3-6 kHz. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 489)

**Delayed and contralateral loss**: SNHL without a fracture line through the capsule ('cochlear concussion') is attributed to otic-capsule microfractures. A delayed, presumed autoimmune SNHL can develop in the opposite, uninjured ear in about 1-11% of patients months to years after a unilateral fracture and may respond to steroids. In children, head trauma accounts for roughly 11% of unilateral SNHL. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 488)

**Diagnosis remains clinical**: suspect PLF with sudden/fluctuating SNHL or vertigo after strain, barotrauma, violent sneeze or nose-blowing. Mondini dysplasia is strongly associated with PLF in children. No preoperative test is reliable (fistula test, ECoG SP/AP, beta-2 transferrin of middle-ear fluid all have limited sensitivity), and absence of visible leak at exploration does not exclude it. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 488) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Balance Disorders", p 454-455)

**Epidemiology**: 7-8% of school-age children report at least one vertigo episode, yet few ever see an otolaryngologist. In a series of over 2000 dizzy children the causes were migraine equivalent 25%, benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood 20%, head trauma 10%, ocular disorders 10%, inner-ear malformations 5%, vestibular neuritis 5%, labyrinthitis 5%, with the rest otitis media, CNS and psychogenic causes. Vestibular neuritis is rare before age 10. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Balance Disorders", p 453-455)

**Migraine variants and mimics**: benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy (recurrent, side-alternating head tilt with pallor/vomiting) is a migraine precursor that may evolve into benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood; image to exclude posterior fossa disease. Basilar-type migraine (reversible brainstem aura, typically adolescent girls, often perimenstrual) is rarer than vestibular migraine (<10% meet criteria). Refractive errors or convergence insufficiency can cause dizziness with headache, so a cycloplegic eye exam is part of the workup. Familial episodic ataxia (autosomal dominant) may respond to acetazolamide; 'tornado epilepsy' can mimic vertigo. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Balance Disorders", p 456-458)

**Pediatric testing choices**: rotary chair (child on a parent's lap, physiologic stimulus, less nausea) makes infants and young children testable and helps confirm bilateral loss, since calorics can be absent when rotation is normal. Bithermal calorics use 30 and 44 C, with ice water if no response; a reduced vestibular response above about 24% (Jongkees) suggests peripheral hypofunction, while directional preponderance is nonlocalizing. Pediatric balance can be screened with the P-CTSIB (foam plus visual-conflict dome) and age-normed motor scales (Peabody, Bruininks-Oseretsky). VEMP amplitudes vary with age, so interpret cautiously. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Vestibular Evaluation", p 414-421)

**SNHL and vestibular loss**: vestibular dysfunction is common in sensorineural loss and its prevalence rises with severity; severe bilateral loss delays head control, sitting and walking while fine motor skills stay normal, and exercise intervention improves motor development. Unilateral cochlear implantation can reduce VOR responses on the implanted side. Severe bilateral loss (Dandy syndrome) gives oscillopsia and instability in the dark or on uneven ground. Middle-ear effusion is a common, reversible cause of imbalance in toddlers. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Balance Disorders", p 458)

**Pediatric tinnitus**: children rarely volunteer tinnitus (about 6.5% spontaneously versus about 34% when asked directly), so ask specifically, especially in children with hearing loss, who report it more often; about 38% of children with cochlear implants report tinnitus, mostly with the device off at night. Peak age of reporting is about 12 years, and anxiety, behavioral and school problems are common associations. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tinnitus in Children", p 447-449)

**Bedside discrimination of pulsatile tinnitus**: venous pulsatile tinnitus diminishes with gentle pressure on the ipsilateral internal jugular vein, while arterial causes do not. Causes in children include AV malformations (27% in one pulsatile series), persistent stapedial artery (~1 in 5000), benign intracranial hypertension, hyperthyroidism and paragangliomas. Myogenic objective tinnitus is most often palatal myoclonus (confirm with palatal EMG; muscle relaxants or botulinum toxin) or stapedius/tensor tympani spasm. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tinnitus in Children", p 449-451)

**Developmental anatomy relevant to neonatal palsy**: at birth there is no mastoid process, so the facial nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen just under the skin behind the tympanic ring and can be injured by forceps or by an adult-style postauricular incision; the mastoid tip covers it by about age 3-5. The facial and abducens motor nuclei develop side by side in the pons, explaining combined VI-VII palsy in Möbius syndrome, and because sensory (nervus intermedius) and motor parts develop separately, congenital palsy often spares taste and sensation. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 259-260)

**NF2 classic criteria taught in this text**: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or a first-degree relative with NF2 plus either a unilateral schwannoma before age 30 or two of meningioma, glioma, schwannoma, or juvenile posterior subcapsular lens opacity. Incidence ~1 in 40,000-90,000; merlin gene on 22q12. Current practice uses the 2022 revised criteria for NF2-related schwannomatosis, which add molecular (NF2 variant) criteria. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 477)

**Infant temporal-bone anatomy**: in infants the cortex over the antrum is cribriform, so mastoid infection easily breaks through to a subperiosteal abscess; the antrum is near adult size at birth while the mastoid process only appears around age 1 and is well formed by 3. Males aged 1-3 are at highest risk of acute mastoiditis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 258-259) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otalgia", p 426)

**Origin of congenital cholesteatoma**: the leading theory is a fetal epidermoid formation, a nest of squamous cells in the anterosuperior middle ear next to the drum that appears between 10 and 33 weeks' gestation and normally involutes by 33 weeks; persistence explains the typical anterosuperior location. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 267)

**Middle-ear spaces from the embryo**: the tubotympanic recess (first pouch) is split by the second arch at week 7 into eustachian tube and tympanic cavity; four sacci (anticus, medius, superior, posticus) pneumatize the middle ear, epitympanum and mastoid. The sinus tympani is bounded by the ponticulus above and subiculum below; the chorda exits anteriorly through the petrotympanic fissure (canal of Huguier). The cochleariform process is a reliable landmark in revision surgery. The infant eustachian tube is ~1.7 cm (half adult length) and nearly horizontal, reaching adult angulation by about age 6. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 256-260)

**Why canal atresia can occur with a normal middle ear**: the lateral one-third (fibrocartilaginous) canal comes from the primary meatus, while the medial two-thirds forms when the meatal plate (solid ectodermal core) canalizes from about week 21 to 28; arrested canalization produces membranous atresia/stenosis with a relatively normal bony canal, drum and middle ear. Isolated external ear anomalies occur in about 1% of newborns, and about 9% of these children have hearing loss. Preauricular sinuses (~84/10,000) are far more common than microtia (~3/10,000). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Developmental Anatomy of the Ear", p 254, 265-266)

**Sinus development milestones (numbers)**: maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are aerated at birth; the maxillary sinus grows in two spurts (first ~3 years, then ages 7-12), reaches the plane of the infraorbital canal by ~2 years and its floor drops from ~4 mm above the nasal floor in infancy to level with it by ~8-9 years. The sphenoid begins pneumatizing at ~3 years and reaches adult size by about 12-15 years; the frontal sinus starts at ~2-3 years, is not radiographically separable from the ethmoid until ~6-8 years, and keeps growing through the teens. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Anatomy of the Paranasal Sinuses", p 921) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Face, and Orbit", p 945)

**Frontal sinus variability**: the frontal sinus is an ethmoid cell that invaded the frontal bone; roughly 60% arise from the fetal frontal recess (draining medial to the uncinate) and about one-third from an anterior infundibular cell (draining lateral to the uncinate, into the infundibulum). Unilateral absence occurs in ~5% and bilateral aplasia in ~4%; a persistent metopic suture prevents midline crossing. Small or absent frontal sinuses are associated with Down, Apert and Treacher Collins syndromes, while hyperpneumatization is seen with acromegaly. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Anatomy of the Paranasal Sinuses", p 916) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Anatomy of the Paranasal Sinuses", p 922) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Anatomy of the Paranasal Sinuses", p 923)

**Sphenoid danger numbers**: the internal carotid artery was clinically dehiscent in the lateral sphenoid wall in ~22% of cadavers and the optic canal in ~4%; intersinus septa may insert directly onto the carotid or optic prominence, so they should not be twisted or fractured. The natural ostium sits about 5 mm lateral to the posterior septum on the anterior wall; total bilateral sphenoid aplasia occurs in ~1%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Anatomy of the Paranasal Sinuses", p 924)

**Keros depths**: Keros classified olfactory fossa depth as type I 1-3 mm, type II 4-7 mm, and type III 8-16 mm (the book prints 3-7 and 7-16 mm). Type III leaves a long, thin lateral lamella unbacked by frontal bone and is the most hazardous for skull-base injury. Also note a low posterior ethmoid height on CT; when it is present, keep posterior dissection inferior and medial. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 958)

**Maxillary sinus hypoplasia trap**: significant hypoplasia occurs in ~3% of patients. Its features are a small sinus with a lateralized medial wall, an atelectatic infundibulum, and a thin hypoplastic uncinate lying against the orbit. The usual landmarks are displaced laterally, so uncinectomy risks orbital entry, and the uncinate must be taken carefully from medial to lateral. It also causes false 'nonclearing opacification' on plain films that has been treated with repeated antibiotics. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 954)

**Why the inferior meatal window failed**: inferior meatal antrostomies closed in most children and ~45% of adults (they need to be at least about 1 x 0.5 cm to stay open), and pediatric symptom control was poor (60% uncontrolled at 1 month, 73% at 6 months). Because cilia keep carrying mucus toward the natural ostium, the middle meatal antrostomy that incorporates the natural ostium replaced it. An ostium that is visible without uncinectomy is likely an accessory ostium. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1057) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1058)

**Pediatric sinus imaging pitfalls**: plain sinus films correlate poorly with CT in children. They have been inaccurate in up to 75% of inflammatory cases, with Waters view false-negative ~32% and false-positive ~49%, so they should not guide surgery. CT/MRI opacification is common in uncomplicated colds: in adults, 27 of 31 recently ill patients had abnormal CT that cleared within 2 weeks without antibiotics, and MRI showed major sinus abnormalities in ~68% of children with a simple URI. An abnormal scan therefore cannot confirm bacterial sinusitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 955) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 957) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1044)

**Pediatric CT protocol pearls**: noncontrast thin coronal/axial CT is the presurgical road map. Contrast is added only for orbital/intracranial complications or suspected neoplasm, and 'limited' sinus CT protocols miss 20-30% of findings and are not for preoperative planning or complications. The lens cannot be shielded, but a sinus CT gives only a few percent of the cataract-threshold dose. Order CT only when surgery is being considered or a complication is suspected, after maximal medical therapy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 956) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 957) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1059)

**Nasal valve numbers**: the internal valve (about 40 mm2 cross-section, versus ~150 mm2 in the main cavity) contributes roughly 50-75% of total airway resistance from nares to alveoli. Inspiratory velocity there approaches 18 m/s, slowing to 2-3 m/s in the cavity. Because resistance is set anteriorly, a small anterior septal deviation causes more obstruction than a large posterior one. Newborn nasal resistance is about four times that of adults and is more variable, so pediatric results must be compared with age-matched norms (airflow rises until ~16 years). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 928) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 929) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 964)

**Rhinomanometry vs acoustic rhinometry**: rhinomanometry measures the transnasal pressure-flow relationship (resistance). Repeating it after maximal decongestion separates the mucosal component from the fixed structural one, but it cannot localize the site of obstruction. Acoustic rhinometry uses reflected sound to map cross-sectional area and volume by distance (it localizes) but says nothing about flow. The two are complementary, and acoustic rhinometry is feasible in newborns and young children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Face, and Orbit", p 949) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Face, and Orbit", p 950)

**Pediatric septoplasty and growth**: postnatal septal cartilage does not appear to be a primary growth center. In cadaver data the cartilage completes most growth by ~age 2, while the perpendicular plate keeps growing into adulthood. Complete septal resection impairs midface growth in animals, but limited, conservative resection of only the deviated segment in children has not shown growth harm. Conservative septoplasty is therefore acceptable even in young children with significant obstruction. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 930)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **Mucociliary clearance numbers**: the 10-15 um mucous blanket has a watery sol layer (where cilia recover) and an overlying gel layer (which the effective stroke moves). It travels on average ~6 mm/min (range 1-20) toward the nasopharynx, except anterior to the inferior turbinate where flow is forward, and clears the nose in 10-20 minutes. A viral cold can impair transport for up to 2 weeks. **Exam clue**: secretions pooled on the nasal floor suggest a mucociliary disorder; the only other cause is total obstruction (adenoid hypertrophy, choanal atresia). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 932) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 933)

**Receptor pharmacology pearls**: alpha-2 receptors mainly constrict the venous capacitance (congestion) vessels and alpha-1 receptors the arteries. Ipratropium blocks cholinergic watery secretion but not the vasodilation/congestion. H1 antihistamines block histamine itch, sneeze and rhinorrhea but not congestion, which is partly blocked by adding an H2 blocker. Oxymetazoline at clinical concentrations does not change ciliary beat frequency, and benzalkonium chloride is ciliostatic in vitro without clinically important effect. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 933)

**Primary atrophic rhinitis (ozena)**: progressive atrophy of mucosa and underlying bone widens the cavity. Paradoxical obstruction comes from loss of normal airflow, with foul-smelling green crusts but little true pus. It is seen mostly in developing regions, with nutritional, iron and endocrine factors implicated. Isolating Klebsiella ozaenae is considered essential for the diagnosis. Distinguish it from secondary atrophic rhinitis after surgery, radiation or granulomatous disease. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 975)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Nasal clues to systemic/infectious disease in children**: sarcoid can show tiny (~1 mm) yellow submucosal nodules on boggy hyperemic mucosa. Diphtheria gives a white-yellow septal membrane with serosanguineous, highly contagious discharge that excoriates the upper lip, and characteristically little fever because the toxin is poorly absorbed from the nose. Rhinoscleroma and leprosy present first with obstruction before necrotic discharge. Granulomatous lesions (GPA, NK/T-cell lymphoma, EGPA, Sporothrix, Coccidioides) look alike and require biopsy, culture and special stains. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 970) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 975) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1039)

**Epidemiology numbers**: incidence is about 1 in 5,000-8,000 births (up to 1 in ~18,500 in large registries), with no sex or side predilection. The unilateral-to-bilateral ratio is ~1.6:1 (the classic 2:1 is inflated by late-detected unilateral cases). Modern CT series show mixed bony-membranous plates in ~71% and pure bony in ~29%, with essentially no purely membranous atresia, replacing the old 90% bony/10% membranous teaching. Major associated anomalies occur in ~47%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 968) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1029)

**Bedside and CT criteria**: suspect atresia when a 6 French catheter cannot be passed into the oropharynx (a mirror or a wisp of cotton under the nares checks airflow). Axial CT parallel to the hard palate, after suction and decongestion, shows the plate, vomer thickening and medial bowing of the pterygoid plates. The normal choanal airspace under age 2 is ~7 mm. **Choanal stenosis** is defined as choanal width under 6 mm on CT plus inability to pass a 6 Fr catheter beyond 32 mm, and it may not need surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1030)

**CHARGE specifics**: choanal atresia is found in 7-56% of CHARGE patients. CHARGE children are more likely to have bilateral disease (unilateral in only 36% versus 81% of non-CHARGE children), have airway obstruction beyond the choanae (tracheostomy needed in 14-30%), and have higher revision rates (~36%). The book's classic diagnosis is 3 or more cardinal features, excluding growth retardation; current practice adds CHD7 testing and major/minor criteria. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1029)

**Approach and timing pearls**: some surgeons use the 'rule of tens' (10 weeks, 10 lb, hemoglobin 10 g/dL) when the airway can be bridged. Transnasal endoscopic repair is now standard for all plate types (meta-analytic success ~85%): mucosal flaps, removal of the plate and about 5 mm of posterior vomer, then selective stenting for up to 4 weeks, with no-stent techniques also reported. The transpalatal route gives excellent exposure for revisions but causes crossbite/malocclusion in up to 50% and risks oronasal fistula. Blind transnasal puncture is obsolete (CSF leak, skull base injury). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1031) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1032)

**Adenoid facies (long-face syndrome)**: chronic nasal obstruction leads to mouth breathing and low tongue posture, producing vertical excess of the lower facial third, lip incompetence, a narrow high-arched maxilla and crossbite tendencies. Unilateral nasal obstruction during sleep triggers frequent large body movements. In young obligate/preferential nasal breathers, it can cause REM-related apnea and, if severe and prolonged, cor pulmonale. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 968)

**Reflux and pediatric sinonasal disease**: in older series, treating reflux in children with CRS improved sinonasal symptoms in ~79-89%. Neonatal nasal obstruction or rhinorrhea with mucosal edema may reflect nasopharyngeal regurgitation of feeds. The book suggests reflux evaluation before ESS in refractory pediatric CRS (lower-level evidence). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 970) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 976)

**Pediatric epistaxis profile**: uncommon under age 2 (look harder for a cause in infants), with peak frequency between 3 and 15 years and up to 60% of young teens reporting nosebleeds. Biopsies of prominent anterior septal vessels show inflammatory infiltrates around thin-walled vessels rather than varices. Usual drivers are URI, allergic rhinitis (rubbing, sneezing), dry winter air, digital trauma and nasal spray technique. Unilateral bleeding with obstruction or foul discharge suggests foreign body or tumor (JNA in adolescent boys, rhabdomyosarcoma with otitis media with effusion or cranial neuropathy). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 981) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 983)

**When to test hemostasis in a child**: recurrent nosebleeds despite preventive care warrant CBC and coagulation studies. In one referral series, 22% were anemic and ~8% had coagulation abnormalities, most often von Willebrand disease. ITP often presents with epistaxis (17% of children with ITP had major hemorrhage), and leukemia rarely presents with epistaxis alone, bleeding when platelets fall below ~20,000. HHT presents with recurrent epistaxis in over 90% of patients (mean onset ~12 years), and children may lack skin or visceral telangiectasias at first. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 983) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 985)

**Pediatric first-line care**: with no active bleeding, an antiseptic or antibiotic cream applied to the anterior septum is about as effective as silver nitrate cautery for recurrent childhood epistaxis. Add humidification, saline, allergy control and correct spray technique (aim laterally; cross-hand method), since 3-20% of steroid/antihistamine spray users bleed. If cautery is needed, do one side at a time or limit bilateral cautery to avoid septal perforation. Most pediatric epistaxis resolves without intervention. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 982) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 984)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Pediatric 'sinus headache' data**: in a case-control study of children with chronic or recurrent headache, only ~7% of headaches were attributable to sinusitis, yet 54% had previously been labeled sinus headache. URI, ABRS and strep pharyngitis are the commonest causes of acute pediatric headache in the ED. Red flags for intracranial disease and neuroimaging include an occipital location, inability to describe the pain, focal neurologic signs, morning or sleep-waking headache, and worsening when lying down. Isolated sphenoid sinusitis is rare in children and gives retro-orbital, vertex or occipital pain that wakes the child, sometimes with visual or cranial nerve signs. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 990) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 991)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **ICHD criteria in children**: pediatric migraine allows attacks of 1-72 hours (versus 4-72 in adults), may be bilateral, and photophobia/phonophobia may be inferred from behavior. Episodic tension-type headache needs at least 10 attacks that are bilateral, pressing and not worsened by activity, without nausea. Cluster headache involves unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis/miosis). The American Academy of Neurology recommends neuroimaging for recurrent pediatric headache when the neurologic exam is abnormal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 989) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 990)

**Pediatric Lyme facial palsy**: in endemic areas, Lyme disease is a leading cause of childhood facial palsy (peak age 5-9 years). Headache at presentation predicts Lyme, palsy can be bilateral, and erythema migrans may be absent. Confirm with a two-tier test (ELISA/IFA, then Western blot). The book treats with oral doxycycline for children 8 and older or amoxicillin under 8, for longer courses (21-28 days) for isolated palsy, and says corticosteroids are contraindicated. Current IDSA/AAP guidance allows short doxycycline courses at any age, generally for about 14-21 days, and does not recommend routine steroids. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 990) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral and Facial Neuropathic Pain in Children", p 998)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Trigeminal neuralgia in children**: rare, with case reports from infancy onward. MRI with MRA of the root entry zone is needed to look for vascular compression or tumor (an epidermoid has been found). Carbamazepine is first-line, then oxcarbazepine. Microvascular decompression is the most effective option when drugs fail; in the largest pediatric series (n = 23), venous compression and long delay to surgery predicted poorer results. Herpes zoster in healthy children is usually mild, and postherpetic neuralgia is uncommon and short-lived. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral and Facial Neuropathic Pain in Children", p 995) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral and Facial Neuropathic Pain in Children", p 996)

**Globe displacement localizes the mass**: frontoethmoid inflammation or mucopyocele pushes the globe down and/or laterally. Maxillary lesions push it up, lacrimal gland or temporal fossa masses push it medially, and an intraconal mass (e.g., optic glioma) causes pure axial proptosis. Proptosis is a difference of 2 mm or more between globes, and pseudoproptosis occurs with contralateral enophthalmos, lid retraction or unilateral high myopia. Forced duction separates mechanical restriction (tumor, abscess) from nerve palsy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1004) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1005)

**Pediatric medical-trial criteria and microbiology**: children 6 or younger with small medial subperiosteal abscesses do especially well with IV antibiotics, because they lack a frontal sinus and have simpler, less anaerobic flora. Good candidates have normal vision and intraocular pressure, minimal gaze restriction, no intracranial concern and normal immunity, with serial ophthalmology exams. Failure to improve within 48 hours, worsening vision or a large abscess calls for drainage. Cover Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group, S. aureus including MRSA, group A strep and anaerobes in complicated cases, and adolescent males carry the highest complication risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications of Rhinosinusitis", p 1066) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications of Rhinosinusitis", p 1069)

**Numbers and rules**: intracranial abscesses larger than ~2.5 cm or causing significant mass effect generally need surgical drainage, together with source sinus surgery. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when mass effect is possible and is usually unnecessary. Antiepileptic coverage is commonly given to children with intracranial abscesses. Steroids are reserved for severe edema or impending herniation. A brain abscess wall matures around day 10, which explains the insidious, antibiotic-masked course, and cavernous sinus thrombosis still carries ~30% mortality. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications of Rhinosinusitis", p 1071) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1009)

**Dermoid vs glioma vs encephalocele at the bedside**: dermoids are firm, noncompressible, nontransilluminating and nonpulsatile, with a midline pit (often with hair) anywhere from the glabella to the columella. About 60% sit on the lower dorsum. Encephaloceles are soft, bluish, compressible, may pulsate or transilluminate, and enlarge with jugular compression (Furstenberg). Intracranial or dural extension occurs in 4-45%. On CT a bifid crista galli and enlarged foramen cecum suggest extension, but the unossified frontonasal region in the first 6-8 months can mimic a bony defect, so MRI is complementary. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1018) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1021) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1024)

**Excision details**: incomplete removal recurs in 50-100%, so the cyst and entire tract (including any intraseptal or skull-base component) must be removed. External rhinoplasty gives exposure and cosmesis comparable to other routes (~5% recurrence), while vertical midline incisions widen in over half of children. For a tract approaching the skull base, a frozen section of the stalk tip can decide the approach: if it is free of epithelium, stop; if not, convert to a combined intracranial-extracranial approach. Avoiding unnecessary craniotomy matters because of its ~5% postoperative seizure risk. Small-window brow craniotomy and endoscopic-assisted techniques are less invasive options. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1024) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1025)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Cleft lip nasal deformity**: in a unilateral cleft, the orbicularis inserts abnormally into the alar base on the cleft side and the anterior nasal spine on the noncleft side. The cleft-side lower lateral cartilage is flattened and displaced posterolaterally with a separated dome, the caudal septum dislocates to the noncleft side, and the alar base is displaced. In a bilateral cleft, the premaxilla projects, the prolabium lacks muscle, and the nose has flared alar bases, a wide flat tip and a short columella. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1028) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 927)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Cleft rhinoplasty timing**: primary rhinoplasty at the time of lip repair (often open) is now favored and does not preclude revision. Intermediate rhinoplasty may be done in two stages (~4-6 years before school, then ~8-12 years after orthodontics/alveolar work). Definitive septorhinoplasty waits for skeletal maturity (~16-18 years). Key maneuvers address vestibular skin shortage (chondrocutaneous advancement), the alar-columellar web, and columellar strut/shield grafts. Improving the nasal airway can unmask or worsen VPI-related speech, so weigh airway against speech. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1028) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1029)

**Pediatric (AAP) criteria differ from the adult guideline**: diagnose ABRS in a child with (1) persistent nasal discharge and/or daytime cough for more than 10 days without improvement, (2) severe onset with fever of at least 39 C plus purulent discharge for at least 3 consecutive days, or (3) worsening around days 6-7 after initial improvement (new or recurrent fever, or more discharge or cough). About 5-10% of URIs in young children meet criteria (~6.7% with strict use). Uncomplicated colds last 5-10 days and peak by days 3-6, any fever is early and short (under 48 h), and discharge quality changes normally. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1040) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1042) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1043)

**Pediatric antibiotic dosing**: for mild uncomplicated pediatric ABRS in a child 2 or older without daycare or recent antibiotics, use amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/day divided twice daily, or 80-90 mg/kg/day where penicillin-nonsusceptible pneumococcus is prevalent. Use high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (80-90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin component) for age under 2, daycare, antibiotics within 30 days, moderate or severe illness, or treatment failure. A single dose of ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM can bridge a vomiting child. Reassess at 72 hours if there is no improvement. TMP-SMX and macrolides are poor choices because of pneumococcal resistance, and second/third-generation cephalosporin cross-reactivity in penicillin allergy is much lower than the historical 8-18%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1048)

**Ostial numbers**: the maxillary ostium is a small tube ~2.5 mm in diameter (~5 mm2) and ~6 mm long, high on the medial wall, so drainage depends on ciliary transport rather than gravity. Individual ethmoid cell ostia are only 1-2 mm. During acute viral rhinitis the maxillary ostium is fully patent only ~20% of the time. Closure creates first positive, then negative, intrasinus pressure that draws nasopharyngeal bacteria in with sniffing or nose blowing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1041)

**Pediatric definition and workup**: in children, recurrent acute sinusitis is defined like recurrent AOM: 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 in 12 months, with complete resolution in between (the adult definition is 4 or more per year). Daycare-driven viral URIs are the usual cause. Evaluate for allergy, cystic fibrosis (sweat test), quantitative immunoglobulins with IgG subclasses and pneumococcal polysaccharide responses, ciliary function, dental apical abscess and reflux before escalating. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1049)

**Pediatric CRS clues**: daytime cough (often worse at night) or throat clearing may dominate over discharge because posterior ethmoid drainage goes to the pharynx. Fever is uncommon, and nonspecific complaints (fatigue, poor school performance) should not be attributed to sinusitis without respiratory symptoms. Widening of the nasal bridge (pseudohypertelorism) has been described. Polyps point to CF or allergy, and any polyp in a child under 12 warrants a sweat chloride test. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1043) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1111)

**Pediatric CRS microbiology**: in chronic persistent disease, ethmoid and maxillary cultures yield mainly alpha-hemolytic strep, S. aureus and coagulase-negative staph (often contaminants), plus S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis. Anaerobes occur in only ~6-8%. Acute exacerbations are driven by the usual ABRS triad. Nasal, throat and nasopharyngeal swabs do not predict sinus pathogens, and middle-meatal sampling had ~75% sensitivity versus maxillary puncture in children with chronic disease. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1046) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1047)

**Outcome numbers for counseling**: adenoidectomy alone succeeds in roughly 50-69% of children with medically refractory CRS (meta-analysis 69%), works best under ~5-6 years, and is the first operation for most pediatric otolaryngologists (~81%). Pediatric ESS, usually anterior ethmoidectomy plus maxillary antrostomy, has a pooled success of ~89% (range 77-100%; 882 children). Results are worse with immunodeficiency, CF, ciliary dyskinesia, younger age and smoke exposure, and revision rates are around 10%. Absorbable packing has made routine second-look anesthesia unnecessary, and most surgeons (~89%) no longer perform it. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1050) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1057) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1061)

**Facial growth and ESS**: an age-matched 10-year cohort (Bothwell) found no quantitative or qualitative facial growth difference after pediatric ESS, despite growth disturbance in piglet models. Families can be told there is no evidence of clinically significant growth effects. Still, be very conservative in the developing frontal recess (do not strip it or dissect above the middle turbinate insertion), and enter the pediatric sphenoid through the posterior ethmoid or superior meatus rather than by enlarging the ostium from the narrow sphenoethmoidal recess. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1060) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1062)

**Absolute indications for pediatric ESS**: (1) complete nasal obstruction from CF polyposis, (2) antrochoanal polyp, (3) intracranial complications, (4) mucocele/mucopyocele, (5) orbital abscess, (6) traumatic optic canal injury, (7) dacryocystorhinitis from refractory sinusitis, (8) fungal sinusitis, and selected (9) meningoencephaloceles and (10) neoplasms. Refractory CRS and recurrent acute sinusitis are relative indications that follow failed medical therapy and adenoidectomy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1059)

**Pre-ESS immune screen in children**: obtain IgG, IgA, IgM (and IgE) plus vaccine titers (tetanus, Hib, pneumococcus) in any child being considered for sinus surgery. Interpret IgG subclass deficiency cautiously, because ~10% of the healthy population has an abnormal subclass level. If a deficiency is found, ESS can still improve symptoms, but families should expect that complete weaning from antibiotics is unlikely. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1059)

**Geography and pediatric AFRS**: AFRS prevalence varies widely, from ~23% of surgical CRS cases in the southern United States to near zero in some northern locations. Dematiaceous molds (Bipolaris, Curvularia, Alternaria, Drechslera) are more common causes than Aspergillus. Allergic mucin shows degenerated eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals with sparse hyphae. In children, slow expansion can remodel the lamina papyracea and skull base, causing proptosis or telecanthus. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1052) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications of Rhinosinusitis", p 1072)

**Pediatric findings and natural history**: seasonal allergic rhinitis is uncommon before a child has had at least two to three pollen seasons, so perennial (dust mite, pet, cockroach) sensitization dominates in infants and toddlers. Look for the allergic salute and its transverse supratip crease, allergic shiners (not pathognomonic), Dennie-Morgan lines, cobblestoned conjunctiva, mouth breathing, and pale blue-gray boggy turbinates. Polyps are unusual in pediatric allergic rhinitis, and a polyp should prompt CF evaluation. A family history of atopy is present in 50-75%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1076) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1077) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1079)

**Pediatric pharmacotherapy safety**: intranasal steroids differ in systemic effect. A year of beclomethasone slowed growth by about 1 cm in prepubertal children, whereas fluticasone, mometasone and ciclesonide showed no growth effect and are preferred. Use the lowest effective dose and remember additive inhaled asthma steroids. Epistaxis occurs in up to ~20% of users, and the cross-hand technique (spray directed laterally) reduces septal trauma. Cetirizine and levocetirizine sedate ~10-15% versus placebo-level sedation with loratadine and fexofenadine. OTC cough and cold combinations are not advised in young children (FDA: avoid decongestants under 2 years). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1084) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1085) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1038)

**Duration and disease modification**: when successful, immunotherapy is usually continued 3-5 years at maintenance dose. Benefit then persists for up to about 10 years after stopping, and immunotherapy may lower the risk of progressing from rhinitis to asthma and of new sensitizations, which is a particular argument in children. (The book predates FDA-approved SLIT tablets; current tablets cover grass, ragweed and dust mite.) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1087)

**Testing pitfalls**: intradermal testing after a negative skin prick test has low predictive value and should not be used for screening. Multi-test devices show poor reproducibility. Food testing is not indicated for isolated rhinitis without a convincing history of immediate reactions. Skin and serum testing are both sensitive but only moderately specific, so test only plausible allergens. Back skin is often used in young children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergic Rhinitis", p 1080)

topic: Ear and Nasal Foreign Body Removal
text: **Nasal foreign body numbers**: peak age is 2-4 years; most children are asymptomatic and insertion is unwitnessed. Unilateral foul mucopurulent discharge is the hallmark but may take time to develop; epistaxis occurs in up to ~7%. About 60% of objects are inorganic (toys, beads), and organic material swells and inflames faster. Button batteries can perforate the septum within as little as 7 hours (12% of nasal foreign bodies in one series). Radiographs help find metallic objects or batteries in uncooperative children with thick secretions. **Rhinolith**: a long-retained object encrusted with mineral salts that can erode into the sinus or palate; it is fractured and removed, rarely through the nasopharynx or by lateral rhinotomy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1089) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1090) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1092)

topic: Ear and Nasal Foreign Body Removal
text: **Removal set-up and aftercare**: restrain the child upright on a parent's lap, with topical lidocaine/oxymetazoline. Have a right-angle hook, 5-7 Fr Frazier suction, alligator forceps, a balloon catheter and an endoscope or microscope ready, and always get behind the object and pull forward. Positive pressure through the mouth with the other nostril occluded can expel unilateral objects. ED removal succeeds in 92-96%, but each failed attempt worsens edema and cooperation. Large nasopharyngeal or small anterior objects carry the highest aspiration risk, and routine antibiotics are not needed after uncomplicated removal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1091) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1093)

**Pediatric nasal fracture pattern**: the cartilaginous, unfused pediatric nasal vault gives greenstick injuries and an 'open book' splaying of the nasal bones over the frontal processes of the maxilla, rather than adult-type displacement. Edema hides them, and crepitus may be absent. Always check for septal hematoma (drain immediately and quilt or pack) and keep CSF rhinorrhea in mind. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1102)

**Reducing a pediatric fracture**: most pediatric nasal fractures need no treatment. When reduction is needed, closed reduction under general anesthesia usually suffices, but greenstick fractures rarely 'snap' into place, and displaced incomplete fractures may require completion osteotomy. Counsel families before reduction that definitive septorhinoplasty may be needed after growth. Septal fractures with loss of central support may need primary reconstruction. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1103)

**Pediatric condyle and dentition rules**: the condyle is the most common pediatric mandible fracture site, often from a fall on the chin with a chin laceration. Under ~3 years, intracapsular crush injuries of the condylar head risk ankylosis and growth disturbance. If occlusion is achievable, treat closed with soft diet and early range-of-motion exercises. If MMF is needed, about 1 week suffices in young children (longer with age), followed by guiding elastics. Fixation depends on dentition: primary (0-5 y) conical teeth make circumdental wires unstable (use splints or Ivy loops), mixed dentition (6-11 y) is hardest (splints or circummandibular/piriform/circumzygomatic wires), and permanent dentition (12+ y) allows standard arch bars. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1100) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1103)

**Pediatric orbital/zygoma differences**: orbital floor and rim fractures are uncommon until the maxillary sinus pneumatizes. Before then, the frontal bone and orbital roof take the impact, and roof fractures can extend intracranially. Zygomatic arch injuries in children are usually greenstick and can be elevated through a Gillies (temporal) or sulcus approach without fixation. Treat displaced ZMC fractures with ORIF. Children with the 'white-eyed' trapdoor floor fracture may show nausea and vomiting with little ecchymosis, so do not wait for late repair, which has inferior results. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1104) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1105)

**Age changes the pattern**: under ~6 years, frontal-region fractures are the most common pediatric facial fractures. Before the frontal sinus develops (~age 5), there is no 'crumple zone', so fractures are greenstick and run up to the vertex or back across the orbital roof, with high rates of associated brain injury. Outcomes of frontal sinus obliteration in children are unknown, so preserve or re-establish the frontal outflow tract when the sinus is present. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1106)

**Pediatric NOE**: the nasoethmoid complex is minimal before age 2 and not prominent until 5-6 years, so NOE fractures are rare in young children. When they occur, they need the same aggressive repair as in adults, reestablishing intercanthal distance and the medial canthal tendon (often via a coronal approach, given associated cranial injury), because rounding and telecanthus are obvious and hard to correct later. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1105)

**Pediatric laceration pearls**: topical LET (lidocaine-epinephrine-tetracaine) gives anesthesia before cleansing. Children form hypertrophic scars more readily, so wide undermining just deep to the subcutaneous fat reduces tension. Align landmarks first (vermilion, brow). Fast-absorbing gut skin sutures under Steri-Strips avoid suture removal, and cyanoacrylate adhesive gives comparable cosmesis for clean low-tension wounds. Give tetanus immunization as indicated. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Nose, Facial Bones, and Paranasal Sinuses", p 1100)

**Fibro-osseous lesions and syndromes**: osteoma is the most common paranasal sinus tumor (~3% of sinus CTs, frontoethmoid predominance). Multiple osteomas suggest **Gardner syndrome** (autosomal dominant, with colorectal polyps that become malignant in essentially all cases, plus supernumerary teeth), which warrants GI referral. Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia may be part of **McCune-Albright syndrome** (cafe-au-lait spots, precocious puberty; activating GNAS mutation), with craniofacial involvement in ~50% of polyostotic and ~25% of monostotic cases. Delay fibrous dysplasia surgery until after puberty unless there is functional compromise. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1114)

**Aggressive pediatric fibro-osseous/giant cell lesions**: psammomatoid (juvenile active) ossifying fibroma occurs in the first two decades, is locally aggressive in the ethmoid and frontal regions (proptosis, facial swelling), may show fluid levels on MRI, and needs complete excision. Ossifying fibroma is well circumscribed with a thick bony rim, unlike the ground-glass, poorly marginated fibrous dysplasia. Central giant cell lesions, about one-third of benign pediatric jaw tumors in one series, are slow and bone-destructive and recur after curettage. Sinonasal desmoid fibromatosis does not metastasize but invades locally, and complete resection is preferred. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1115) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1116)

**Pediatric sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy**: rhabdomyosarcoma (embryonal or alveolar) is the most common primary nasal/sinus malignancy in children and can be congenital. It presents as a friable mass with obstruction and epistaxis, sometimes with ipsilateral otitis media with effusion, deep facial pain or a sixth nerve palsy (parameningeal spread). Lymphoma is the most prevalent malignancy across the nose, nasopharynx and sinuses, and extranodal nasal NHL (including NK/T-cell lymphoma with angioinvasive necrosis) does worse than Waldeyer ring Hodgkin disease. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma in children presents with a posterior triangle node and unilateral otitis media with effusion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 983) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1109) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1112) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1118)

**Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma**: it is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood (mean age ~7; rapid unilateral proptosis, often superonasal). Biopsy (or excision if it can be done without morbidity), then chemoradiation per Intergroup protocols. The globe is spared in over 90%, exenteration is reserved for resistant tumors, and 3-year survival is ~93%, the most favorable head and neck site. Radiation cataract is the common visual cost. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1011)

**Nasal and periocular hemangiomas**: nasal tip hemangiomas involute slowly and can deform developing alar cartilages, leaving fibrofatty residua, so earlier treatment or surgery may be justified. Periorbital (often superonasal) hemangiomas threaten amblyopia from visual-axis occlusion or astigmatism, which is an indication for treatment. Intranasal hemangiomas present with unilateral obstruction and epistaxis. The book lists Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy among hemangioma complications; current understanding attributes it to kaposiform hemangioendothelioma/tufted angioma rather than common infantile hemangioma. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1010) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1109) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1110)

**Orbital and imaging specifics**: exophthalmos is the most common sign of orbital involvement and is present in about 14% of JNA patients. The CT hallmarks are erosion of the pterygoid plates with anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary wall. MRI better separates tumor from obstructed secretions at the cribriform plate and cavernous sinus and suits serial follow-up. Office biopsy should be avoided. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1013) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1116)

**Pediatric papilloma spectrum**: vestibular squamous papillomas are common in children. They are 1-3 mm cauliflower-like growths on the septum or vestibular skin that often recur and need close follow-up (HPV-related spread to the ear canal has been reported). Inverted papilloma is rare in children; with older open techniques recurrence was 25-75%, and 10-15% have associated SCC (true malignant transformation under 2%), mainly in adults. A choanal polyp arising anywhere other than the maxillary sinus should raise suspicion for inverted papilloma. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1111)

**Retention cyst vs mucocele**: maxillary mucous retention cysts (2.7-9.6% prevalence on imaging, any age) arise from blocked seromucinous gland ducts. They appear as dome-shaped, well-marginated densities, often resolve, and are usually incidental. A mucocele is an expansile, epithelium-lined collection that remodels bone. Remove a retention cyst only when it obstructs the ostium and the symptoms truly match, after excluding dental, migraine and vascular pain causes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1113)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Veau classification**: Veau I involves the soft palate only; Veau II involves hard and soft palate but stays posterior to the incisive foramen (secondary palate only); Veau III is a complete unilateral cleft lip and palate; Veau IV is a complete bilateral cleft lip and palate. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1166)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Cleft lip spectrum and epidemiology**: Cleft lip with or without palate occurs in roughly 1 in 500-1,200 births, is more common in boys and on the left, and is accompanied by cleft palate about 75% of the time; bilateral clefts are about 15% of clefts. A microform cleft shows vermilion notching and a groove with intact lip skin, an incomplete cleft preserves a nasal sill (Simonart band), and a complete cleft disrupts lip, sill and alveolus. Isolated cleft palate (about 1 in 2,000) is a separate entity with no sex predilection and is twice as likely as cleft lip to be part of a syndrome. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1162)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
