text: **Repair timing and the rule of 10s**: Typical sequence: nasoalveolar molding from birth to 3 months, lip repair at 2-4 months (classic rule of 10s: at least 10 weeks old, 10 lb, hemoglobin 10 g/dL), palatoplasty at 9-14 months, speech surgery at 3-5 years, alveolar bone grafting at 7-9 years (mixed dentition), and orthognathic surgery at 14-18 years. Primary rhinoplasty is usually done at the time of lip repair. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1164)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Lip and palate repair techniques**: Millard rotation-advancement is the most widely used unilateral lip repair: it keeps the Cupid bow, puts closure tension under the alar base and uses the C-flap to lengthen the columella. For the hard palate, von Langenbeck uses bipedicled mucoperiosteal flaps, while the Bardach two-flap repair uses flaps on the greater palatine pedicle. The soft palate is closed by intravelar veloplasty or a Furlow double opposing Z-plasty, which also lengthens the velum; vomer flaps help close the nasal layer in wide or bilateral clefts. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1166)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Premaxillary setback risk**: In bilateral clefts, setting back a protrusive premaxilla is a last resort, because the premaxillary-vomer suture is a growth center. Early setback risks midface retrusion and a concave profile. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1166)

**Submucous cleft rarely needs surgery**: Only a minority of children with an overt submucous cleft (bifid uvula, zona pellucida, notched posterior hard palate) develop VPI. When surgery is needed, gap size, palate length, lateral wall motion and closure pattern guide the choice; the Furlow Z-plasty is the most-reported repair, with pharyngeal flap or intravelar veloplasty as alternatives. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1167)

**Medialized carotids in 22q11.2 deletion**: Velocardiofacial syndrome (22q11.2 microdeletion, diagnosed by FISH or microarray) is the most common syndrome with a palatal anomaly as a key feature, although only about 9% have an overt cleft. The internal carotid arteries may run medially behind the posterior pharyngeal wall, so image the course of the vessels before a pharyngeal flap, sphincter pharyngoplasty or tonsil surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1170)

**Airway escalation numbers**: About half of infants with Robin sequence are managed with prone or side positioning alone. Of those who need more, about half do well with a nasopharyngeal airway alone, for an average of about 44 days (range 16-104), with inpatient oximetry. Tongue-lip adhesion works best in nonsyndromic infants; mandibular distraction is favored in syndromic infants; tracheotomy is reserved for multilevel obstruction (e.g., subglottic stenosis, sphincteric pharyngeal collapse) or major neurologic or pulmonary comorbidity. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1169)

**Sher endoscopic obstruction types**: Endoscopy in Robin sequence shows four obstruction patterns: type 1, the tongue falls back to the posterior pharyngeal wall (true glossoptosis); type 2, the tongue pushes the velum against the posterior wall; type 3, the lateral pharyngeal walls move medially; type 4, sphincteric circumferential collapse. Types 3-4 respond poorly to tongue-based procedures. Incidence is about 1 in 8,500-14,000. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1169)

**Treacher Collins airway threshold**: Treacher Collins syndrome (autosomal dominant, TCOF1 on 5q32) is a bilateral expression of Tessier clefts 6, 7 and 8, with malar and zygomatic hypoplasia, a hypoplastic mandible, microtia, ossicular malformation with conductive loss, and sometimes absent parotid glands. An oropharyngeal airway diameter under 1 cm is linked to sudden death and is an indication for tracheotomy. Mandibular distraction often allows later decannulation; bone-anchored hearing devices address the conductive loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1172)

**Down syndrome oral and airway features**: Children with trisomy 21 develop progressive lip enlargement, true or relative macroglossia with a fissured tongue by about age 5, a high narrow palate, a narrow nasopharynx (platybasia), pharyngeal hypotonia, delayed and missing teeth, and periodontal disease. Their chronic rhinorrhea and otitis respond poorly to adenoidectomy unless true adenotonsillar obstruction is present. Tongue reduction helps oral hygiene but has no proven speech benefit. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1171)

**Absolute vs relative indications**: Absolute indications for adenotonsillectomy (greatest risk of death or major morbidity) are adenotonsillar hyperplasia with OSA, failure to thrive or abnormal dentofacial growth, suspected malignancy, and hemorrhagic tonsillitis. Relative indications include obstruction-related dysphagia or speech problems, recurrent or chronic pharyngotonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, streptococcal carriage and halitosis; adenoidectomy alone is added for otitis media and recurrent adenoiditis or rhinosinusitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1193)

**Tonsil and adenoid grading**: Tonsil size is graded 1-4 with the tongue relaxed, by how much of the oropharyngeal width is filled: 1 is 0-25%, 2 is 25-50%, 3 is 50-75%, and 4 is 75-100%. The grade correlates poorly with PSG severity. On endoscopy (Parikh), adenoid grade 1 touches nothing, grade 2 touches the torus tubarius, grade 3 adds the vomer, and grade 4 touches the soft palate at rest. On a lateral neck film, an adenoid-nasopharynx ratio above 0.73 suggests significant hypertrophy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1197)

**Response rates by phenotype**: Adenotonsillectomy resolves OSA in more than 80% of normal-weight children but in fewer than 30% of obese children; about 30% of obese children have OSA, roughly 10 times the rate in lean children. Residual disease is also likely in Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, achondroplasia, mucopolysaccharidoses, cerebral palsy, and mandibular or midface hypoplasia. Enuresis is present in up to half of children with sleep-disordered breathing and resolves in about 60% after surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1201)

**Down syndrome perioperative checklist**: About 10-20% of children with trisomy 21 have atlantoaxial instability. Neck pain, hyperreflexia or clonus calls for neurosurgical or orthopedic evaluation, and an atlas-dens interval above 4 mm on flexion-extension films warrants further assessment. Plan an endotracheal tube about one size smaller than predicted (small subglottis), keep neck extension gentle, admit overnight after tonsillectomy, and limit opioids; respiratory complications are about 5 times more common than in controls. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1204)

**Sickle cell and outpatient selection**: For sickle cell disease, transfuse to a hemoglobin of about 10 g/dL, give generous IV hydration, keep the patient warm and treat pain well to avoid a crisis. Outpatient tonsillectomy is reasonable for healthy children over about 3 years old. Admit children much younger than 3, those with severe OSA, those who live far away, and those with Down syndrome, craniofacial anomalies, bleeding disorders or obesity. The chapter used AHI >15 as its severe threshold, but the current AAO-HNS trigger for overnight monitoring is AHI >=10 or nadir <80%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1205)

**Grisel syndrome**: Grisel syndrome is nontraumatic atlantoaxial subluxation from inflammatory laxity of the transverse ligament after adenoidectomy, pharyngeal infection, or anesthetic injected into the prevertebral space. It is more likely after a recent URI. It presents about a week after surgery with neck pain and torticollis, and an atlas-dens interval above 4 mm in a child confirms it. Treat with immobilization and an urgent neurosurgical consult. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1211)

**Delayed complications of adenotonsillectomy**: Velopharyngeal insufficiency after adenotonsillectomy is usually temporary (6 weeks to 6 months) and becomes clinically significant in about 1 in 1,500-3,000 cases. Persistent cases often involve an unrecognized submucous cleft or a 22q11 deletion; give speech therapy after 6 months and consider pharyngoplasty after 6-12 months. Nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal stenosis comes from removing too much mucosa, especially at several levels at once. Tonsil tags are found in 9-28%, and regrowth after intracapsular surgery in about 0.5-6%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1211)

**Intraoperative hazards**: After intubating a severely obstructed child, falling saturation with pink frothy secretions means postobstructive (negative-pressure) pulmonary edema: give PEEP, reintubate if needed, and diurese gently. In children aged 5-7, loose incisors can be knocked out by the mouth gag; if a tooth is missing, get a chest film. Burns of the oral commissure are the tonsillectomy complication most often litigated; prevent them with insulated cautery tips and a moist barrier between metal retractors and the lips. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1210)

**Tonsil asymmetry and lymphoma**: Most apparent tonsil asymmetry in children is benign (pillar effacement or true benign asymmetry). Tonsil lymphoma usually comes with rapid enlargement over weeks, nodes larger than 3 cm, dysphagia, night sweats or fever. An asymptomatic child with asymmetry can be watched for several months. Excise when the tonsil grows, when there are B symptoms or mucosal change, or in transplant patients, where PTLD is a risk. Routine histology of normal tonsils finds occult malignancy in only about 0.01% of specimens. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1195)

**PTLD presenting as adenotonsillar hypertrophy**: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder affects about 5-10% of organ recipients; it is more common after heart or lung transplant and with potent T-cell suppression. It is EBV-driven B-cell expansion, and Waldeyer ring and the cervical nodes are its most common head and neck sites. New tonsil or adenoid enlargement or OSA in a transplant child calls for adenotonsillectomy for both diagnosis and airway relief, along with reduced immunosuppression. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1271)

**Strep diagnostics and carriers**: Rapid antigen testing is highly specific but has only moderate sensitivity (about 60-90%), so a negative rapid test should be followed by culture when strep is suspected. An ASO titer above about 333 Todd units, or a 2-fold rise, confirms recent infection; titers peak at 3-6 weeks. GAS carriage affects about 5-40% of children. Carriers rarely spread disease or develop sequelae, so do not test children with clearly viral features such as cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, hoarseness or oral ulcers. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1199)

**When to treat strep carriage**: Eradication (e.g., clindamycin or rifampin-containing regimens), and tonsillectomy if that fails, is reserved for carriers with a family history of rheumatic fever, ping-pong spread within the family, a personal history of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, or a school outbreak. In the Paradise trial, untreated control children averaged only 1.17, 1.03 and 0.45 episodes in years 1-3, which shows how often recurrent tonsillitis resolves on its own. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1202)

**Recurrence and quinsy tonsillectomy**: Peritonsillar abscess recurs in about 10-15% of patients. Routine tonsillectomy after a first abscess is not indicated. About 20-30% of patients already meet criteria for tonsillectomy (e.g., 2-3 tonsillitis episodes in the prior year); for them, a quinsy (hot) tonsillectomy or an interval tonsillectomy after drainage is reasonable. Tonsillectomy is also the definitive option for very young or uncooperative children and for inadequately drained abscesses. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1195)

**Rates, mortality and the sentinel bleed**: Primary hemorrhage occurs in about 0.2-2.2% and secondary hemorrhage in 0.1-3%, with an overall rate of about 1.5% and the highest risk in older males. Tonsillectomy mortality is about 1 in 16,000-35,000, roughly a third from primary bleeding and most of the rest from anesthesia. In a series of catastrophic outcomes, most deaths followed repeated delayed bleeds; more than 60% had 2-7 sentinel bleeds before the fatal event, at a median of day 6. Repeated or uncontrollable bleeding with normal coagulation studies should prompt angiography for a vascular anomaly or pseudoaneurysm. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1211)

**Technique and NSAIDs**: In the UK National Prospective Tonsillectomy Audit, hot techniques (diathermy or coblation) for both dissection and hemostasis had about 3 times the secondary hemorrhage rate of pure cold-steel dissection with ties or packs. Coblation works at about 45-85 C, versus about 400 C for monopolar cautery. NSAIDs other than ketorolac do not increase bleeding; bleeding rates with ketorolac have been reported at 4.4-18%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1208)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **von Willebrand disease protocol for tonsillectomy**: von Willebrand disease affects about 1% of people, and type 1 (80-90%) responds to desmopressin, while types 2 and 3 usually do not. A typical tonsillectomy protocol is desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 30 minutes before surgery, at 12 hours, and then daily until the fossae heal; aminocaproic acid about 50 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days to counter salivary fibrinolysis; half-maintenance fluids around each dose; and at least 23-hour observation. Watch for hyponatremia and tachyphylaxis, and switch to vWF-containing factor concentrate if they occur. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1205)

**Gas-exchange and UARS thresholds**: Clinically important nocturnal hypoxemia was defined as saturation below 89% for more than 5% of total sleep time, and hypoventilation as end-tidal CO2 above 50 Torr for more than 10% of total sleep time. Upper airway resistance syndrome can produce symptoms with an AHI below 1.5 through RERAs and flow-limited events. PLMD needs more than 5 limb movements per hour. Clinical history predicts OSA poorly: only about 55% of children suspected clinically have OSA on PSG. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Sleep Disorders", p 1226)

**Pediatric PAP indications and growth effects**: CPAP or BiPAP is indicated for persistent OSA after adenotonsillectomy, when surgery is contraindicated or declined, for complex central plus obstructive apnea, for severe OSA before or after surgery, and for pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale. Long-term mask use in a growing child can cause midface hypoplasia and maxillary dental compression, so plan periodic cephalometric or orthodontic review. Rapid maxillary expansion and nasal anti-inflammatories are nonsurgical options. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Sleep Disorders", p 1227)

**Anesthetic sensitivity in pediatric OSA**: Children with OSA are more sensitive to opioids and inhaled anesthetics and can have delayed emergence. Nitrous oxide can raise pulmonary artery pressure, so use it cautiously in children at risk for pulmonary hypertension. In one series of children under 6, postoperative respiratory complications occurred in 9.8% of those under 3 versus 4.9% of older children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Sleep Disorders", p 1228)

**HIV oral disease in children**: About half of HIV-infected patients have an oral complaint at diagnosis. In children the common findings are candidiasis (which can mark antiretroviral failure), recurrent HSV or large aphthous ulcers lasting more than a month, and bilateral parotid enlargement, whereas hairy leukoplakia and Kaposi sarcoma are uncommon. In one study, oral Candida was the earliest sign of HIV in infants younger than 15 months. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1269)

**GI, polyposis and nutritional clues**: Crohn disease causes cobblestoned buccal mucosa, deep linear ulcers, lip swelling and mucosal tags. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome causes flat brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa. Gardner syndrome causes jaw osteomas, supernumerary or unerupted teeth and odontomas. Plummer-Vinson syndrome is iron deficiency, glossitis and dysphagia from esophageal webs, with a raised risk of pharyngeal and esophageal carcinoma. Niacin deficiency gives a beefy red tongue, riboflavin deficiency a magenta tongue, zinc deficiency hypogeusia, and scurvy a hemorrhagic gingivitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1274)

**Hematologic and immunodeficiency clues**: About 10% of leukemias show oral infiltrates, such as spongy gingival hyperplasia (seen in at least a third of children with leukemia), petechiae and ulcers. Oral GVHD (lichenoid lesions) occurs in up to 80% after bone marrow transplant. ITP presents with gingival bleeding and sublingual hematoma. Clues to primary immunodeficiency include severe early periodontitis with tooth loss (leukocyte adhesion deficiency, Chediak-Higashi, Kostmann), a double row of teeth from retained primary teeth plus candidiasis (hyper-IgE syndrome), and conical teeth or hypodontia (ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1276)

**Drug-induced gingival overgrowth and stomatitis**: Generalized gingival overgrowth is caused by phenytoin, cyclosporine and calcium channel blockers, as well as leukemia, Sturge-Weber syndrome and hereditary gingival fibromatosis (autosomal dominant, appearing as the permanent teeth erupt). Phenytoin overgrowth appears within months and regresses after the drug is stopped. Heavy metals (lead, bismuth) leave a gingival line. Broad-spectrum antibiotics can cause a beefy, depapillated tongue from Candida overgrowth. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Mouth and Pharynx", p 1305; Ch "Inflammatory Disease of the Mouth and Pharynx", p 1186)

**Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome**: Recurrent facial palsy with orofacial (usually lip) swelling and a fissured tongue is Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome. It belongs to the orofacial granulomatosis spectrum, with chronic granulomatous cheilitis (cheilitis granulomatosa of Miescher). In a child it can be the first sign of Crohn disease, so get a GI evaluation, and include sarcoidosis (Heerfordt syndrome: uveitis, parotid swelling, facial palsy) in the differential for recurrent palsy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1274)

**Pediatric and viral sialadenitis**: Neonatal suppurative parotitis is mostly due to S. aureus, about 40% of cases occur in premature infants, and IV antibiotics usually clear it without recurrence. Mumps has an incubation of 14-21 days and is contagious from about 3 days before the swelling until it resolves. It can also involve the gonads, meninges and pancreas, and it produces clear rather than purulent ductal saliva. Bilateral cystic parotid enlargement from benign lymphoepithelial cysts is essentially pathognomonic of HIV and is managed with antiretrovirals, aspiration or sclerotherapy rather than excision. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1282)

**When surgery is needed**: Recurrent parotitis usually stops by puberty with hydration, sialogogues, massage, and sialendoscopy in selected cases. In the rare refractory case that needs gland surgery, a total rather than superficial parotidectomy is generally required, because leftover deep-lobe tissue keeps getting infected. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1282)

**Pediatric salivary mass epidemiology**: Most pediatric salivary masses are vascular (in one series of 324, 87% were vascular anomalies: 59% hemangioma and 27.5% lymphatic malformation), and only about 3% were malignant. A solid epithelial salivary tumor, however, is more likely malignant in a child than in an adult: about half of epithelial parotid tumors in children are malignant, most often low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma followed by acinic cell carcinoma. A malignancy in a child under 10 tends to be high grade. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is also the most common radiation-induced salivary cancer. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1284)

**Higher recurrence in children**: After superficial parotidectomy, pleomorphic adenoma recurs in about 19.5% of children versus about 1% of adults. This is attributed to capsule violation and to parotid tumors being mistaken for upper neck nodes and enucleated. Plan a formal parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection from the start; enucleation alone carries up to 30% recurrence. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1286)

**Sialoblastoma**: Sialoblastoma is a rare embryonal salivary tumor of newborns, present at or shortly after birth. It is mitotically active and locally aggressive, and it occasionally metastasizes to the neck. Wide excision is the treatment. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1285)

**Approach by level**: A ranula above the mylohyoid can be removed transorally together with the sublingual gland, which recurs less than marsupialization alone, while preserving the lingual nerve and Wharton duct. A plunging ranula below the mylohyoid usually needs a transcervical approach along with removal of the sublingual gland. Submandibular duct relocation for drooling causes ranulas or cervical cysts in about 8-13% unless the sublingual glands are removed at the same time. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Management of Drooling (Sialorrhea)", p 1294)

**Tongue involvement**: The oral cavity, especially the tongue, is the most common site of lymphatic malformation. Lesions appear as pale fluctuant mucosa with clear vesicles, and diffuse involvement causes macroglossia and an open-bite malocclusion. About 7% of tongue lymphatic malformations come with a cervical lymphatic malformation, and 80-90% are evident by age 2. Treatment options include sclerotherapy (OK-432, bleomycin), CO2 laser for superficial vesicles, and staged excision. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Mouth and Pharynx", p 1300)

**Tongue embryology**: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue comes from the first-arch lateral lingual swellings and tuberculum impar; its general sensation is V3 (lingual nerve) and its taste is the chorda tympani (VII). The posterior third comes from the hypobranchial eminence (copula) of arches 3 and 4 and is supplied by IX and X. The intrinsic muscles come from occipital somites (XII). The foramen cecum at the apex of the sulcus terminalis marks where the thyroid begins its descent. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Embryology and Anatomy of the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus", p 1130)

**Lingual thyroid**: Lingual thyroid sits between the foramen cecum and the vallecula as a smooth, red, vascular midline mass. It is more common in females and often presents with dysphagia, muffled voice, dyspnea or bleeding. It is frequently the only functioning thyroid tissue, and about 3% become malignant. Get a thyroid uptake scan and thyroid function tests. Biopsy is discouraged because of bleeding and necrosis risk. Symptomatic tissue is treated with suppression or ablation and thyroid replacement, or with excision and autotransplantation into muscle. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Mouth and Pharynx", p 1302)

**Developmental airway protection**: In infants the larynx sits at about C1-C3, with the epiglottis overlapping the soft palate. This separates breathing from swallowing until about 4-6 months, and the larynx reaches the adult C6-C7 level after puberty. A coordinated suck-swallow-breathe pattern appears at about 32 weeks of gestation. The cough reflex is absent in about 75% of premature infants and 50% of newborns, so laryngeal penetration often causes apnea or bradycardia rather than cough. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Dysphagia", p 1314)

**Aspiration tests beyond MBS/FEES**: A radionuclide salivagram (tracer placed in the mouth, imaged for about 2 hours) detects aspiration of saliva in children who cannot take a meal study, but it cannot show penetration. A gastric technetium milk scan shows reflux-related aspiration. In children with a tracheotomy, dyed feeds that appear in tracheal suction show aspiration, and placing dye in the stomach separates reflux from swallowing aspiration. In cerebral palsy, about 38% aspirate on VFSS and about 97% of those events are silent. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Functional Abnormalities of the Esophagus", p 1333)

**Pediatric FEES and FEESST details**: In children, apply anesthetic in the nose only (oxymetazoline and lidocaine 1:1, or lidocaine gel on the scope tip for infants and fragile children) so that hypopharyngeal sensation is preserved. In infants, premature spillage to the vallecula can be a normal developmental pattern. Blue dye No. 1 has been linked to methemoglobinemia in infants with a leaky gut, so use green food coloring or a colored vitamin instead. On FEESST, a laryngeal adductor reflex threshold above about 4.5 mmHg correlates with a history of aspiration pneumonia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Dysphagia", p 1319)

**Pediatric cricopharyngeal achalasia**: In infants and children, cricopharyngeal achalasia presents with choking, nasal regurgitation and poor feeding. It is usually secondary to CNS or neuromuscular disease (hypoxic injury, Chiari II, syringobulbia, myotonic or oculopharyngeal dystrophy), and a cricopharyngeal bar on VFSS can be seen in normal children. Small children can improve as the muscle matures. A stepwise plan is VFSS (with manometry if available), then dilation or botulinum injection (whose effect fades over months), and myotomy only for refractory cases with good pharyngeal contraction. Transient pharyngeal incoordination of the newborn usually resolves within about 2 weeks with tube feeding. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Functional Abnormalities of the Esophagus", p 1330)

**Achalasia diagnosis and pediatric features**: Only about 4-5% of achalasia presents before age 15, and children often present with growth failure and recurrent aspiration pneumonia after a 2-3 year delay. Associations include trisomy 21 and Allgrove (triple A) syndrome (achalasia, alacrima and ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency; autosomal recessive). Barium shows a dilated esophagus with a smooth bird-beak taper, and there may be a mid-esophageal air-fluid level with no gastric bubble. Manometry confirms a high LES pressure, failure of LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. Endoscopy rules out a stricture or mass. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Functional Abnormalities of the Esophagus", p 1330)

**Achalasia treatment**: Nitrates and calcium channel blockers are only temporizing. Botulinum relief lasts months, and the resulting fibrosis can complicate later myotomy. Pneumatic dilation (about 300 mmHg) helps older children but was uniformly ineffective under age 9. Laparoscopic Heller myotomy (4-6 cm on the esophagus and 1-2 cm onto the cardia) is the preferred definitive treatment. Reflux follows myotomy in 10-60%, so add an anterior Dor fundoplication: in a randomized trial, pathologic reflux occurred in about 48% after myotomy alone versus about 9% with Dor. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Functional Abnormalities of the Esophagus", p 1331)

**Spastic disorders, scleroderma and Barrett**: Diffuse esophageal spasm is defined by simultaneous contractions in more than 20% of wet swallows. Nutcracker esophagus has a mean distal amplitude above about 180 mmHg (220 mmHg has been proposed), and hypertensive LES has a resting pressure above 40 mmHg with normal peristalsis. In pediatric chest pain series, 44-78% had an esophageal cause. In scleroderma (75-85% have esophageal involvement), distal peristalsis is weak or absent and LES pressure is low, which causes severe reflux. Barrett esophagus occurs in about 2.5-13% of children with GERD and requires yearly surveillance biopsy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Functional Abnormalities of the Esophagus", p 1332)

**Lipid-laden macrophage index**: A lipid-laden macrophage index above 100 on bronchoalveolar lavage has been used as a marker of aspiration from reflux. In children it does not correlate with impedance-pH reflux events or esophagitis, so do not use it alone to diagnose or treat GERD. Microscopic esophagitis is present in about 40% of normal-looking mucosa, which is why biopsies are taken routinely. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Functional Abnormalities of the Esophagus", p 1329)

**EoE diagnostic criteria and findings**: Diagnosis requires symptoms of esophageal dysfunction plus a peak of at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field, confined to the esophagus, with other causes excluded; take biopsies from both proximal and distal esophagus. Endoscopic signs are longitudinal furrows, white exudates, concentric rings (trachealization or felinization), crepe-paper mucosa and a narrow-caliber esophagus, but endoscopy can look normal and barium is insensitive. EoE affects males about 3 times as often as females, and 42-93% of affected children have another atopic disease. Presentation changes with age: feeding refusal in infants, vomiting and pain in school-age children, and dysphagia or food impaction in adolescents. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Eosinophilic Esophagitis", p 1338)

**EoE therapy and dilation safety**: Options include elimination diets (a six-food elimination diet controls about 74%; an amino-acid elemental formula controls about 90% but often needs tube feeding), swallowed topical steroids (viscous budesonide or swallowed fluticasone, with candidiasis as the main side effect), and PPI (pediatric dose about 1 mg/kg twice daily for 8-12 weeks). The book uses the older PPI-responsive esophageal eosinophilia concept; current consensus counts PPI responders as EoE and treats PPI as first-line therapy, and dupilumab is now approved for EoE. Dilation carries about a 0.8% perforation risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Eosinophilic Esophagitis", p 1342)

**ENT associations of EoE**: In one series of 144 children with EoE, about a quarter had eustachian tube dysfunction and a quarter had sleep-disordered breathing. A third to a half of EoE children seen by otolaryngologists have atypical symptoms such as cough, hoarseness or throat clearing. EoE has been linked to subglottic stenosis and laryngeal edema, so treat it before airway reconstruction. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Eosinophilic Esophagitis", p 1337)

**Coin vs battery and imaging pitfalls**: A CR2032 lithium cell (20 mm wide, 3.2 mm thick, 3 V) is about the size of a penny (19 mm) or nickel (21 mm), and radiographs magnify by about 20%. Always get AP and lateral views: a lateral view shows a coin stack and the step-off of a battery. A hand-held metal detector cannot tell a coin from a battery and should not replace films. Pennies are about 95% zinc and can corrode the mucosa if retained. Faintly radiopaque bones are best seen on lateral views, and a retained radiolucent object may show up only as periesophageal swelling or late stridor. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Pharynx and Esophagus", p 1349)

**Alternatives for uncomplicated coins**: An asymptomatic child with a coin, seen within 24 hours, with no airway symptoms and no known esophageal disease (a simple case), can be re-imaged at about 24 hours because many coins, especially distal ones, pass on their own. Other options are bougienage into the stomach (near-zero complications), Foley balloon extraction under fluoroscopy (over 90% success), and flexible endoscopy. Rigid esophagoscopy (about 2% complications) is kept for complex cases: airway symptoms, prolonged retention, prior esophageal surgery or failed simpler methods. Biopsy every food impaction, because over half show esophagitis or stricture. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Pharynx and Esophagus", p 1348)

**Choking-hazard foods**: The foods most often fatal to young children are hot dogs, carrots, grapes, meat and peanuts. Nuts are a particular aspiration risk because they are dense and aerodynamic once bitten. Risk factors are a lack of molars, older siblings, male sex and inadequate supervision. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Pharynx and Esophagus", p 1347)

**The 3 Ns and delayed vascular deaths**: Remember the 3 Ns: the Negative pole is the Narrow side on the lateral view, and that is where Necrosis occurs. Severe injury can develop within 2 hours. The CR2032 is behind most fatal cases, and the risk of major complications or death rose about 6.7-fold between 1985 and 2009. Most deaths were from aortoesophageal fistula, sometimes weeks after removal, so follow significant erosion with serial esophagram and, if needed, MRI. A battery that has passed the esophagus should be re-imaged in about 1-2 weeks to confirm it has been passed. Swallowing several magnets, or a magnet with a battery, can cause bowel pressure necrosis even beyond the stomach. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Pharynx and Esophagus", p 1350)

**Endoscopy timing and the window to avoid**: CONFLICT within sources: the site gives both 24-48 hours and within 24 hours. The book recommends endoscopy at 24-72 hours in symptomatic children. Lesions may be underestimated before 24 hours, and endoscopy should be avoided between days 5 and 15, when the esophageal wall is weakest. Stop advancing the scope at the first severe (circumferential or necrotic) burn. Having two or more of drooling, vomiting and stridor predicts an esophageal burn better than any single sign. Current pediatric guidance favors endoscopy within about 24 hours (generally after 12 hours), and all sources agree on avoiding the subacute window. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1372)

**Why titratable reserve matters**: Agents with pH below 3 or above 12 cause rapid injury, but the titratable reserve (how much acid or base it takes to bring the pH to 8) predicts damage better than pH alone. For example, hair relaxer has a pH near 13 but a low reserve and causes little injury. Household bleach is dilute and near neutral and rarely burns the esophagus. Sodium hydroxide causes necrosis at concentrations as low as about 1-2%, and solutions above about 22% go through the full wall. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1367)

**Stricture risk and dilation**: Stricture forms after about 77% of Zargar 2b burns and essentially 100% of grade 3 burns, and grades 0-2a rarely stricture. Start dilation at about 3-4 weeks after barium mapping; dilation that begins late (after about 6 weeks) has more perforations and recurrences. Balloon (radial) dilation tears less than bougies, which exert longitudinal shear. Retrograde dilation over a string through a gastrostomy is the safest for long strictures. Caustic strictures resist dilation more than peptic or anastomotic strictures (success about 60-80%). The book still recommended steroids for grade 2a burns, whereas current reviews treat their benefit as unproven. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1373)

**Late carcinoma risk**: After a severe caustic burn, the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is roughly 1,000 times higher, with a latency of 13-71 years, and up to 7% of patients with esophageal carcinoma have a childhood caustic ingestion. Patients with caustic strictures need lifelong surveillance even without symptoms. For strictures that need dilation indefinitely, esophagectomy with gastric pull-up or colon interposition is an alternative. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1377)

**Pediatric perforation differs from adult**: In children, perforation is mostly iatrogenic (dilation of caustic or atresia-repair strictures, tubes, endoscopy) and is often recognized early, so nonoperative care succeeds more often than in adults (mortality as low as about 4% vs up to 50%). That care is 10-14 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics, chest tubes for collections, NPO for at least 5-7 days with TPN, tube or gastrostomy feeding, and contrast study before feeding. Neonatal perforations occur most often at the pharyngoesophageal junction above the cricopharyngeus, and in older children in the thoracic esophagus. A chest film is abnormal in about 88% of cases, so a normal film does not exclude perforation. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Trauma to the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus in Children", p 1360)

**Oral commissure electrical burns**: Electrical burns of the oral commissure typically happen at age 3-4 from mouthing a live cord, with arc temperatures above 2,500 C, and they are always deeper than they first look. Edema lasts 7-10 days, then the eschar separates, and labial artery bleeding is possible in the second to third week. Early commissure splinting worn for 6-12 months or longer reduces the need for later commissuroplasty (about 35% vs 86% with observation in one series). Delayed surgical reconstruction is the alternative. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Trauma to the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus in Children", p 1357)

**Lip, tongue and rabies essentials**: Lip defects under about 30% of lip length can be closed primarily after precise vermilion alignment, while larger defects need Abbe, Estlander or Karapandzic flaps. Tongue lacerations shorter than about 2 cm that are not bleeding usually heal without suturing. After a bite from a possible rabies carrier, observe the animal for 10 days, or give immediate prophylaxis if the animal is unavailable or suspect: human rabies immune globulin 20 IU/kg infiltrated into the wound as far as possible, plus vaccine on days 0, 3, 7 and 14 (a day-28 dose is added only if immunocompromised under current ACIP). Human bites most often involve the ear and become infected more often than animal bites. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Trauma to the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus in Children", p 1356)

topic: Cranial Nerve Examination / Skull Base Localization
text: **Palatal signs of vagal lesions**: With a unilateral vagal lesion, the palate sits low on the weak side and pulls toward the normal side on phonation, and the posterior pharyngeal wall shifts toward the intact side (the Vernet curtain sign). Palatal weakness lets a patient puff the cheeks only when the nose is pinched, whereas facial weakness prevents puffing either way. Palatal plus vocal fold paralysis places the lesion high (brainstem or jugular foramen), while a vagal lesion below the hyoid causes only vocal fold dysfunction. A unilaterally absent gag localizes, but a bilaterally reduced gag can be normal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neurologic Disorders of the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus", p 1382)

topic: Cranial Nerve Examination / Skull Base Localization
text: **Pediatric bulbar syndromes**: Avellis syndrome is ipsilateral palatopharyngeal paresis with contralateral hemiparesis or sensory loss. Mobius syndrome is congenital bilateral VI and VII palsy, sometimes with other cranial nerves involved. Chiari I and II malformations can present with dysphagia, central apnea and bilateral vocal fold paralysis that need early decompression. Infant botulism comes from spores (e.g., in honey) and causes constipation, ptosis and weak feeding. Myotonic dystrophy in a newborn causes severe facial weakness with a tented upper lip and dysphagia. Oculopharyngeal dystrophy causes ptosis and dysphagia that responds to cricopharyngeal myotomy. Isolated hypoglossal palsy can be postviral or follow tonsillectomy, third-molar extraction or carotid dissection. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neurologic Disorders of the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus", p 1386)

**Palatal myoclonus**: Palatal myoclonus is rhythmic palatal contraction, about 10-200 beats per minute, from a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle (central tegmental tract or contralateral dentate nucleus, causing inferior olivary hypertrophy). It can present as objective clicking tinnitus from repeated eustachian tube opening. It is uncommon in children, often resolves on its own, and can be treated with antiepileptics. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neurologic Disorders of the Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus", p 1387)

**Adenoid facies and dentofacial growth**: Chronic nasal obstruction from adenotonsillar hypertrophy is associated with long-face syndrome: increased lower facial height and gonial angle, a high narrow palate and posterior crossbite. Cause and effect has never been proven in humans, so adenotonsillectomy for orthodontic reasons alone is considered only with significant hypertrophy. Adenoid facies is an open mouth, flat midface and dark circles under the eyes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1194)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Cervicofacial actinomycosis**: Actinomyces israelii is an oral commensal that becomes invasive after dental work, poor hygiene or radiation, always with companion bacteria. It forms a slowly enlarging, woody, relatively painless mass with multiple sinus tracts draining sulfur granules, and it crosses tissue planes. Treatment is prolonged high-dose penicillin (often 6 weeks IV, then months of oral therapy), with doxycycline as the alternative for penicillin allergy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1283)

**Collapse-pattern types and synchronous lesions**: Endoscopic collapse is commonly typed as type 1 (prolapse of redundant arytenoid/cuneiform supraglottic mucosa), type 2 (foreshortened aryepiglottic folds), and type 3 (posterior displacement of the epiglottis). Synchronous airway lesions occur in up to 27% of infants with laryngomalacia, so when disease is severe enough for surgery the whole airway is examined at the same anesthetic. Laryngomalacia is not more common in premature than term infants, which argues against simple cartilage immaturity as the cause. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1519)

**Natural history timeline and late-onset forms**: Stridor usually begins within the first 2 weeks of life, worsens over the first months, peaks and plateaus around 6 months, and most infants are symptom-free by 18-24 months, although some persist for years. Late-onset variants are described by presentation: feeding-disordered, sleep-disordered, and exercise-induced laryngomalacia. Pectus excavatum can result from severe chronic obstruction. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1517)

**PSG as an indication and outcome caveats**: A strongly abnormal polysomnogram in an infant with laryngomalacia is itself a reason to consider supraglottoplasty. Supraglottoplasty can reduce laryngeal penetration and aspiration in severe laryngomalacia, but this benefit is less reliable in children with multiple medical comorbidities. Over-resection can cause supraglottic stenosis, and milder postoperative narrowing may present only as recurrent, prolonged 'croup' with viral illnesses. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Stridor: Presentation and Evaluation", p 1480) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1489) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1520)

**Definition in preterm infants and leak-test sizing**: A subglottic lumen under 4 mm in a term newborn or under 3 mm in a premature infant defines subglottic stenosis. Sizing starts with a deliberately small endotracheal tube (to avoid dilating the stenosis); if a leak occurs below 10 cm H2O the next size is tried, and the tube that leaks between 10 and 25 cm H2O is taken as the airway size and compared with the age-expected size to give the Myer-Cotton percentage. The full larynx and distal airway are inspected first to classify the lesion as soft/membranous or firm/cartilaginous and to find synchronous lesions. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1520)

**Congenital subtypes and acquired injury stages**: Congenital SGS is membranous (soft, circumferential thickening from submucosal fibrosis or mucous gland hyperplasia) or cartilaginous (small or elliptical cricoid with lateral shelves); most congenital cases are cartilaginous, so laser is generally not advised. Acquired post-intubation lesions progress through gland hyperplasia, retention (subglottic) cysts, granulation, and finally mature fibrosis. Contributors include oversized or mobile tubes, repeated intubation, cuff pressure, nasogastric-tube-promoted reflux, infection (including MRSA), and low birth weight; in neonates no intubation duration is truly safe. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1520) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Acquired Disorders of the Larynx and Trachea", p 1555) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1582)

**Predictors of endoscopic failure and grade-based approach**: Endoscopic (laser) treatment is likely to fail with prior failed endoscopic procedures, loss of cartilage framework, circumferential scar more than 1 cm in vertical height, posterior commissure involvement, or exposure of perichondrium/cartilage. Laser works best for lesions no taller than about 0.5-1 cm involving up to 50-70% of the circumference, and lasering more than half the circumference in one session is discouraged. As a rule grade I is managed endoscopically or observed, grade II by either route, and grades III-IV almost always need open surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1521) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Acquired Disorders of the Larynx and Trachea", p 1557)

**Endoscopic outcome numbers and mitomycin**: With CO2 laser radial incisions plus dilation, near-normal lumen was achieved in about 92% of grade I, 46% of grade II and 13% of grade III stenoses (Monnier). Balloon dilation gives immediate improvement in about 90% but durable resolution in only about half, often after several sessions; balloons apply radial force without the shear of bougies and are filled with saline. Topical mitomycin C is commonly applied at 0.4 mg/mL for about 2 minutes, but proof of benefit in children is limited. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1583) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1587) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Acquired Disorders of the Larynx and Trachea", p 1558)

**Graft harvest and carving details**: Costal cartilage is usually taken from the right 5th or 6th rib (incision in the future breast crease in girls), leaving the inner perichondrium behind; check for pleural breach by disconnecting positive pressure, filling the wound with saline and giving a Valsalva. The graft's perichondrium faces the lumen, lateral flanges prevent prolapse, and an anterior graft is cut about 5 mm longer and 2 mm wider than the defect with knots tied laterally because the graft is fed by overlying strap muscle. Thyroid ala grafts (taken at least 1 mm above the cords) suit small defects but cannot be flanged; auricular cartilage is too weak to sit between cricoid edges and is best as a stomal cap. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1594) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1595) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1606)

**Single-stage intubation durations and extubation rules**: Typical stenting intubation after single-stage surgery: anterior cricoid split about 10 days, anterior costal graft 0-5 days, posterior graft 5-10 days, anterior plus posterior grafts 7-14 days, cricotracheal resection 0-5 days, slide tracheoplasty 0-3 days; beyond about 2 weeks the tube itself risks new stenosis. The 24-36 hours after extubation are the danger period; after three failed extubations a temporary tracheotomy should be reconsidered, and a child who is difficult to intubate should not be single-staged. Double-stage repairs usually use a suprastomal stent for 2-8 weeks; failure risk rises with uncontrolled reflux, eosinophilic esophagitis, an 'active' larynx and Pseudomonas or MRSA colonization. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1593) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1594) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1607)

**Anterior cricoid split and posterior split variants**: The anterior cricoid split divides the lower thyroid cartilage, the cricoid and the first two tracheal rings in the midline for a neonate who repeatedly fails extubation despite adequate lung reserve (weight above about 1500 g); the child is reintubated with a tube a half to one size larger for about 7-10 days and extubation succeeds in about 66-78%. In infants under about 9 months (over 1500 g) with symptomatic SGS, an anterior graft with a posterior cricoid split can work without a posterior graft because the posterior split heals quickly during 7-10 days of tube distraction. The cricoid split's role has shrunk since high-flow nasal cannula reduced the number of chronically intubated premature infants. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1521) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Acquired Disorders of the Larynx and Trachea", p 1559) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1595)

**Outcome numbers by grade and procedure**: For acquired SGS, single-procedure decannulation is about 81-88% for grade II (97% after two) and 78-81% for grade III (91% after revision); grade IV did poorly with expansion alone (37-50%) but exceeds 90% with partial cricotracheal resection. One large series reported 94% decannulation after CTR, with vocal fold paralysis the main predictor of failure; Down syndrome, EoE and MRSA also lowered success. Only about half of children have a normal or near-normal voice after LTR, and CTR is an effective salvage after failed LTR. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1522) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1581) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1600) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1606)

**Cricotracheal resection pearls**: CTR suits severe stenosis with at least a small margin of normal airway below the vocal folds; extended CTR adds a posterior cricoid split and graft when posterior glottic stenosis coexists. The anterior cricoid arch and anterior two-thirds of the lateral cricoid are removed while preserving the cricothyroid joints, where the recurrent laryngeal nerves are most vulnerable; the posterior plate is thinned subperichondrially and an existing stoma can be kept if two healthy rings separate it from the stenosis. In children under 2 the folds sit low inside the thyroid cartilage, so the airway is first transected at the lower edge of the cricothyroid membrane; suprahyoid release and chin-to-chest sutures reduce anastomotic tension. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1599) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1600) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Acquired Disorders of the Larynx and Trachea", p 1561)

**Petiole prolapse after laryngofissure**: Dividing the thyroepiglottic ligament during a complete laryngofissure can let the epiglottic petiole fall back, causing exercise intolerance and obstructive sleep apnea, often with CPAP dependence. It is best judged by polysomnography or drug-induced sleep endoscopy (rigid endoscopy and cine MRI are unreliable). Repair pexies the petiole to the thyroid cartilage through a laryngofissure with a high suprastomal stent for at least 6 weeks, and prophylactic pexy sutures are advised whenever a full laryngofissure is done. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1602)

**Epidemiology and etiologic split**: Vocal fold paralysis is the third most common congenital laryngeal anomaly causing stridor, after laryngomalacia and congenital SGS; unilateral and bilateral cases are about equally frequent. Congenital paralysis is usually bilateral and about half have other anomalies; about 70% of acquired cases stem from congenital neurologic disease (myelomeningocele, Arnold-Chiari, hydrocephalus) or its surgery, while unilateral palsy is most often iatrogenic (PDA ligation, especially under 1500 g, cardiac or esophageal surgery) and left-sided. Bilateral palsy may show paradoxical motion, the folds drawn in on inspiration and opened passively on expiration. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1524) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1603)

**Diagnostic pitfalls**: Diagnosis is by awake flexible laryngoscopy, ideally recorded for slow-motion review because infants breathe fast; ultrasound can also show immobility. Under general anesthesia, coordinated motion rules out paralysis but absent motion cannot be interpreted. Once paralysis is found, image the head and chest for neurologic and cardiovascular causes, and examine under anesthesia with arytenoid palpation when fixation, web or scar is suspected. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1524) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1603) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Stridor: Presentation and Evaluation", p 1480)

**Recovery timeline**: Infant vocal fold paralysis usually resolves within 6-18 months, and up to 50% of congenital bilateral cases recover within the first 2 years; recovery is unlikely if there is no improvement by 2-3 years. Paralysis due to raised intracranial pressure often responds to early shunting or posterior fossa decompression. Unilateral palsy rarely needs surgery (liquids can be thickened), whereas bilateral palsy usually, but not always, needs a temporary tracheotomy, with close growth monitoring if managed without one. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1524) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1603)

**Glottic-widening options and outcomes**: A meta-analysis found about 40% decannulation after endoscopic CO2 laser arytenoidectomy versus 74-100% after various open procedures in children. A narrow (4-6 mm) posterior cricoid cartilage graft, placed openly without full laryngofissure or endoscopically, or vocal fold lateralization (at least two posteriorly placed sutures through the vocal process) gives the best balance of airway, voice and aspiration; acquired bilateral palsy often needs more than one operation. Screen for aspiration first, simply with a food-dye test in a tracheotomized child, and delay or avoid widening if baseline aspiration is present. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1583) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1603)

**Associated anomalies and syndromes**: Clefts have associated anomalies in about 56%, most often tracheoesophageal fistula (20-27%) and tracheomalacia (about 80%); over 6% of children with TEF have a cleft, which is missed in about three-quarters until aspiration persists after TEF repair, so a cleft should be excluded in every TEF patient. Syndromic associations include Pallister-Hall (autosomal dominant: hypothalamic hamartoblastoma, hypopituitarism, imperforate anus, polydactyly) and Opitz G/BBB (hypertelorism, hypospadias, cleft lip/palate, dysphagia). Redundant mucosa between the arytenoids at endoscopy should raise suspicion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1526) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1604)

**Repair approach, results and failure**: Most type I-II clefts are repaired endoscopically (success over 80%), for example with a single-layer mass closure using mattress sutures, the top one through both cuneiform cartilages; clefts below the folds generally need an open (anterior laryngofissure or transtracheal) offset two-layer closure, with an interposition graft such as tibial or sternal periosteum when failure risk is high (revision, prior TEF repair, Opitz). Preliminary tracheotomy, gastrostomy and fundoplication each improve the odds of success, and uncontrolled reflux lowers it. Breakdown occurs distally as a fistula or proximally as recurrence, usually within weeks; mortality ranges 11-46% and reaches 93% for clefts extending into the thoracic trachea. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1527) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1604) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1605)

**Epidemiology and endoscopic features**: Subglottic hemangioma makes up about 1.5% of congenital laryngeal anomalies, with a female predominance of about 2-2.5:1; 85% present before 6 months (often as 'croup' at 6-8 weeks) and about half have a cutaneous hemangioma, while about 63-65% of infants with beard-distribution facial hemangiomas have airway involvement. Endoscopy shows a compressible, smooth, pink or blue submucosal mass, more often left-sided; examine with spontaneous ventilation without intubation (the tube compresses the lesion), and biopsy is usually unnecessary. AP high-kV neck films show asymmetric subglottic narrowing in about half; untreated mortality has been reported at 30-70%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1527) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1642) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1643) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1605)

**Propranolol details and second-line options**: Propranolol is typically dosed at 2-3 mg/kg/day in 2-3 divided doses, often for more than a year; adverse effects include hypoglycemia, bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm and somnolence, and some lesions rebound after weaning. Systemic steroids alone resolve only about 25% (prednisone up to about 4 mg/kg/day, then alternate-day dosing to limit growth suppression); CO2 laser succeeds in about 89% but causes stenosis in about 6-25%, especially with bilateral or circumferential disease, so it is staged. Open excision through an anterior laryngofissure avoids tracheotomy in about 85%, and interferon alfa (risk of spastic diplegia in infants) or vincristine are reserved for refractory or massive cervicofacial disease. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1644) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1645) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1528)

**PHACE components and natural-history numbers**: PHACE(S) comprises posterior fossa malformations, segmental head/neck hemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects (coarctation), eye anomalies and sternal/supraumbilical defects; because intracranial arterial anomalies can cause strokes, brain MRI/MRA screening is required. Infantile hemangiomas are 3 times more common in girls, 60% occur in the head and neck, proliferate for about 6-10 months, and about 50% have involuted by age 5 and 70% by age 7; multiple cutaneous lesions should prompt a search for visceral (especially hepatic) hemangiomas. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1527) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1642)

**Pediatric saccular cysts**: A saccular cyst differs from a laryngocele because its lumen does not communicate with the larynx and it holds mucus, not air; lateral cysts extend into the false fold and aryepiglottic fold, while anterior cysts bulge medially between the true and false folds. Congenital saccular cysts present in the first days of life with inspiratory stridor, a muffled cry and dysphagia. Loss of tone at anesthetic induction can cause complete obstruction, so perform awake flexible laryngoscopy first and secure the airway in the OR before any sedated imaging. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1522) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1602)

**Saccular cyst treatment**: Needle aspiration confirms a saccular cyst but rarely cures it; endoscopic unroofing or excision to the saccular orifice often needs repeating. Recurrent cysts, or (in the view of some authors) all congenital saccular cysts, are best removed through an external approach that incises the thyrohyoid membrane along the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, protecting the superior laryngeal nerve. Tracheotomy is usually avoidable, but a few days of intubation may be needed. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1524) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1602)

**Classification systems and associations**: Pathologic tracheomalacia shows a cartilage-to-membranous-wall ratio of about 3:1 to 2:1 (normal 4.5:1) with more than 50% luminal collapse; cervical tracheomalacia collapses on inspiration. Benjamin divides it into primary and secondary forms, and the major airway collapse (MAC) system groups type I intrinsic weakness (prematurity, EA/TEF, mucopolysaccharidoses), type II extrinsic compression (vessels, cysts, tumors, thymus, goiter) and type III acquired (prolonged ventilation, tracheotomy, severe infection). Associations include cardiovascular anomalies (20-58%), bronchopulmonary dysplasia (up to 52%), reflux in up to 78% of severe cases, and neurologic impairment (8-48%). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Trachea and Bronchi", p 1533)

**Practical management points**: Most primary tracheomalacia resolves by about 2 years; bronchodilators may worsen collapse by relaxing tracheal smooth muscle, while antireflux therapy can help. Paralysis, deep sedation or positive-pressure ventilation during bronchoscopy can mask malacia, and flow-volume loops show a truncated expiratory limb. Pediatric airway stents (silicone or metal) carry a stent-related mortality of about 13% from granulation, migration, erosion and bleeding, so they are emergency-only. After EA/TEF repair, tracheomalacia occurs in about 75% but is clinically significant in only 10-20%; bronchomalacia is more often left-sided (about 36% vs 22%), and Williams-Campbell syndrome (absent subsegmental cartilage) causes bronchiectasis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Trachea and Bronchi", p 1534) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Trachea and Bronchi", p 1535) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Trachea and Bronchi", p 1539) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Trachea and Bronchi", p 1543) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1588)

**Croup treatment kinetics and intubation rules**: Nebulized racemic epinephrine works within 10-30 minutes but wears off within about 2 hours, so children can be discharged after a 2-3 hour observation; corticosteroids take up to 3 hours for peak effect and oral dosing is as effective as nebulized. Heliox (usually 80% helium/20% oxygen) lowers turbulent flow but cannot be used if more than 40% oxygen is needed. If intubation is required, use a tube smaller than age-predicted, extubate when an air leak develops (usually 2-3 days), and perform endoscopy if no leak appears by about 5 days. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1548)

**Croup epidemiology, scoring and recurrent croup**: Croup peaks at 1-2 years (range 6 months-3 years), is most often caused by parainfluenza type 1, and about half of affected children have a normal neck radiograph; intubation is needed in only about 2% of hospitalized children. The Westley score (consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, retractions; 0-17) is used mainly for research. For recurrent croup, endoscopy is ideally done 3-4 weeks after an episode once edema subsides; in one series about 47% had reflux and 25% an anatomic lesion (SGS or laryngomalacia), and reflux-associated cases presented younger with shorter intervals between episodes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1547) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1548)

**Post-Hib epidemiology shift**: Conjugate Hib vaccination cut US epiglottitis in children under 5 from 41 to 1.3 per 100,000 (1987-1997); Hib fell from about 90% of pediatric cases to about 32-63%, and the mean age of patients rose (5.8 to 14.6 years in one center), so 84-97% of cases are now adults. In adults Hib causes only 11-20%, blood cultures are negative in up to 85%, onset is slower, and an artificial airway is needed far less often (about 21% vs 68% in children). Vaccine failure (about 2.2 per 100,000 vaccinees) clusters in children with prematurity, malignancy, Down syndrome or immunodeficiency (most often IgG2, then IgA); average intubation for pediatric epiglottitis is about 2.8 days. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1551) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1552)

**Intraoperative hazards specific to children**: Never incise the cricoid; avoid a nasogastric tube or esophageal stethoscope during the operation because the esophagus can be mistaken for the trachea, and remember that a high innominate artery or the neonatal carotid can mimic or overlie the trachea. Minimal pretracheal dissection limits pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum (3-9%), and a chest radiograph (or scope through the tube) confirms tube tip position. Relieving obstruction can cause apnea, arrhythmia or hypotension from rapid CO2 washout and post-obstructive pulmonary edema (treated with positive pressure and diuretics); percutaneous techniques are avoided except in adolescents. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1570) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1571) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1572)

**Tube sizing and key numbers**: Approximate tracheostomy tube inner diameters: under 1000 g 2.5 mm; 1000-2500 g 3.0; neonate-6 months 3.0-3.5; 6-12 months 3.5-4.0; 1-2 years 4.0-5.0; beyond 2 years (age in years + 16)/4; length matters because a long tube can abrade the carina or enter the right mainstem. The first tube change is usually at 5-7 days; prolonged ventilation is the indication in over half, bronchopulmonary dysplasia is now the most common diagnosis, and incidence peaks under 1 year. Tracheotomy-related mortality is 0.5-3.3% (accidental decannulation or plugging), pulse oximetry is the best home monitor, and suctioning should pass just beyond the tube tip for no more than 30 seconds. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1566) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1568) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1573) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1574) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1577)

**Tracheocutaneous fistula and decannulation details**: Persistent tracheocutaneous fistula is rare after a few weeks of cannulation but occurs in over 50% after more than a year (overall 11-20%); excision with layered closure risks subcutaneous emphysema, so a small drain or overnight small tube may be used. Chronically ventilated children should be off support for several weeks before decannulation, airway endoscopy should precede it (removing suprastomal granulation; managing suprastomal collapse by excision, suturing to skin or single-stage tracheoplasty), and the child is observed in a monitored setting overnight because obstruction may appear only in sleep. Neurologically impaired children often fail from secretion clearance problems despite a normal airway. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1574) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Tracheotomy", p 1575)

**First aid and prevention**: A child who can cough, gag or speak has partial obstruction and should not receive first aid, because finger probing or inverted back blows can impact the object in the glottis; blind finger sweeps are never done. For complete obstruction, infants under 1 year get five back blows then five chest thrusts, older children get abdominal thrusts, and an unresponsive child gets CPR for about a minute before EMS activation. Prevention: no nuts, popcorn, seeds or round hard candy before age 4-5, cut hot dogs and grapes into small pieces, and toys for under-3s must not fit the Small Parts Test Fixture (31.7 mm diameter); balloons are dangerous at all ages. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1610) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1611) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1622)

**Diagnostic accuracy numbers**: A choking history is elicited in about 80% and is the most sensitive clue (about 97% sensitive, 63% specific); 20-50% of foreign bodies are diagnosed more than a week late. Only about 15% are radiopaque, chest films are normal in up to 40% (air trapping is the commonest sign, 32-66%), plain-film accuracy is about 67%, and CT is nearly 100% sensitive but only about 70% specific. Neck films are often diagnostic for laryngeal objects but a normal film cannot exclude a tracheal one; tracheal foreign bodies give an audible slap, palpable thud and an asthmatoid wheeze heard best at the open mouth. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1613) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1614) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1615) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1616) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Radiologic Evaluation of the Pediatric Airway", p 1431)

**Epidemiology and lodging sites**: Children under 3 account for about 74% of cases (and over three-quarters of deaths), boys outnumber girls 2:1, vegetable matter makes up 55-95% (nuts about 39%; oily nuts inflame and dried beans swell), and plastic toy parts are inert and radiolucent; school supplies such as pen caps dominate after age 5. Laryngeal foreign bodies (1-7%) are usually flat, sharp objects lodged in the sagittal plane, often in infants under 1 year; tracheal ones are 3-12% and are more likely with tracheomalacia or weak effort. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1611) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1612)

**Valve terminology**: In Bluestone's foreign-body chapter, bypass-valve obstruction gives a normal film; check-valve obstruction (air enters but cannot leave) causes hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away and is typical of acute bronchial foreign bodies; stop-valve (complete) obstruction gives atelectasis; and true ball-valve obstruction (air leaves but cannot enter) is rare and also causes atelectasis with shift toward the affected side. Many radiology texts, including Bluestone's radiology chapter, loosely call the hyperinflation mechanism 'ball-valve', so read answer choices by the physiology described. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1615) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Radiologic Evaluation of the Pediatric Airway", p 1431)

**Extraction technique pearls**: Give an anticholinergic, spray the larynx with lidocaine, keep spontaneous ventilation (especially for laryngotracheal objects) and avoid positive pressure that drives the object distally; inspect and clear the normal side first and use the largest bronchoscope that passes easily. Grasp past the equator of round objects, turn the object into the sagittal plane, anchor it to the scope tip and remove scope, forceps and object as a unit; sheathe sharp points by advancing the scope over them, and if the object is stripped off in the larynx push it back into a bronchus (preferably the original one). Stop after about 60 minutes and treat edema with steroids and racemic epinephrine before a second attempt; always make a second pass to look for residual fragments, and avoid routine postoperative steroids, which were linked to more persistent pneumonia and atelectasis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1617) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1618) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1619) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1620) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1621) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1622)

**Pediatric tracheobronchial injury clues**: In children, blunt laryngotracheal injury most often follows bicycle handlebar falls (mean age about 10; penetrating injuries about 12), and pliable cartilage means soft-tissue injury exceeds fractures. Rib fractures accompany tracheobronchial rupture in about 24% of children (vs about 90% of adults), so their absence does not exclude injury; a continued air leak despite a chest tube is the key clue, about 80% of ruptures involve a mainstem bronchus, 15% the trachea and 5% distal bronchi, and mortality reaches 30% (half within the first hour). Esophageal injury is the most commonly missed associated injury (15-50% of penetrating cases); contrast swallow alone is only 50-90% sensitive, so combine with esophagoscopy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1627) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1628) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1630)

**Pediatric airway and tracheal repair choices**: Awake tracheotomy under local anesthesia is not feasible in most children, so the airway is secured in the OR after inhalational induction, usually by rigid bronchoscopy with tracheotomy over the scope (or skilled intubation over a flexible scope with a surgical backup). Tracheal tears involving less than one-third of the circumference, especially posterior ones with opposed edges and a lung that re-expands, may be managed nonoperatively; larger tears are closed with interrupted absorbable sutures preserving lateral blood supply, and a tracheotomy tube should not be placed through a simple anterior laceration. Esophageal tears are closed in two layers with a vascularized flap between trachea and esophagus to prevent fistula, and surgery for vocal fold paralysis is delayed about a year. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1631) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1632) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1633)

**Epidemiology, transmission and prognostic numbers**: Incidence is about 4.3 per 100,000 children and 1.8 per 100,000 adults; mean age at juvenile diagnosis is about 3.8 years, and first-born children of teenage mothers delivered vaginally are at highest risk. Over half of affected children are born to mothers with active condylomata, yet the risk to an exposed neonate is only about 1 in 400; cesarean delivery lowers but does not abolish risk and may be offered. Diagnosis before age 3 makes a child 3.6 times more likely to need more than four surgeries a year (average about 20 procedures), tracheal spread occurs in 17-26% and pulmonary spread in 1-6% (with about 16% cancer risk), and tracheotomy promotes distal spread, so it is avoided when possible. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1636) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1637) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1638)

**Other adjuvants and surgical complications**: Intralesional cidofovir (about 5-7.5 mg/mL every 2-3 weeks) produced durable remission in about half of severe pediatric cases; a review found about 2.7% reversible dysplasia, so consent, renal/blood monitoring and serial histology are advised. Interferon alfa can cause growth slowing and spastic diplegia in infants; indole-3-carbinol and photodynamic therapy have modest roles, antireflux therapy is recommended (reflux in about 90%, and treating it reduces webs), and radiation is contraindicated. Delayed laser complications such as webs occur in 13-35%, mostly at the anterior and posterior commissure, so residual disease is accepted there; the 585-nm pulsed dye and 532-nm KTP lasers can be used awake in the office. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1640) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1641) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1642)

**Pediatric laryngotracheobronchial malignancy**: Over two-thirds of pediatric laryngeal malignancies are mesenchymal; embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is most common (mean age about 9, treated with chemoradiation, with surgery for biopsy/debulking) followed by squamous cell carcinoma (about 12, well differentiated and without usual risk factors); boys outnumber girls about 3:1 and the supraglottis is the most common site. Primary tracheal tumors are rare in children (about 64% benign) and cause symptoms only after about 50% obstruction, so they are often mistaken for asthma. Bronchial tumors in children are mostly malignant: carcinoid is the most common (endobronchial removal recurs in 60-75%, so open resection with nodes; about 90% survival) and inflammatory pseudotumor is the most common benign one. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1647) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1648) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1649)

**Granular cell tumor and laryngeal neurogenic tumors**: Granular cell tumor is a Schwann-cell-derived lesion most common on the tongue; the larynx is involved in about 7-10%.
