In adults about half show pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, so a superficial biopsy can be misread as squamous cell carcinoma; it is multicentric in 10-15%, recurs in 2-8% after endoscopic excision, and is malignant in 1-3%. Pediatric granular cell tumors favor the glottis and subglottis, and laryngeal neurofibromas (often with NF1) arise on the arytenoid or aryepiglottic fold, with plexiform lesions infiltrating and recurring, so subtotal debulking is acceptable. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1646)

**Silent aspiration biology and test performance**: Cough is absent in about 75% of premature infants and 50% of newborns; infants respond to aspiration with the laryngeal chemoreflex (apnea, bradycardia, glottic closure and swallowing) rather than coughing. Videofluoroscopy is the test of choice; FEES adds saliva assessment and air-pulse sensory testing of the laryngeal adductor reflex. A lipid-laden macrophage index over 100 is more than 90% sensitive but nonspecific; dye tests detect only gross aspiration; gastroesophageal scintigraphy is low-yield (positive in 6% vs 39% by videofluoroscopy in cerebral palsy), and a radionuclide salivagram detects saliva aspiration; chronic aspiration injures the superior segments of the lower lobes and the posterior upper lobes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1487) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1488) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1489) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway and Laryngotracheal Manifestations of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease", p 1500)

**Escalation ladder**: Gastrostomy is indicated for an unsafe swallow, poor nutrition, oral feeding taking more than about 3 hours a day, or nasogastric dependence, but it can worsen reflux; Nissen fundoplication controls reflux in about 90% overall but fails in about 27% of neurologically impaired children and does nothing for saliva aspiration. Cricopharyngeal achalasia can be treated with botulinum toxin, balloon dilation or myotomy. For intractable life-threatening aspiration, laryngotracheal separation (proximal trachea closed) or diversion (proximal trachea joined to the esophagus) is definitive and has been reversed when laryngeal function returned; a cuffed tracheotomy is only a temporizing step. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1489) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1490) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Aspiration: Etiology and Management", p 1491)

**Older empiric-PPI algorithm versus current practice**: Bluestone 5e suggests empiric acid suppression for suspected pediatric extraesophageal reflux: a PPI at about 1.5 mg/kg/day given once 30 minutes before breakfast, plus bedtime ranitidine, escalating to twice-daily PPI after 6-12 weeks or for 'end-stage' disease such as laryngotracheal stenosis. Current NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN guidance discourages empiric PPIs for extraesophageal symptoms (cough, wheeze, stridor) in infants without proven GERD, and ranitidine was withdrawn from the US market in 2020, so the site's targeted approach reflects current practice. Pepsin in BAL fluid correlates with proximal reflux and may be more specific than lipid-laden macrophages. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway and Laryngotracheal Manifestations of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease", p 1500) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway and Laryngotracheal Manifestations of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease", p 1504)

**Pediatric larynx dimensions and descent**: In the newborn the lower cricoid lies at about C4 and the epiglottic tip at C1, and the epiglottis meets the soft palate, which favors nasal breathing during suckling. The larynx descends to C5 by age 2, C6 by age 5 and its adult C6-7 level by about 15. The newborn glottis is about 7 mm (AP) by 4 mm and the subglottis 4-5 mm, the vocal process makes up 60-75% of the fold at birth (membranous fold dominant by age 3), the folds stay halfway between the thyroid notch and lower thyroid border, the trachea grows from about 4 to 12 cm, and the newborn trachea is 3 times as compliant as a 1-year-old's and 6 times an adult's. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Developmental Anatomy and Physiology of the Larynx, Trachea, Esophagus, and Lungs", p 1402) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Developmental Anatomy and Physiology of the Larynx, Trachea, Esophagus, and Lungs", p 1403)

**Pediatric posterior glottic stenosis**: In children, posterior glottic stenosis usually follows prolonged intubation (risk rises with tube size, agitation, inflammation and oral tubes) and often coexists with subglottic stenosis and cricoarytenoid fixation; it can mimic bilateral vocal fold paralysis. Diagnosis needs rigid endoscopy with an attempt to splay the vocal folds, because flexible examination is unreliable. Treatment is usually posterior cricoid split with a cartilage graft (open, or endoscopic in selected isolated cases); restenosis is at least 15%, but isolated interarytenoid bands (Bogdasarian-Olson type I) do well with endoscopic division. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1602) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1603) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Airway Stenosis: Minimally Invasive Approaches", p 1588)

**Lateral neck film criteria**: On a lateral soft-tissue neck film in an infant or young child, retropharyngeal swelling means prevertebral soft tissue wider than the adjacent vertebral body at C1-C4, with loss of the shelf marking the top of the cervical esophagus. The film must be taken in extension during inspiration because flexion or expiration creates false thickening; gas without trauma strongly suggests abscess. On CT, a retropharyngeal process pushes parapharyngeal fat anterolaterally and a parapharyngeal process pushes it posteromedially, and sterile 'danger space' edema is common, so not every low-density area is drainable pus. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Radiologic Evaluation of the Pediatric Airway", p 1427) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Radiologic Evaluation of the Pediatric Airway", p 1428)

**Pediatric scope sizing and normal findings**: Approximate Storz bronchoscope sizes: premature 2.5; newborn-3 months 3.0; 3-18 months 3.5; 1-3 years 3.7; 3-5 years 4.0; 5-10 years 5.0; over 10 years 6.0. Use the largest scope that passes without resistance, and remember that an inserted telescope narrows the ventilating lumen. Anterior pulsatile flattening from the innominate artery is normal unless it obstructs more than 70% of the lumen, the normal cartilage-to-trachealis ratio is about 4:1, and a right upper lobe bronchus arising above the carina ('pig' or tracheal bronchus) is often linked to other tracheal and cardiovascular anomalies.
